# Finding liquid leaders before a potential expansion

Source: [Raghee Horner](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/19vezVGc8Z/). Downloaded duration: 54.101 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The clip describes a watchlist funnel: identify strong sectors, find stronger individual stocks within them, require tradability, and wait for a pause near an important high before planning a trade. Its purpose is candidate selection and preparation. It does not supply a mechanical prediction that a particular stock will accelerate.

## How to do it

1. Choose a market universe and a consistent comparison period. Rank sectors, then compare candidate stocks with their own sector. The video provides the hierarchy but no ranking formula or lookback.
2. Remove names whose activity or price movement is unsuitable for the intended trade size. Define minimum turnover, spread, and volatility explicitly; the speaker gives no numerical thresholds.
3. Inspect higher-high structure and proximity to meaningful reference prices, including monthly or annual highs. Record those levels before a later breakout can influence their selection.
4. Wait for contraction or a pullback rather than treating the first new high as an obligation to buy. The illustration contrasts extension, retracement, and a tighter pause.
5. Specify an entry condition, a price that invalidates the idea, a target, and a position size before entering. A watchlist inclusion is not itself an order.

## Making the workflow reproducible

Additional research choices are needed. For example, sector strength could mean trailing return against a benchmark, and stock strength could mean return against its sector over the same dates. Contraction could be defined using a falling recent range or an ATR percentile. These are possible operational definitions, not parameters established in the clip. Freeze the definitions before evaluating later data.

An illustrative risk calculation is quantity = planned monetary risk / (entry minus stop), rounded down to permitted units and adjusted for costs. If entry is 50 and invalidation is 48, a 100-unit risk budget permits at most 50 shares before costs. A gap can still lose more than that plan.

## What remains open and how to evaluate it

The lesson leaves the timeframe, universe, sector map, strength window, liquidity limits, contraction threshold, exact trigger, target method, and exit timing unspecified. A complete implementation needs those choices. Compare the same base entry with and without sector selection, stock-relative-strength selection, and contraction; otherwise it is difficult to know which feature helped. Use the membership and sector information available at the historical date, include unsuccessful candidates, and measure net results on later periods. The attractive charts in the clip are examples, not a full sample of outcomes.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 0–19s introduces the sector-to-stock and liquidity funnel; 19–33s discusses structure and important highs; 33–41s discusses contraction and pullbacks; 41–49s calls for a complete risk plan.

Reviewed using: manual synthesis of complete machine transcript, page metadata, and timestamped sampled frames.

[Downloaded video](video.mp4) · [Page description](video.description) · [Timestamped machine transcript](transcript.txt) · [Sampled frames](frames/contact-sheet.jpg) · [Metadata](video.info.json) · [Integrity record](source.json)

Machine transcripts may misrecognize names, numbers, and music. Settings and claims that could not be established are identified above. Any implementation examples added in this writeup are research choices, not extra rules attributed to the video.

Load the longest frozen strength, contraction and liquidity windows, plus the preceding year if annual highs are used; obtain sector/benchmark warm-up over the same sessions.

Use [docs/daily-bars-api.md](../../docs/daily-bars-api.md) and [data/history.py](../../data/history.py): snapshot `list_history_symbols(market=...)`, then `load_daily_bars(symbol, market=...)`. PH keys use `.PS` through `core.market.ph_history_symbol`. Use `core.market.get_market` for separate USD/PHP reporting, New York/Manila session calendars and PH long-only eligibility. Fetch enough pre-start history (or all history), then filter locally; newest-N can omit an old interval entirely and bulk’s 2,000-bar cap is not historical pagination. Pre-start bars only warm features/state. Sort/validate completed, finite OHLCV and conflicting/duplicate sessions; preserve missing sessions and zero/missing-volume status. `None` from `load_daily_bars` means failure; `[]` means no bars. Preserve this distinction before candle/frame conversion and report insufficient warm-up separately. Symbol enumeration currently collapses remote errors to `[]`: propose an explicit failure status before treating an empty universe as success. Bulk helpers can return partial maps after chunk failure; reconcile every requested symbol, retry missing keys and bound concurrency/cancellation. ## Results and validation

Freeze interpretation, parameters and execution before testing. Expose only completed decision bars and prior data to the adapter; close-generated signals fill no earlier than the next tradable open. Limit/stop orders become eligible only after their conditions are known. Preserve pivot confirmation, external publication and higher-frame availability times. Test prefix invariance by changing/removing future bars and requiring unchanged earlier features, signals and orders. Use raw market prices for fills, keeping synthetic Heikin-Ashi/regression prices as features.

For fully specified trades, report candidate/accepted/rejected/expired/unfilled counts, trade and signal/fill timestamps, rule/level evidence, fees/slippage, net expectancy/R where defined, win rate, profit factor, realized/unrealized P&L, marked-to-market equity, exposure, turnover and drawdown by market. Compare a frozen baseline with identical dates/universe/costs; label independent-notional versus finite-capital accounting. Without entry/exit rules, report event coverage and predeclared forward-return/MAE/MFE horizons or forecast calibration, leaving trading P&L unavailable. Outcome windows never enter features and are censored at end_date with incomplete horizons reported.

Use fixtures alongside [core/test_stream_backtest.py](../../core/test_stream_backtest.py), [core/test_rule_backtest.py](../../core/test_rule_backtest.py), [core/test_backtest_service.py](../../core/test_backtest_service.py) and [web/test_paper_api.py](../../web/test_paper_api.py): source positives/near-misses, date boundaries, warm-up without orders, missing/invalid data, owner/remote parity, `.PS` and market isolation, enumeration/auth/partial-bulk failures, progress/cancel/retry and valid no-signal runs. Freeze end-date treatment (mark open positions or labeled liquidation), with last-bar orders unfilled if no later eligible bar exists. Use untouched later holdouts and retain all trials, failures and costs.

## Gaps and assumptions

### Writeup: What remains open and how to evaluate it

The lesson leaves the timeframe, universe, sector map, strength window, liquidity limits, contraction threshold, exact trigger, target method, and exit timing unspecified. A complete implementation needs those choices. Compare the same base entry with and without sector selection, stock-relative-strength selection, and contraction; otherwise it is difficult to know which feature helped. Use the membership and sector information available at the historical date, include unsuccessful candidates, and measure net results on later periods. The attractive charts in the clip are examples, not a full sample of outcomes.

**Practical next step:** Write and approve a small explicit research specification resolving the source gaps above, then validate numeric/event fixtures and a short causal replay before a full historical run. Missing rules should block the faithful trading mode; a labeled feature/event study may be the practical first milestone.

**Proposed assumptions, not source facts:** the experiment catalog/API paths, adapters, daily-stock adaptation, warm-up/seed conventions where unspecified, next-open execution convention, costs/slippage, sizing, finite-account policy, same-bar ordering and end-date handling are design proposals. Keep source-established values and unresolved alternatives in separate manifest fields. Claims of institutional activity, guaranteed moves, AI confidence or advertised profitability require independent evidence; OHLCV labels alone cannot establish them.

An anchored volume-weighted average price measures the average traded price, weighted by volume, starting at a deliberately chosen event. The lesson uses it to interpret positioning after a catalyst. Price above the average suggests that a representative buyer since the anchor has a favorable mark; price below suggests the opposite. This is an approximation to aggregate positioning, not a record of every participant's entry or proof that particular traders still hold inventory.

She also wants participation to support the interpretation and discusses resetting the anchor after an event that substantially changes positioning.

# Anchored VWAP as a positioning filter

Source: [Raghee Horner](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1D5Q6NNV5v/). Review used the downloaded video, its page description, machine transcription, and timestamped frames. This is an explanation of the lesson, with implementation suggestions identified separately.

## What it does

An anchored volume-weighted average price measures the average traded price, weighted by volume, starting at a deliberately chosen event. The lesson uses it to interpret positioning after a catalyst. Price above the average suggests that a representative buyer since the anchor has a favorable mark; price below suggests the opposite. This is an approximation to aggregate positioning, not a record of every participant's entry or proof that particular traders still hold inventory.

The presenter emphasizes choosing a trading direction with this information. Merely crossing the line is not presented as a complete entry system. Her event examples include company results, important announcements, central-bank decisions, and a pronounced selling climax. She also wants participation to support the interpretation and discusses resetting the anchor after an event that substantially changes positioning.

## How to reproduce the analysis

1. Open a chart with reliable price and traded-volume data. Identify an event that was already observable when the analysis would have been made.
2. Place the anchored VWAP drawing or indicator at that event's bar. Record the exact timestamp, timeframe, session selection, and price source so another person can reproduce it.
3. Observe how subsequent bars behave relative to the average. Record sustained holding above it, holding below it, and repeated crossings separately.
4. Compare participation around the event with the instrument's usual activity. The video asks for stronger participation but supplies no numerical relative-volume threshold.
5. Use the positioning interpretation to filter a separately defined setup. Choose that setup's entry confirmation, invalidation, and exit before trading; the clip does not specify them.
6. Re-anchor only after a new qualifying event. Keep the earlier anchor in the research record so a later favorable chart cannot silently replace the original decision.

## Calculation and interpretation

An explicit implementation can calculate `AVWAP[t] = sum(price[i] * volume[i], i=anchor..t) / sum(volume[i], i=anchor..t)`. For bar data, typical price `(high + low + close) / 3` is one possible convention; the presenter does not specify a source, so this choice must be labeled as an implementation assumption. Trade-level and bar-level calculations can differ. The average is undefined before any qualifying volume exists.

Illustrative arithmetic: 100 units at 20 and 300 at 22 produce an average of 21.50. A later mark of 22 is above that average, but this alone does not establish whether buying at 22 offers an attractive outcome.

## What the video leaves open

There is no fixed timeframe, objective event classifier, participation cutoff, stop distance, target, or holding period. The chart illustrations do not establish a measured success rate. A flat average crossed repeatedly can be a poor directional filter. Thin trading and missing volume can distort it; foreign-exchange tick counts and centralized exchange volume are different inputs.

## Research and bot implementation notes

These are additional implementation suggestions. Save anchor selection at the time it becomes known, calculate from bars available then, and test the underlying setup with and without the filter on later data. Compare fixed anchor policies rather than selecting the best-looking anchor after the move. Include turnover, fees, slippage, and rejected setups. A filter can reduce trading frequency while also excluding profitable trades.

Evidence map: approximately 0–7s introduces the tool; 7–23s discusses positioning, event selection, and participation; 25–38s explains the directional filter; 38–45s discusses changing the anchor. Local evidence: [video](video.mp4), [transcript](transcript.txt), [sampled frames](frames/contact-sheet.jpg), [metadata](video.info.json), [integrity record](source.json).

# Opening range: trend breakouts and failed-breakout reversals

Source: [Raghee Horner](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1E3MHdzEoy/). Reviewed the narration through its machine transcript, page metadata, and timestamped frame samples. The lesson includes two different market regimes; its reversal example should not be implemented as an unconditional breakout trade.

## What it does

The opening range establishes three intraday reference prices: its high, low, and midpoint. The speaker combines those prices with the previous regular-session close and the current trend environment. Above the previous close she favors bullish opportunities; below it she favors bearish opportunities. A directional breakout is considered differently from a failed excursion in a sideways market.

The illustrated schedule is the US cash opening half-hour: 09:30 through 10:00 Eastern. She explicitly checks a five-minute chart for market condition. The previous close is the prior cash session's 16:00 reference. These are the video's example conventions, not a universal schedule for every instrument.

## How to do it

1. Before the session, draw the prior regular-session close.
2. Collect the high and low of the opening half-hour. At 10:00, freeze `range_high`, `range_low`, and `midpoint = (high + low) / 2`.
3. Compare current price with the prior close to establish the permitted directional bias.
4. Inspect the five-minute structure. Sustained directional movement and overlapping range behavior should be classified separately. The speaker does not provide a numerical trend/chop formula.
5. In a trend, watch a break of the opening boundary in the allowed direction and evaluate a pullback to support or resistance. A touch or excursion alone does not establish follow-through.
6. In chop, watch for a sweep that returns into the range. A low-side failure with price still above the prior close fits the bullish bias. A high-side failure below the prior close fits the bearish bias.
7. For the illustrated return-to-range idea, the range edge is the entry area, the midpoint is an initial objective, and the far boundary is a possible subsequent objective. These inward targets belong to a reversal into the range. They are not outward breakout targets.

# Choosing tools for trend, participation, volatility, and sector context

Source: [Raghee Horner](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1FUnggm7Ez/). Reviewed the machine transcription and timestamped video frames. This clip ranks tools according to the presenter's preferences. It does not demonstrate a complete entry-and-exit strategy or establish that the rejected tools are universally ineffective.

## What it does

The presenter favors tools that describe market context. She chooses moving averages for trend, volume-at-price profiles for participation by price, volatility ranges for movement context, and sector analysis for understanding an index's drivers. She is less interested in MACD crossover signals, isolated volume spikes as directional evidence, and a put/call measure that she considers mismatched to the index being analyzed.

The most concrete configuration is a trio of 34-period exponential averages: one calculated from bar highs, one from closes, and one from lows. The remainder of the tools are discussed conceptually without reproducible numerical settings.

## How to build a research chart from the lesson

1. Add three EMAs with length 34 and sources high, close, and low. Keep the timeframe constant when comparing their shape. This creates a channel around the price series.
2. Observe channel slope and price location as trend context. The video does not give an angle threshold, crossover entry, stop, or exit rule, so do not silently introduce one as the speaker's method.
3. Add a volume profile for an explicitly chosen period. Note where trading was concentrated and where participation was sparse. A profile bins volume by price; a conventional volume histogram bins it by time. They answer different questions.
4. Add a measure of typical movement only after defining its calculation and window. The speaker endorses volatility ranges but does not specify ATR length, standard-deviation bands, or a particular proprietary formula.
5. Compare the instrument's sector or industry with the broader index. Identify which components matter to the chosen benchmark and whether leadership is concentrated or broad.
6. Use that context to evaluate a separately written trade plan. Nothing in the clip defines a standalone executable signal.

## Why the distinctions matter

A volume spike shows unusual activity but does not by itself say whether future returns will be positive or negative. A volume profile adds location, but neither type of display proves who is buying or selling. Likewise, EMA smoothing removes detail and introduces lag; the clip's preference for those averages is not evidence that lag disappears.

For the put/call discussion, the presenter argues that a broad aggregate may not describe the most influential stocks in a concentrated benchmark. The practical question is whether the options measure covers the same instruments, period, and weighting as the hypothesis. The clip does not calculate a corrected ratio or provide a dataset. Its approximate statement about a small group dominating the S&P should be understood as commentary, not a verified current component-weight table.

## Implementation details left unspecified

The timeframe, EMA initialization, profile anchor and bin size, volatility formula, sector-ranking horizon, trade trigger, position sizing, stop, and target are all open. An EMA implementation can use `EMA[t] = alpha * source[t] + (1-alpha) * EMA[t-1]` with `alpha = 2/35`; declare the initialization and warmup. Profile calculations require sufficiently detailed volume information, and a daily OHLCV bar alone does not reveal the exact volume traded at each price.

## How to evaluate it

As an additional research step, test each contextual feature separately against the same frozen base strategy. Compare later-period net results and trade counts before stacking features. Correlated indicators can duplicate the same trend information. A persuasive tool comparison needs measured outcomes rather than a count of attractive chart examples.

Evidence map: approximately 0–11s covers the EMA channel; 11–17s MACD; 17–28s volume profiles; 28–34s spikes; 34–44s volatility; 44–68s options sentiment; 68–89s sectors. Local evidence: [video](video.mp4), [transcript](transcript.txt), [frames](frames/contact-sheet.jpg), [metadata](video.info.json), [integrity](source.json).

# Turtle Soup: a failed excursion outside a trading range

Source: [Raghee Horner](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1CQDw4tZP9/). This short clip points viewers to its page caption. The procedural details below come from the downloaded `video.description`, supported by the visible title in sampled frames. Its machine transcript contains no useful instructional narration and should not be treated as the strategy source.

## What it does

The post describes a range that first attracts orders at its boundaries, then experiences an unsuccessful breakout, followed by a move back toward the opposite boundary. The tradable observation is the failed excursion and recovery into the range. The caption attributes the behavior to institutional stop triggering, but a chart alone cannot establish the intent of market participants.

Its use of the Turtle Soup name refers here to this particular range-reentry description. The post does not give a historical lookback such as a fixed number of daily bars, so a reader should not silently substitute a different strategy that shares the name.

## How to reproduce the described setup

1. Find a pre-existing tight range and mark its high and low before the breakout. Decide in advance how much history and how much width qualify as a range; neither is specified.
2. Wait for price to move outside one boundary. This is an observation phase, not yet the reversal entry.
3. Require price to return inside the original range by a confirmation buffer. The caption illustrates roughly 10–20 Dow index points or 3–5 S&P index points. These are price units in those examples, not universal ticks, percentages, or settings for every asset.
4. Look for an additional small-scale structure cue or inside bar. The post suggests these as extra confirmation but does not define an exact trigger or order type.
5. For an upside failure, evaluate a short after recovery below the range high. For a downside failure, evaluate a long after recovery above the range low.
6. Put invalidation beyond the excursion's extreme, with a declared execution allowance. The original range boundary and the actual sweep extreme are different prices.
7. Use the opposite range edge as the stated objective. Calculate the available reward relative to the stop distance before assuming that the advertised 3-to-1 relationship is possible.

## Worked interpretation

Illustrative numbers, not numbers from the video: a range spans 100–110, price briefly reaches 112, and a short is evaluated at 109 after recovery. A stop at 113 risks 4 units and a target at 100 offers 9, or 2.25R before costs. Calling that setup 3R would be incorrect. A different entry or invalidation changes the ratio, and the far boundary may never be reached.

## Missing rules and failure cases

The caption does not define timeframe, maximum time outside the range, candle-close requirements, a formal inside-bar trigger, buffer scaling, session, news exclusions, or a time exit. A genuine directional breakout can keep extending and repeatedly punish attempted fades. Conversely, demanding a large reentry buffer can leave little room to the opposite side. A level selected after the reversal creates a misleadingly clean example.

## How to test or implement it

Additional implementation suggestions: freeze range boundaries when the setup becomes eligible, create explicit states for outside-range excursion and recovery, and invalidate stale setups. Record the extreme as it develops instead of using a later high or low. Test index-point buffers only on their intended instrument; specify a separate volatility- or tick-based adaptation for other markets. Model spread, gaps, commissions, and the possibility that entry and stop both fall inside one OHLC bar. The post's profitability and reward/risk assertions are promotional claims, not independently verified results.

# A seven-stage preparation routine before intraday trading

Source: [Raghee Horner](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1GwQqepy1d/). Reviewed the machine transcription and the progressively displayed checklist in timestamped frames. This is a preparation process, not an indicator formula or a complete trading system.

## What it does

The routine organizes information before the trader commits to a session. It starts with a lesson from the previous session, establishes overnight context and reference levels, checks scheduled catalysts, and ends with a written conditional plan and a short screen break. The aim is to make decisions more deliberate. The speaker's personal profitability history is a claim in the video, not a measured result established by this review.

## How to do it, in the video's order

1. **Review the previous session.** Read the trade journal and write one specific lesson before looking at the new session. Distinguish a process error from an ordinary losing outcome. A useful lesson describes an action that can be checked later.
2. **Review overnight movement.** Note whether Asian, European, or US trading generated a meaningful move. Record the affected instrument and the period being compared. The lesson does not give a numerical definition of meaningful.
3. **Draw reference prices.** Mark the prior session's high and low and the current premarket high and low. The speaker explicitly treats these as context rather than automatic entry signals. Keep the data windows visible so regular-session and extended-session extremes do not get confused.
4. **Check scheduled events.** Note relevant economic releases, policy appearances, and company results. The presenter mentions Forex Factory as one calendar example. The useful output is a timestamped event list in the chart's timezone, not a prediction of the result.
5. **Write a conditional plan.** State the market condition, permitted direction, preferred entry zone, required trigger, and price that would invalidate the idea. A bullish opinion without a condition for changing it is incomplete.
6. **Write circumstances for abstaining.** The examples include ambiguous price action and major-news volatility. Turn those concepts into rules that can be followed in real time, rather than deciding after a loss that the situation was unclear.
7. **Take a brief reset.** The presenter suggests about five minutes away from screens. Return to wait for the defined setup instead of treating the opening bell as an obligation to trade.

## A reusable worksheet

| Field | What to record before the session |
|---|---|
| Prior-session lesson | One observable behavior to repeat or change |
| Overnight context | Instrument, session, direction, notable move |
| Reference levels | Prior high/low; premarket high/low; window definitions |
| Scheduled events | Time, timezone, instrument relevance, planned restriction |
| Market state and bias | Conditional assessment and what changes it |
| Trade plan | Zone, confirmation, invalidation, exit plan |
| Abstention rule | A condition that prevents a new trade |
| Reset and readiness | Completion time and readiness to follow the plan |

## What is added and what remains unspecified

The worksheet format and the instruction to make conditions objectively checkable are implementation suggestions. The clip does not define a quantitative trend classifier, a standard premarket window, an event blackout duration, a position size, or profit objectives. It also does not establish that a routine alone creates positive expectancy. Those decisions belong to the independently tested setup used after preparation.

For a bot, store a dated plan containing only information available before eligibility begins. Session windows, holidays, and event timestamps must be explicit. A later edit should create a revision rather than overwrite what was actually known. Evaluate adherence and strategy outcomes separately: following the routine and making money on a particular day are different measurements.

Evidence map: about 0–19s introduces preparation and review; 19–31s covers overnight context and levels; 31–46s covers the calendar; 46–65s covers conditional planning and abstention; 65–71s covers the reset. # Bearish change of character followed by a retest

Source: [Time To Trade](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/19zUgo18Vf/). Reviewed the narration via machine transcription and the timestamped illustrated sequence. The displayed chart is labeled as a 15-minute example. The source's live-chart branding does not establish that the animation is an independently verifiable live trade.

## What it does

The lesson contrasts continuation within an uptrend with the first structural warning of reversal. A sequence of higher highs and higher lows describes the initial trend. Breaking a prior high is called a break of structure in the direction of that trend. Breaking beneath the latest relevant higher low after upward progress stalls is labeled a change of character.

The proposed entry waits for a recovery toward the broken support and rejection from below. That is a support-to-resistance retest idea. It reduces the need to sell immediately after a sharp decline but can miss a move that never retests. A structural warning is not certainty that a lasting downtrend will follow.

## How to do it

1. Identify the upward swing sequence and mark the latest higher low that supports the trend interpretation.
2. Track whether the next rally achieves a fresh high. In the demonstration it fails, forming a lower high.
3. Wait for price to close below the relevant higher low. The narration says break; the saved caption explicitly specifies a closing break and describes a close at 1.0896 below 1.0905. This changes the structural assessment; the presenter distinguishes it from a continuation break above a high.
4. Keep the broken level on the chart. Wait for price to pull back toward it from underneath.
5. Evaluate a short only when price rejects that area. The video does not specify a precise candle pattern, close requirement, zone width, or pending-order price.
6. Place the stated invalidation above the lower high. The lower high is a structural point; it should not be confused with an arbitrary fixed distance from entry.
7. Define an exit objective before testing or trading. The clip shows subsequent downward movement but supplies no reproducible target, partial-exit rule, trail, or time stop.

## Important implementation choices

A detector needs a formal swing definition. A pivot that requires several later bars is not known on the pivot's own timestamp. If a two-sided swing algorithm is selected, its confirmation delay must be respected. Use the caption’s completed-close convention for the CHoCH break; a wick-only version would be a separate research variant. The retest rejection still has no exact closing-bar or candle-pattern rule.

Define the rejection event and maximum wait for a retest in advance. A research version might require a bar to touch the resistance area and close below it, then become eligible on a later executable price. That is an additional rule, not a detail supplied by the speaker. A rally that reclaims resistance or exceeds the intended lower high can invalidate the bearish scenario.

## Worked example and validation

Illustrative prices: swings rise from 100 to 106, pull back to 103, and then stall at 105. A move below 103 is the structural warning. Recovery to the 103 area followed by rejection is the proposed entry sequence, with invalidation beyond 105. These are teaching numbers, not prices transcribed from the chart. Net reward depends on an independently selected exit and costs.

For research, preserve the swing level known at each bar, count every eligible break and failed retest, and compare the retest entry with immediate-break entries on later data. Include spread and slippage. A strategy that sells can be implemented only where the instrument and account permit that position; a bearish signal can instead serve as a long-entry exclusion in a long-only study.

Evidence map: approximately 0–18s establishes trend and continuation; 18–31s shows the structural change; 31–42s shows the retest, rejection, and stop; the closing animation shows a favorable continuation without statistical validation. Local evidence: [video](video.mp4), [transcript](transcript.txt), [frames](frames/contact-sheet.jpg), [metadata](video.info.json), [integrity](source.json).

# Distinguishing a failed breakout from acceptance beyond a level

Source: [Bull Trading FX](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/19mqpLV3S7/). Downloaded duration: 14.773 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The animation compares two paths after an obvious boundary is crossed. One quickly rejects and returns into the former range; the other holds beyond the boundary, consolidates or retests, and continues. The longer caption adds structure-shift confirmation for reversal ideas and displacement with a pullback for continuation ideas. Its assertions about institutional intentions are explanatory claims; candle shapes cannot prove the identity or intent of counterparties.

## How to do it

1. Mark a prior high, low, or range boundary using information already available.
2. Observe the first excursion without immediately deciding it is a lasting break.
3. For a failure candidate, require recovery inside the original area and examine whether local structure turns against the excursion. A wick through the boundary followed by a close inside is the caption's central visual cue.
4. For a continuation candidate, look for a strong close outside and subsequent holding or retesting on that side. The caption suggests a pullback toward an imbalance or the origin of the displacement.
5. Compare the event with higher-timeframe context. The caption mentions four-hour and daily charts but supplies no exact context classifier.
6. Define the entry, invalidation, and exit for the chosen branch before placing an order. The video does not provide numerical execution rules.

## Operational definitions still needed

Choose whether acceptance means one close, several closes, a minimum distance, or a minimum elapsed time; those alternatives are not interchangeable. Define displacement relative to prior ranges rather than using future price movement to decide which candle looked strong. If implementing a three-bar bullish fair-value gap, one possible convention compares the first bar's high with the third bar's low, but the caption does not specify a formula, minimum size, or fill requirement. Record any chosen convention as an added research assumption.

## Failure cases and validation

A candle can close outside and still reverse later. A wick can reject and then be exceeded. The labels summarize observed behavior over a chosen horizon; they do not identify a guaranteed outcome at the first touch. In replay, retain the original boundary, log every first break, and record what was known when each decision became eligible. Compare rejection and continuation branches separately with fixed expiry, costs, and execution assumptions. A stop beyond an excursion and a target at a prior swing are possible research rules, not instructions fully specified in this clip.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The 0–4s slides introduce the false-break scenario; around 6–9s the paths are compared; about 10–14s the failure and holding sequences are displayed separately. The page description contains the more detailed procedural discussion.

Reviewed using: manual synthesis of the saved page description and all eight timestamped frame samples; no useful narration was detected.

# Fair-value-gap selection and three distinct entry strategies

Source: [Cy forex 5](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1LwHpPwfy9/). Downloaded duration: 684.145 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This eleven-minute tutorial defines a three-bar gap, proposes five quality filters, and then describes inversion, Fibonacci-confluence, and higher/lower-timeframe confirmation variants. These are distinct strategy branches with different triggers; they should not be merged into one rule that claims whichever entry looked best afterward. The repeated profitability and high-win-rate assertions are unsupported by a complete dataset or trade ledger.

## Gap geometry and five selection filters

For a bullish example, compare the first bar's high with the third bar's low and box the interval when the former is lower. The bearish mirror compares the first bar's low with the third bar's high. A large middle candle alone is insufficient. This geometry does not prove that no trades occurred through the middle candle's range.

The proposed filters are: use a gap before its first retest; reject the original bullish interpretation after a close through its lower boundary, with the bearish mirror separately defined; prefer relatively larger gaps when several exist; prefer bullish candidates in the lower half of the selected advance and bearish candidates in the upper half of a decline; avoid a nearby opposing major reference; and favor a gap associated with a break of structure. The video calls this five filters because freshness and invalidation are discussed together.

To divide the selected move, the source visibly uses TradingView’s Gann Box drawing with price levels 0, 0.5, and 1 (the settings dialog is readable around 234s). The practical feature is the midpoint; the speech recognition renders the tool name inconsistently. The source gives no minimum gap size, near-level distance, or formal swing algorithm.

## Baseline midpoint entry

After choosing a gap, calculate its midpoint and wait for a return there. The source places invalidation at a break of the gap. This is a location-based entry description; exact order type, buffer, and candle-close convention remain open. If a resting limit is selected, it must already exist before the touch. If a closing-bar confirmation is required, it cannot also be assumed filled retrospectively at an earlier touch.

## Strategy 1: inversion after the original gap fails

1. Identify a gap whose original directional support/resistance interpretation has been broken.
2. Wait for a return toward that same area from the opposite side.
3. For the shown failed bullish gap, evaluate a short as the area is retested as resistance.
4. Put invalidation above the gap and use an objective twice the entry-to-stop distance.
5. The speaker treats the inversion as a one-use opportunity and discards repeatedly traversed versions. The exact definition of broken, retest confirmation, and maximum waiting time needs an independent rule.

## Strategy 2: gap near a 61.8% retracement

1. Mark candidate gaps in a chosen advance.
2. Apply a Fibonacci retracement to that same swing and select the gap closest to the 61.8% level. The anchor direction and displayed percentage convention must be preserved; different chart tools can reverse the labels.
3. Wait for price to return to the selected gap. The bullish example requires the confirming candle to close within or above it.
4. Enter the long only under a declared executable timing convention, put invalidation beneath the gap, and set the stated objective at 2R.
5. Closest is not necessarily overlapping; the source supplies no distance tolerance or tie-break rule.

## Strategy 3: higher-timeframe trend and lower-timeframe momentum

1. On the example four-hour chart, use a 200-period EMA to choose directional eligibility: above it favors bullish gaps and below it bearish gaps.
2. Select a fresh gap in the permitted direction and wait for a return.
3. Move to the example one-hour chart for MACD confirmation. The bearish example waits for a downward cross. The source does not fully specify MACD inputs or whether cross means the signal line or another plotted reference.
4. Use the gap's invalidation area for the stop and an objective of twice the risk.
5. The supplemental table shows these higher/lower pairs: weekly/daily, daily/four-hour, four-hour/one-hour, and one-hour/fifteen-minute. They are source examples, not proof that these combinations are optimal.

## A reproducible research specification

Additional choices must settle indicator sources and warmup, pivot confirmation, gap size, freshness, partial touches, invalidation, nearby-level distance, entry timing, stop buffers, position size, session, and expiry. Keep separate states for fresh original gaps, failed gaps, and eligible inversion retests. Store when every higher-timeframe bar actually completed; do not use its final EMA, MACD, or structure inside earlier lower-timeframe bars. A selected swing high used for discount/premium must already be knowable when the decision is made.

## Failure modes and evaluation

A fresh or large gap can fail, price can leave without reaching its midpoint, and a momentum confirmation can arrive after favorable reward/risk has disappeared. A 2R target defines an intended payoff, not the probability of achieving it. Test each branch separately, compare each added filter against the same base rule, include losses and unfilled orders, and use later data with spread/slippage. The tutorial gives detailed hypotheses but no independently demonstrated universal success rate.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximate chapters: 45–109s geometry; 123–360s quality filters; 369–401s midpoint entry; 410–490s inversion; 492–572s Fibonacci; 574–672s multi-timeframe setup. The timeframe table is directly readable in [supplement-674s.jpg](frames/supplement-674s.jpg).

Reviewed using: manual reading of the complete machine transcript, saved caption, recognized frame text, and direct inspection of an additional frame at 674s containing the timeframe table.

[Downloaded video](video.mp4) · [Page description](video.description) · [Timestamped machine transcript](transcript.txt) · [Sampled frames](frames/contact-sheet.jpg) · [Metadata](video.info.json) · [Integrity record](source.json)

Machine transcripts may misrecognize names, numbers, and music. Settings and claims that could not be established are identified above. Any implementation examples added in this writeup are research choices, not extra rules attributed to the video.

# A claimed 05:30 UK gold activity window: useful research hypothesis, incomplete trading rules

Source: [FXDSniper](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1CUaEmaFHc/). Downloaded duration: 68.939 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This is a promotional presentation of a time-of-day hypothesis. The author claims that gold became active near 05:30 UK time during five selected mornings. He favors observing the direction of emerging activity rather than predicting direction before the window. Neither the indicator's calculation nor a complete executable setup is disclosed. The animation describes market movement, not a verified trade ledger.

## How to study the observable idea

1. Identify the exact gold product, price feed, bar interval, and quotation convention. A pip in one gold feed need not equal another feed's tick.
2. Convert the stated UK clock time using an actual UK timezone. Do not assume the same UTC offset throughout the year.
3. Record price range, return, spread, and an explicit activity measure before and after the observation time. The source calls the event a volume injection but supplies no threshold or formula.
4. Decide before testing how directional control would be recognized, how long the window lasts, and whether a first move that reverses is eligible for a second signal. The source itself acknowledges sweeps and two-way movement.
5. Define entry, invalidation, target, sizing, and expiry separately. These are missing research specifications, not recoverable settings of the advertised indicator.

## Why the advertised total is not strategy profit

The page highlights an aggregate of 3,563 pips, while the daily values and two-way Wednesday presentation require reconciliation. Adding displayed excursions can include movement that one directional position could not capture. The companion clip at item 020 lists 431, 1,143, 1,113, 591, and 285; their arithmetic sum is 3,563, but they remain selected price excursions. That is not net realized return, a complete set of fills, or evidence that the reversal was known in advance. The exact dates, entry timestamps, rejected signals, position sizes, costs, and losses are not established.

## A reproducible evaluation

Additional research choices: freeze a pre/post interval and a causal activity rule, then compare the distribution of movement around 05:30 with adjacent times over many later sessions. Stratify by volatility regime and major scheduled events. Evaluate a separately frozen trading rule using executable prices and transaction costs. Compare with unconditional gold volatility at those times so ordinary intraday seasonality is not mistaken for a unique edge. An opening push can reverse, activity can arrive elsewhere, and a high-spread window can be less tradable despite a large range. The promotional indicator cannot be reconstructed from this video alone.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Source: [writeup.md](writeup.md). Planning only: this document proposes future integrations and does not implement a tab, strategy or engine. Source snapshot SHA-256: `40200a5c9392092eb58613fd2154f90d1bba08f9b855ce6991d2b9b89ac4b0fe`.

## Experiment overview

This is a promotional presentation of a time-of-day hypothesis. The author claims that gold became active near 05:30 UK time during five selected mornings. He favors observing the direction of emerging activity rather than predicting direction before the window. Neither the indicator's calculation nor a complete executable setup is disclosed. The animation describes market movement, not a verified trade ledger.

**Proposed evaluation scope:** Evaluate the particular setup or indicator sequence described here on a frozen historical universe. First produce causal features and candidate events; promote it to a trade simulation only after the unresolved entry, invalidation, exit and sizing decisions below have an explicit versioned specification. A daily-equity adaptation must be labeled when the source uses another interval or product.

## Rules and inputs

**Evidence boundary:** The source interpretation below retains the writeup’s own wording, including its qualifications, corrections and explicitly added research examples. A numbered procedure can contain a proposed operational choice; it is not automatically a rule attributed to the video. No unstated timeframe, conventional default, mirrored trade or numerical stop/target becomes source-backed through inclusion here.

### Writeup: How to study the observable idea

1. Identify the exact gold product, price feed, bar interval, and quotation convention. A pip in one gold feed need not equal another feed's tick.
2. Convert the stated UK clock time using an actual UK timezone. Do not assume the same UTC offset throughout the year.
3. Record price range, return, spread, and an explicit activity measure before and after the observation time. The source calls the event a volume injection but supplies no threshold or formula.
4. Decide before testing how directional control would be recognized, how long the window lasts, and whether a first move that reverses is eligible for a second signal. The source itself acknowledges sweeps and two-way movement.
5. Define entry, invalidation, target, sizing, and expiry separately. These are missing research specifications, not recoverable settings of the advertised indicator.

### Writeup: Why the advertised total is not strategy profit

The page highlights an aggregate of 3,563 pips, while the daily values and two-way Wednesday presentation require reconciliation. Adding displayed excursions can include movement that one directional position could not capture. The companion clip at item 020 lists 431, 1,143, 1,113, 591, and 285; their arithmetic sum is 3,563, but they remain selected price excursions. That is not net realized return, a complete set of fills, or evidence that the reversal was known in advance. The exact dates, entry timestamps, rejected signals, position sizes, costs, and losses are not established.

**Experiment input contract (proposed):** timestamped open, high, low, close and volume, market/session identity, versioned source interpretation and all declared parameters. Additional datasets and source-specific dependencies below are mandatory only for the branch that needs them. A signal-only study can proceed once its event definition is complete; trade P&L additionally requires explicit entry/fill, invalidation, exit and sizing policies.

## Proposed integration

Treat the 05: 30 UK claim as an event-window study before considering a strategy. London daylight-saving changes and gold session/feed data matter; US/PH daily equity bars cannot establish this clock-specific effect.

The future Experiments page would extend [web/app.py](../../web/app.py) and [web/templates/base.html](../../web/templates/base.html), using Paper’s [template](../../web/templates/paper.html) and `initPaper` in [web/static/app.js](../../web/static/app.js) for US/PH controls, status, tables and chart inspection. Register this directory’s source ID/digest; requests freeze market, inclusive dates, parameters, universe/data hashes and execution policy. Retain pre-start zone/anchor state when required. If the source leaves these windows open, finalize them before declaring a minimum; insufficient history produces a per-symbol not-ready reason, not fabricated values.

Preserve that routing in workers, with existing credentials and no silent CSV/Yahoo/TradingView fallback.

Snapshot each market’s available symbols, optionally narrowed by explicit tickers; current membership/delistings and corporate-action adjustments are unverified. ### Writeup: A reproducible evaluation

Additional research choices: freeze a pre/post interval and a causal activity rule, then compare the distribution of movement around 05:30 with adjacent times over many later sessions. Stratify by volatility regime and major scheduled events. Evaluate a separately frozen trading rule using executable prices and transaction costs. An opening push can reverse, activity can arrive elsewhere, and a high-spread window can be less tradable despite a large range. The promotional indicator cannot be reconstructed from this video alone.

Freeze interpretation, parameters and execution before testing. Expose only completed decision bars and prior data to the adapter; close-generated signals fill no earlier than the next tradable open. Limit/stop orders become eligible only after their conditions are known. Preserve pivot confirmation, external publication and higher-frame availability times. Test prefix invariance by changing/removing future bars and requiring unchanged earlier features, signals and orders. Use raw market prices for fills, keeping synthetic Heikin-Ashi/regression prices as features.

For fully specified trades, report candidate/accepted/rejected/expired/unfilled counts, trade and signal/fill timestamps, rule/level evidence, fees/slippage, net expectancy/R where defined, win rate, profit factor, realized/unrealized P&L, marked-to-market equity, exposure, turnover and drawdown by market. Compare a frozen baseline with identical dates/universe/costs; label independent-notional versus finite-capital accounting. Without entry/exit rules, report event coverage and predeclared forward-return/MAE/MFE horizons or forecast calibration, leaving trading P&L unavailable. Outcome windows never enter features and are censored at end_date with incomplete horizons reported.

Use fixtures alongside [core/test_stream_backtest.py](../../core/test_stream_backtest.py), [core/test_rule_backtest.py](../../core/test_rule_backtest.py), [core/test_backtest_service.py](../../core/test_backtest_service.py) and [web/test_paper_api.py](../../web/test_paper_api.py): source positives/near-misses, date boundaries, warm-up without orders, missing/invalid data, owner/remote parity, `.PS` and market isolation, enumeration/auth/partial-bulk failures, progress/cancel/retry and valid no-signal runs. Declare gap-through-stop and conservative same-bar stop/target ordering; daily OHLC cannot reveal intrabar order. Freeze end-date treatment (mark open positions or labeled liquidation), with last-bar orders unfilled if no later eligible bar exists. Use untouched later holdouts and retain all trials, failures and costs.

## Gaps and assumptions

The writeup does not define a complete reproducible trading contract. Treat any missing executable detail in its procedure as unresolved; a familiar name or attractive historical display does not supply the omitted formula.

**Practical next step:** Write and approve a small explicit research specification resolving the source gaps above, then validate numeric/event fixtures and a short causal replay before a full historical run. Missing rules should block the faithful trading mode; a labeled feature/event study may be the practical first milestone.

**Proposed assumptions, not source facts:** the experiment catalog/API paths, adapters, daily-stock adaptation, warm-up/seed conventions where unspecified, next-open execution convention, costs/slippage, sizing, finite-account policy, same-bar ordering and end-date handling are design proposals. Keep source-established values and unresolved alternatives in separate manifest fields. Claims of institutional activity, guaranteed moves, AI confidence or advertised profitability require independent evidence; OHLCV labels alone cannot establish them.

# A five-app research workflow, with product claims left unverified

Source: [John.Trading](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1F2bJCkQXM/). Downloaded duration: 18.0 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What the video does

This is a product-list montage rather than a trading setup. It names TradingView for charts, Liquid for trading and following other traders, Forex Factory for scheduled releases, Stocktwits for market conversation, and Yahoo Finance for company events and headlines. The Liquid slide also advertises access associated with private-company markets. Those are claims shown in the clip, not verified current capabilities or recommendations from this review.

## How to reproduce the information workflow

1. Create an instrument watchlist in a charting tool and record the instrument, exchange, timeframe, and whether the displayed data are delayed.
2. Maintain a scheduled-event list with its timezone visible. Convert important times into the chart's timezone before interpreting a pre-event move.
3. Use social discussion to discover subjects for research. Verify the underlying announcement or filing independently before treating a popular post as fact. Attention and positive expected return are different observations.
4. Keep a separate company-news and results calendar, and date the information used in a trade plan.
5. If evaluating any execution platform, independently establish its identity, supported products, custody, eligibility, costs, and order behavior before considering an account. The montage does not provide that information.

## What cannot be reproduced from this video

No app version, official download link, account tier, jurisdiction, market-data entitlement, integration configuration, entry signal, risk plan, or exit method is supplied. The brand name Liquid alone is insufficient to identify a financial product with confidence. Private-company exposure may involve a product different from owning the underlying company; the clip does not establish the legal or economic structure. Do not infer a particular service from its icon and transfer funds on that basis.

## Research and bot implications

The useful abstraction is a separation of chart data, scheduled events, social attention, and verified news. A bot would need documented data sources and timestamps for each, rather than screenshots of consumer apps. Save when a headline became available, avoid attributing later edits to an earlier time, and keep social indicators separate from confirmed events. This is an added workflow interpretation. The video supplies no evidence that using these five apps produces a trading edge, and reproducing the workflow does not require buying subscriptions or opening an account.

The product slides occur at roughly 5s (TradingView), 8s (Liquid), 10s (Forex Factory), 13s (Stocktwits), and 15–18s (Yahoo Finance). The clip's references to 2027 are part of its promotional framing.

# Beginner day-trading orientation, Part 1: planning, psychology, and chart setup

Source: [Jooviers Gems](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1ExeWhD1Fm/). Downloaded duration: 1258.009 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What this particular upload contains

The video is explicitly labeled Part 1 in its final frame. It introduces intraday trading, emphasizes habits and planning, and then distinguishes a charting platform from an execution platform. It ends as the speaker begins to explain candle anatomy. Although the introduction promises a preferred strategy, backtesting instruction, and a way to use other capital, this upload does not reach those sections. A complete file can therefore still be only the first part of a longer lesson; the missing material must not be invented.

## The eight process themes

The speaker asks learners to follow a written plan, approach trading with consistent businesslike structure, set risk parameters, avoid making exits according to imagined spending, understand sample-size variation, wait patiently for eligible setups, practice historical review, and seek constructive peer feedback. These are process themes rather than a tested signal. The suggested daily practice duration is roughly half an hour to an hour; the video does not show a complete historical-testing protocol in this part.

## How to apply the useful planning content

1. Write the intended market, session, setup definition, risk budget, and maximum activity before practice starts. The speaker identifies these planning fields but supplies no single completed strategy specification.
2. Keep a journal recording whether each simulated decision followed those rules. Separate a compliant loss from a rule-breaking decision that happened to make money.
3. Express the planned loss numerically rather than relying only on emotional comfort. The video's examples of dollar risk are illustrative, not a recommended size for the reader.
4. Review a sufficiently broad sample and track net outcomes, losses, and adverse excursions, not win rate alone.
5. If using peers for review, compare the same documented rules and evidence. A community or paid mentorship is not necessary to reproduce the planning exercise.

## The demonstrated platform workflow

The speaker uses TradingView to inspect and annotate charts and refers to Tradovate for execution. The speech transcript misrenders the broker name in several places; do not use those transcribed spellings as links. He demonstrates opening the chart interface, clearing unwanted studies, and finding market-data subscription settings. He warns that the displayed feed can be delayed without the appropriate entitlement. This is a description of the video's workflow, not confirmation of current product menus, pricing, access, or a recommendation to buy a subscription. Before simulation, record the actual instrument and feed latency; historical replay and a delayed live display are different modes.

## Corrections to claims in the lesson

The speaker's claim that choosing a risk amount makes trading effectively risk-free is incorrect. A planned stop does not guarantee its execution price, and leverage can magnify losses. The video is explicitly labeled Part 1 in its final frame. It introduces intraday trading, emphasizes habits and planning, and then distinguishes a charting platform from an execution platform. It ends as the speaker begins to explain candle anatomy. Although the introduction promises a preferred strategy, backtesting instruction, and a way to use other capital, this upload does not reach those sections. A complete file can therefore still be only the first part of a longer lesson; the missing material must not be invented.

### Writeup: The eight process themes

The speaker asks learners to follow a written plan, approach trading with consistent businesslike structure, set risk parameters, avoid making exits according to imagined spending, understand sample-size variation, wait patiently for eligible setups, practice historical review, and seek constructive peer feedback. These are process themes rather than a tested signal. The suggested daily practice duration is roughly half an hour to an hour; the video does not show a complete historical-testing protocol in this part.

### Writeup: How to apply the useful planning content

1. Write the intended market, session, setup definition, risk budget, and maximum activity before practice starts. The speaker identifies these planning fields but supplies no single completed strategy specification.
2. Keep a journal recording whether each simulated decision followed those rules. Separate a compliant loss from a rule-breaking decision that happened to make money.
3. Express the planned loss numerically rather than relying only on emotional comfort. The video's examples of dollar risk are illustrative, not a recommended size for the reader.
4. Review a sufficiently broad sample and track net outcomes, losses, and adverse excursions, not win rate alone.
5. If using peers for review, compare the same documented rules and evidence. A community or paid mentorship is not necessary to reproduce the planning exercise.

The speaker uses TradingView to inspect and annotate charts and refers to Tradovate for execution. The speech transcript misrenders the broker name in several places; do not use those transcribed spellings as links. He demonstrates opening the chart interface, clearing unwanted studies, and finding market-data subscription settings. A hundred or thousand trials likewise does not guarantee exactly 80 or 800 wins. Trading outcomes can be dependent and the process can change, so a larger sample does not by itself prove a stable edge. Finally, a high win rate can lose money when average losses and costs outweigh gains; expectancy needs the outcome sizes as well as their frequency.

For the initial incomplete-specification state, report the missing dependencies and any captured configuration/signal evidence; trading metrics remain unavailable. Product slogans, floating P&L, dashboards and selected chart rectangles are not validated performance.

Limit/stop orders become eligible only after their conditions are known. Preserve pivot confirmation, external publication and higher-frame availability times. Test prefix invariance by changing/removing future bars and requiring unchanged earlier features, signals and orders. # Three illustrative gold-session paths: consolidation, continuation, and reversal

Source: [Marketmentor0](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/18hhvPkPhv/). Downloaded duration: 37.863 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The screen presents a session-based story for XAU/USD across Asia, London, and New York. It shows three schematic rows rather than a quantitative algorithm: Asian consolidation followed by a downward London move and further New York weakness; Asian upward movement followed by a London pause and New York continuation; and upward movement through Asia and London followed by a New York reversal. The wording and arrows in the diagram provide firmer evidence than the corrupted speech transcription.

## How to use the diagram for observation

1. Define the three session windows and their timezones for the gold instrument being studied. The clip names sessions but provides no start/end times.
2. Record each session's open, high, low, close, total range, and net movement using only completed data.
3. Classify the first session as a pause or directional move using a declared rule. Do not assign the label after seeing New York.
4. Observe whether London extends, reverses, or pauses relative to that earlier behavior.
5. Treat the proposed New York path as a hypothesis and record both matching and nonmatching outcomes. The diagram supplies no entry confirmation or point at which a forecast becomes invalid.

## Missing settings and interpretation limits

The three rows are examples; they do not cover all possible session sequences. Terms such as consolidation and continuation have no numerical definition here. There is no timeframe, minimum range, volatility adjustment, stop, target, position size, or expiry. The top row's reversal label is not tied to a clearly quantified prior trend. The transcript does not justify confidently translating every spoken phrase, so these notes do not present a cleaned-up translation as established narration.

## How to turn it into a testable study

Additional research work could classify each session using net move divided by range, then estimate later-session outcomes conditional on the first two labels. Set thresholds on training data and test on subsequent periods. Use local-market timezone rules rather than hardcoded UTC offsets, define the gold product precisely, and include holidays and exceptional news days. Report the unconditional New York distribution alongside each conditional pattern. Otherwise a common session path can appear predictive simply because the comparison ignores its normal frequency. The diagram does not establish a universal daily gold algorithm.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

All three rows are visible by approximately 5s; the first is emphasized through about 16s, the second around 16–23s, and the third around 23–30s. This review relies on those visible labels and arrows, not a confident reconstruction of garbled words.

Source: [Trade with Pat](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/19rxHCduyg/). Downloaded duration: 43.45 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The principle is conditional entry at a reference zone, not automatic selling of every high.

## How to reproduce the illustrated short

1. Mark a support area and resistance area using prior price history. Freeze their boundaries before the new approach. The speaker does not explain how much history or what qualifies a zone as extreme.
2. Wait for price to reach resistance. Do not open the illustrated trade while price is between the zones.
3. Look for a small candle and then a larger bearish engulfing candle. Define precisely whether engulfing applies to bodies or entire ranges; the clip's spoken description does not settle that distinction.
4. Use the completed confirmation to make the short eligible. The exact fill price and order type are not specified, so a backtest must add an executable timing convention.
5. Put invalidation above resistance as described. Specify any buffer and decide whether the relevant boundary is the premarked zone or the new excursion high.
6. The visual short-position tool extends toward the lower range edge. Treat that displayed support area as the example objective; the narration does not give a universal target formula.

## Illustrative risk arithmetic

Additional teaching example: if a research rule sells at 105, invalidates at 107, and targets support at 100, planned reward is 5 units against 2 units of risk, or 2.5R before costs. The actual executable result can differ. A candle-close confirmation followed by a gap must not be filled retroactively at the already-known close.

## Missing rules, failure cases, and validation

The video leaves the zone algorithm, engulfing definition, signal expiry, minimum reward/risk, sizing, spread limits, and news handling open. Strong momentum can break resistance instead of reversing; a large confirmation candle can also consume much of the available distance to support. Test every qualifying approach and retain failed examples. Compare zone-plus-trigger entries with the same trigger used without a zone, using later data and realistic costs. A bullish support trade is the conceptual mirror, but the fully illustrated example is bearish and a mirrored long rule is an implementation extension.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximately 0–18s emphasizes location; 19–26s shows the approach to resistance; 26–34s identifies the engulfing cue and entry; 34–43s displays the stop above the upper zone and an objective near the lower edge.

# Trend-and-pullback scalping with candle confirmation and a fifteen-minute context check

Source: [AM Trader](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1DcCTLRGEn/). Downloaded duration: 1909.075 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The tutorial combines swing-based trend interpretation, support/resistance role reversal, a candle signal at a pullback, and higher-timeframe agreement. It is framed through stories about Dow, Wyckoff, and Homma. Those historical attributions, purported quotations, extraordinary wealth claims, universal applicability, and numerical edge claims are not established by the chart examples. The actionable content is the observable sequence described below, not the historical authority used to promote it.

## Trend and location framework

The speaker classifies higher highs/higher lows as an uptrend, lower highs/lower lows as a downtrend, and overlapping horizontal movement as a range. The intended entries follow a retracement within a trend. A resistance break followed by a return to that area supplies a potential long location; a support break followed by a recovery toward it supplies a potential short location. Ranges are generally excluded from the basic scalping branch.

The tutorial also describes accumulation, markup, distribution, markdown, springs, and upthrusts as context. Those labels can describe a completed history, but identifying them before the outcome requires explicit rules. A low-side excursion is not known to be the final spring merely because a later rally occurred. Claims about which participant caused a candle cannot be proved from OHLC alone.

## The four candle families discussed

A hammer-style candle has a relatively small upper-positioned body and a long lower shadow; the source uses it as a possible support rejection. A shooting-star-style candle has the opposite geometry and is used around resistance. A doji has an open and close close together and is discussed as a pause whose meaning depends on location. An engulfing pattern compares the body of the newer candle with the prior candle's body; the bullish and bearish versions are paired with support and resistance respectively.

The source supplies no wick/body ratios, doji tolerance, minimum candle size, or engulfing edge convention. Those must be implementation choices. The spoken Japanese names and historical stories are not necessary to define the geometry.

## The final stated workflow

1. Begin on the one-minute chart and identify a clean trend, an impulse, and a retracement to a meaningful level. The introduction also mentions five-minute use, but the final worked process uses one minute.
2. Wait for the selected candle signal at that location.
3. Check whether the planned entry, invalidation, and objective offer at least 2R; otherwise the stated filter rejects the trade.
4. Inspect the fifteen-minute chart for structural/contextual agreement. If it contradicts the one-minute idea, the speaker stays out.
5. Return to the one-minute chart and execute under a declared timing rule, with invalidation beyond the relevant support or resistance.
6. The worked short uses a doji at resistance in USD/JPY; the worked long uses a bullish engulfing-style candle at support in NZD/USD. These are examples from the source, not current market instructions.

## Important ambiguities in the examples

The earlier doji explanation says to wait for the following candle to resolve uncertainty, while the final short enters at the doji's close. Those are different triggers. A reproducible version must select one and retain that choice.

The source also describes a 2R minimum while using a higher-timeframe resistance area as a long objective. If that level offers less than the required ratio at the actual fill, the trade should fail the declared filter rather than be silently relabeled 2R. A prior resistance target also does not guarantee profit if price reverses before reaching it.

The fifteen-minute context must be available before entry. Using the final outcome of a fifteen-minute candle to approve a one-minute entry that occurred earlier inside it would look ahead. An explicit completed-higher-bar policy is an added implementation choice that avoids that timing mistake.

## How to make a causal implementation

Define pivot lookback and confirmation delay, level width, break-close conditions, retracement eligibility, candle geometry, higher-timeframe alignment, maximum wait, order type, stop buffer, position size, and exit policy. Store the level and signal timestamps. A close-based confirmation can make a trade eligible after the close, but cannot establish an already-executed fill at that close without a separate executable order model. Never widen a stop or choose another historical level after seeing the outcome while claiming the original plan remained fixed.

## Failure modes and validation

One-minute patterns are vulnerable to spread and execution noise; apparent support can fail, trend classification can lag a reversal, and higher/lower frames can disagree for long periods. Candle labels do not reveal a certain next move. Test each candle branch separately against the same location rule, then assess the contribution of the fifteen-minute filter on later data. Include all losses, missed fills, costs, and changes in regime. The source's statements about a 65% edge or eliminating most poor trades are claims without a supplied statistical study. Its statement that chart analysis makes news irrelevant should not be taken as evidence that event-driven gaps or execution risk disappear.

# Reading market state through swing structure, reversal patterns, and Wyckoff-style phases

Source: [AM Trader](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1FgVDHX11a/). Downloaded duration: 898.705 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This fifteen-minute lesson layers three forms of chart description: trend/range classification, familiar reversal-pattern structures, and a four-phase market-cycle story. It is primarily a context framework. It repeatedly suggests that reading the structure improves timing, but does not supply one complete entry, stop, target, and sizing algorithm or a statistical demonstration of profitability.

## Method 1: trend and the current leg

1. Label confirmed swing highs and lows. Rising pairs support an uptrend interpretation; falling pairs support a downtrend; more horizontal overlap suggests a range.
2. Within a trend, distinguish an advance in the main direction from a retracement against it. The speaker favors waiting for the latter to finish rather than chasing the extended impulse.
3. Use earlier support/resistance as candidate locations for that change. A former ceiling can become support after a break, and a former floor can become resistance.
4. Watch the reaction at the location, including rejection wicks or a failed excursion. The video does not define a numerical completion/entry trigger for the leg.

## Method 2: reversal-pattern confirmation

The lesson shows a double top, head-and-shoulders, triple top, double bottom, and triple bottom, despite briefly calling the list four patterns. For the topping patterns, repeated inability to extend upward is followed by a break of the intervening support/neckline. For the bottoming patterns, repeated inability to extend lower is followed by a break of intervening resistance. The change is not confirmed merely because two similar highs or lows can be drawn retrospectively.

An implementation needs pivot confirmation, tolerance between repeated extremes, maximum separation, neckline construction, and a break condition. A sloping neckline, horizontal neckline, wick break, and closing break can produce different eligibility dates. None is fully quantified by the source.

## Method 3: the four-phase narrative

The speaker describes a lower range as possible accumulation, an upward expansion as markup, an upper range as possible distribution, and a decline as markdown. A downside false break followed by recovery is called a spring; an upside false break followed by recovery inside is treated as an upthrust-like trap. The illustrated lower-range recovery precedes a rise, and the upper-range failure precedes a decline. These names organize a scenario but cannot prove hidden institutional inventory or intent.

## How to use the framework without hindsight

Additional implementation choices: define the timeframe and causal swing rule first, mark only levels known then, and record uncertain classifications rather than forcing every bar into a perfect cycle. A range near the recent low is not automatically accumulation; it can be a pause before another decline. Keep the observed break/recovery separate from a later confirmed trend. If comparing pattern and phase labels, save both as-of classifications so later relabeling does not manufacture predictive accuracy.

## Missing execution rules and evaluation

The lesson lacks a complete instrument/session specification, entry order, stop placement, target formula, position size, maximum holding period, and handling of conflicting frameworks. The claim that identifying a retracement is enough to know when to make money is not established. To research it, select a frozen entry system and compare each contextual layer separately on later data. Count failed necklines, false recoveries, trend resumptions, ambiguous ranges, and costs. Describing an already-completed move accurately is different from making a profitable decision before the outcome.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximate chapters: 45–237s trends and legs; 241–354s support/resistance and retracement examples; 354–578s the five reversal patterns; 610–898s four phases, spring-like recovery, and upper-range failure.

Reviewed using: manual reading of the complete machine transcript in timestamped sections, supported by recognized screen text; the generic repost caption contains no method-specific detail.
