# Five selected gold mornings at a fixed UK time: excursion totals versus executable returns

Source: [FXDSniper](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1Fm47MfTjL/). Downloaded duration: 45.208 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This second FXDSniper clip illustrates the same time-window premise as item 012. The stated observation time is 05:30 UK. The author wants to observe increased activity first and then follow whichever side appears dominant. The clip presents selected daily movement figures rather than a reproducible indicator or complete trading system.

## How to reproduce the observation

1. Choose the exact XAU instrument and feed and record what a pip means in its quotation.
2. Mark 05:30 using a timezone-aware UK clock.
3. Observe the transition from quieter trading into greater price activity. Define any volume or range threshold independently because the source does not supply one.
4. Track direction after the event and include failed first moves. Wednesday is explicitly represented as an initial rise and a later decline.
5. Keep the displayed excursion study separate from any proposed entry/exit rule. A tradable version requires a trigger, invalidation, target, permissible reversal behavior, position size, and window end; none is fully specified.

## Arithmetic and evidence limits

The caption's daily amounts are 431, 1,143, 1,113, 591, and 285 pips, summing to 3,563. Wednesday's 1,113 combines 133 upward with 980 downward. That addition is arithmetically consistent, but capturing both legs would require timely reversal or separate trades. The video does not establish those executable decisions or their costs. Its rounded spoken values are not a precise trade accounting record. The selected week also lacks a complete timestamped sample, all losses, and a method for defining each measured move's endpoints.

## How to evaluate it

As an additional research specification, predefine the observation horizon and direction rule, freeze them, and test subsequent sessions. Compare activity around this time with other morning intervals. If measuring potential range rather than trading return, label it as range and include all eligible dates. For an actual strategy, use causal order timing, spread and slippage, and declared rules for a first move that fails. Elevated movement does not guarantee a favorable entry, and a claimed repeated window can disappear outside the selected sample. An undisclosed external indicator is not a reproducible numerical setting.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximately 5–11s establishes the clock time; 11–33s lists selected excursions; 33–45s gives the timing-first description and promotes the external indicator. Around 34s, the recognized summary frame lists all five amounts.

# Daily SMA context with intraday VWAP and a 9/20 EMA trend filter

Source: [Momentum.](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1dRRUw4JZY/). Downloaded duration: 74.9 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The presenter describes a reduced chart layout for stock trading. Daily simple averages give broader context, while a one-minute chart uses VWAP and a pair of exponential averages for intraday interpretation. He explicitly says these tools do not tell him the exact entry; price action and volume still matter. His rejection of other indicators is a personal selection, not a controlled performance comparison.

## Configuration and procedure

1. On the daily chart, add simple moving averages with lengths 20, 50, and 200. Use them to observe broader positioning and trend. The source does not specify a precise daily eligibility rule.
2. On the one-minute chart, add VWAP and EMAs of lengths 9 and 20.
3. Use price relative to VWAP as a contextual bias. The presenter describes price above as buyer-favored and below as seller-favored. This is an interpretation of average price, not proof that all buyers are profitable or that particular institutions control the market.
4. When the 9 EMA is above the 20, he looks for pullbacks. When the shorter average is below the longer, he avoids the illustrated long opportunities. That avoidance is not automatically a short-entry instruction.
5. Require a separate price/volume setup before entry. The clip does not define it.

## How to make the chart reproducible

Additional implementation choices include the EMA price source, initialization and warmup, VWAP reset/session convention, inclusion of extended hours, and data adjustments. A standard EMA can use alpha = 2/(length+1); it carries exponentially decaying historical weight rather than abruptly forgetting everything older than the named length. Define a pullback objectively and decide whether only completed one-minute bars count. Save the daily context using information available before the intraday signal.

## Failure modes and evaluation

A short average can cross repeatedly in a range. Price can remain far from VWAP during a strong move; the presenter's magnet analogy is not a guaranteed mean-reversion trigger. A VWAP filter and EMA filter can also duplicate similar directional information. Missing rules include the exact setup, stop, target, risk fraction, expiry, liquidity requirements, and event handling. Test a frozen base entry with and without each filter on later data, report net results and excluded trades, and model the execution difficulty of one-minute small-cap trading. The clip's claims about widespread indicator use are not evidence that a particular setup has positive expectancy.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 25–32s gives the daily SMA lengths; 32–46s describes one-minute VWAP; 48–56s gives the 9/20 relationship; 63–70s explicitly says price and volume, rather than the indicators alone, determine actual execution.

# A bullish Wolfe-wave-style illustration with numbered pivots and a projected target

Source: [Zenix Arixon](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1A2SbKbtUM/). Downloaded duration: 18.102 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The animation labels five alternating turning points, highlights a potential buying area near point 5 after an excursion beneath a channel boundary, and projects an upward path to a sloping target line. A later chart segment is shown reaching that target. The title calls it a bullish Wolfe wave. The drawing is an example geometry, not a complete specification of every condition associated with that pattern name.

## How to reproduce what is shown

1. Identify the alternating low/high turning points shown as 1 through 5, using an independently declared swing rule.
2. Draw the visible channel and its lower boundary through the earlier lows. Note the fifth point's excursion beneath that area.
3. Draw the illustrated rising projection through the earlier numbered reference points; the graphic appears to use the 1-to-4 alignment as a target guide. Preserve that reading as a visual interpretation, since the clip supplies no spoken geometric formula.
4. Mark an entry zone around the fifth-point excursion and a stop area below it, as shown by the position overlay.
5. Evaluate a return toward the sloping projection. The animation labels a later point 6 at the favorable outcome; that future point is an outcome label, not information available when point 5 forms.

## Turning a picture into a rule

Additional implementation choices include swing confirmation, channel-fitting method, permissible slope, pivot spacing, excursion depth, entry confirmation, exact stop buffer, and whether the target is fixed at entry or moves with time along the projected line. A line through (time1, price1) and (time4, price4) can be extended algebraically, but the formula alone does not establish a valid setup. Freeze the selected pivots and line when the pattern becomes eligible instead of refitting them after seeing the target reached.

## Failure cases and validation

A fifth-point low can keep falling, the recovery can fail, or the target projection can be too distant to offer a practical holding period. The video does not specify instrument, timeframe, order type, sizing, maximum wait, geometric tolerances, or statistics. Its loading animation and trade overlay are presentation elements rather than test results. A causal study should include all candidate geometries under one frozen definition, delayed pivot recognition, unfilled entries, invalidations, costs, and later-period results. The pattern name alone does not justify importing absent rules from a different source.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Around 3–8s the channel and numbered pivots appear; 10–13s adds the entry area, target projection, and stop; 15–18s reveals the favorable continuation. The original page description names the bullish pattern but supplies no numerical rules.

# Three valleys and a river: breakout recovery followed by an illustrated short projection

Source: [Forex signal active](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/18DK8YcPTd/). Downloaded duration: 21.133 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The clip draws three descending troughs, a falling resistance line, and a rebound after the line is broken. It then illustrates a short around a later rebound high and a downward measured projection. A briefly shown instructional page names two possible trades in the pattern, rather than a single unconditional short. No useful strategy narration was detected.

## How to follow the two illustrated phases

1. Mark the three troughs and their intervening rallies using only pivots already recognizable. Draw the descending resistance line shown over the rallies.
2. For the page's first phase, a close above that line is the initial reversal condition, with the described long entry just beyond the breakout candle's high. This is distinct from the short emphasized later in the animation.
3. Measure the reference decline from the page's A to B points. The visible text associates a later short at C with a rebound of at least roughly 62% of that reference range; another line mentions a 62–78% area for the first trade's objective. These readings come from the displayed page, whose right-hand text is partly occluded.
4. For the later short illustration, the stop is drawn above C and the downward projection is labeled AB = CD. That means a projected price distance comparable to the original A-to-B decline measured from C, not a demonstrated fixed success probability.
5. Specify the exact confirmation at C independently. The animation marks a turn retrospectively without a fully stated real-time entry trigger.

## Important ambiguities

The supporting page is partly covered by a hand and cropped text. Its entire stop/exit wording cannot be read reliably, so it would be wrong to reconstruct every sentence. The animation does not establish the instrument, timeframe, pivot tolerances, maximum formation length, line-fitting convention, buffer, order type, sizing, or time exit. A later C high is not known to be a final high while price is still rising.

## How to research the idea

Additional research choices: formalize the three-trough sequence, delay pivot confirmation, freeze the resistance line, and separately log the breakout-long and rebound-short branches. If using an A-to-B range and retracement threshold, define their endpoints and update policy before the test. A close above a trendline can fail; a rebound can continue far beyond the intended short zone; a projected equal-distance target can remain unreachable. Compare each branch with its own entry, invalidation, and executable costs. The video supplies an attractive example, not evidence that both phases can consistently be captured.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The first 6s draws the troughs and resistance; around 9s it marks the later short; the instructional page is visible at 11.99s; the last samples show a stop above the rebound high and a favorable decline along the projected path.

# Two conditional breakout paths from rising support beneath horizontal resistance

Source: [Fx Trading.01](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1QfPosb3se/). Downloaded duration: 15.999 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

A silent chart markup shows rising lows beneath a relatively flat resistance area. The author draws alternative upward and downward paths with corresponding long and short position overlays. The key observation is conditional direction selection after a boundary breaks. The final overlay text refers to one-side trading, rather than showing that both opposing trades should be opened simultaneously.

## How to reproduce the illustrated markup

1. Identify a sequence of higher lows and draw a rising support boundary through prior points.
2. Mark the repeated upper reaction area as resistance. The graphic includes a midpoint-style label but does not explain an indicator calculation; do not infer a Fibonacci system from that label alone.
3. Keep an upward continuation scenario that becomes eligible only after price escapes above resistance under a declared confirmation rule. The visible long overlay places invalidation back beneath the breakout area.
4. Keep a separate downward scenario for failure through rising support. The short overlay places invalidation back above the relevant break area.
5. Activate only the branch whose previously defined trigger actually occurs. The arrows are alternative projections, not simultaneous future facts.

## Rules needed for an executable version

The video does not specify close-versus-wick breaks, a retest requirement, exact entry timing, stop buffer, target formula, formation duration, number of touches, timeframe, instrument, position size, or order expiry. The displayed risk/reward rectangles illustrate placement but their small changing numbers do not establish universal parameters. Additional implementation choices should define the boundary-fitting and breakout rules explicitly and freeze the geometry before eligibility.

## Failure cases and evaluation

Converging boundaries can produce multiple false breaks. A line chosen after the future move can make the setup look clearer than it was. Price can break in one direction and reverse into the other, so a two-branch strategy also needs cancellation and reentry rules. Evaluate all qualifying formations with chronological data, causal pivot availability, executable next-price fills, and costs. Compare the two branches separately and retain cases that never break or expire. The graphic demonstrates planning possibilities rather than an audited winning trade or a complete named pattern algorithm.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Around 2–5s the support and resistance areas are added; 7s displays the short scenario; 9s adds the long alternative; 11–16s shows both paths and a one-side-trade annotation.

Reviewed using: manual inspection of all eight timestamped frame samples and saved description; no instructional speech was detected.

# VWAP weighting and the 9/20/50 EMA chart layout

Source: [Momentum.](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/19mHhkb8Zp/). Downloaded duration: 49.968 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This clip explains two indicator families: volume-weighted average price and exponential moving averages. Its central comparison is that a high-volume price change moves VWAP more strongly than a similar low-volume change. It then describes an upward bias when the 9 EMA is above the 20 and mentions a 50 EMA. It does not provide a complete entry-and-exit system, despite the rhetorical description of only two lines.

## How to reproduce the layout

1. Add VWAP to a chart with a defined session and meaningful volume input.
2. Add exponential averages of lengths 9, 20, and 50. The video does not give a separate trading rule for the 50.
3. Observe price above or below VWAP as context.
4. Observe whether the 9 EMA is above the 20. The presenter uses that upward relationship to look for pullbacks.
5. Specify a separate pullback trigger, invalidation, and exit before evaluating trades. None is fully taught in this short lesson.

## Calculation details and a correction

A research implementation can express VWAP as cumulative sum(price times volume) divided by cumulative volume from the selected reset. Bar-level typical price or close is an implementation choice unless the source is established. As a teaching example, 100 units at 10 and 900 at 11 yield 10.90; reversing those volumes yields 10.10. The named EMA period controls the decay rate. An EMA is not a strict rolling window containing only the last 9, 20, or 50 candles; older observations retain declining influence. That distinction corrects the clip's simplified lookback explanation.

## Missing rules, failures, and evaluation

The timeframe, session reset, source price, crossover versus persistent-state interpretation, pullback depth, trigger, stop, target, size, and maximum holding period are open. Trending averages can lag reversals, and repeated crossings can create poor signals in sideways price. A move away from VWAP can extend rather than revert. To evaluate this layout, freeze one causal entry and compare it with and without VWAP and EMA conditions on later data, including costs and every eligible setup. Treat the opening cluttered chart as the starting point being removed, not as a list of required indicator settings.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Roughly 5–26s explains volume weighting and VWAP context; 26–42s names the 9, 20, and 50 EMAs and describes the short-above-long relationship. Screen text around 31s confirms the three EMA labels.

Reviewed using: manual synthesis of full machine transcript and recognized visual labels; garbled OCR rows were excluded from factual claims.

# A bearish rejection block formed by upper wicks

Source: [MrRhay World](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EL5no7TAZ/). Downloaded duration: 47.11 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The example uses five-minute XAU/USD near an old high. Upper wicks with lower-closing candle bodies define a potential rejection area. The proposed trade waits for a return into that area, sells around its midpoint, invalidates above the wick extreme, and targets a prior low-side reference. This is a specific retracement-entry idea; the existence of wicks does not prove that institutions deliberately took stops.

## How to reproduce the demonstrated sequence

1. Identify and mark a prior high before the new approach.
2. Observe price reaching that area and leaving upper wicks while bodies close lower.
3. Draw the rejection zone from the highest relevant body boundary to the highest wick. The source's phrasing does not fully define which candles form the cluster, so a detector needs a fixed grouping rule.
4. Calculate the zone midpoint as (upper boundary + lower boundary)/2.
5. Wait for a retest into that midpoint area and evaluate the illustrated short. The clip does not specify a required additional candle confirmation or whether the order is a resting limit.
6. Place invalidation above the highest wick and use the identified low-side liquidity reference as the objective. Buffer and exact target selection remain unspecified.

## Operational example and causal constraints

Additional teaching example: if the chosen body boundary is 100 and the wick extreme is 102, the midpoint is 101. With a declared stop at 102.20 and target at 97, nominal reward is 4 against 1.20 of risk, about 3.33R before costs. These are illustrative prices, not the video's levels. The zone cannot be considered complete before the relevant candles close. If a resting order is chosen, model whether it was actually live before a subsequent touch and how a gap or spread affects its fill.

## Missing rules and failure modes

The clip leaves cluster selection, significance of the old high, minimum wick size, maximum wait, allowed retests, spread limits, sizing, and stop buffer open. Price can resume upward, fail to revisit the midpoint, or first touch the target without filling the entry. The displayed successful result and reward/risk overlay are an example, not a verified distribution. Test every qualifying zone, retain invalidations and unfilled orders, and compare midpoint entry with a separately defined confirmed-rejection entry on later data. # A bullish rebound after a three-swing rise breaks its support line

Source: [Signal Street](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/19oU9nb1Zo/). Downloaded duration: 26.213 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The animation shows three rising swing peaks, a rising line under their intervening lows, a break downward, and then a long from a later low labeled C. It projects a recovery using an AB = CD-style measured distance. Although some peak labels say valley, the visible peaks and rising support are the more reliable description of this particular drawing. This is different from simply buying an upward trendline breakout.

## How to reproduce the shown analysis

1. Mark the alternating swings and rising support line visible in the initial chart.
2. Observe the subsequent downward break rather than assuming the support must hold.
3. Identify the later low labeled C in the illustration. The source marks a long there, with a stop area beneath C.
4. Use the displayed prior reference distance A-to-B to project a comparable upward C-to-D distance. The clip labels this equal-distance relation and shows a target line above.
5. Require an independently specified real-time reversal trigger before treating C as an actionable low. The clip reveals the favorable low retrospectively; it does not tell the viewer exactly when that low becomes confirmed.

## What remains unspecified

There is no instrument, timeframe, formal pivot rule, definition of A and B beyond the drawing, minimum retracement, entry confirmation, exact stop buffer, order type, position size, maximum waiting period, or management after entry. The risk/reward overlay and later target-hit label demonstrate one chosen outcome, not a historical sample. A detector cannot know the final low of the decline in advance.

## Operational interpretation and validation

Additional research choices could require a small structural recovery or completed rejection bar after the support break before a long becomes eligible. That rule would be new, and it can materially worsen the entry compared with the retrospective C marker. Freeze the reference measurement, compute D from the actual eligible entry context, and use a stop policy that exists before a later touch. Test every qualifying formation, including declines that continue through C and rebounds that fall short of the projected distance. Report net reward and drawdown with costs. A measured projection is a scenario, not an obligation for price to travel that far.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximately 0–8s labels the swings and support; 11–15s shows the break and later C low; 18–22s adds entry, stop, and equal-distance target geometry; the final frame reveals a successful rebound.

## What it does

The clip illustrates regular divergence between price swings and MACD: a higher price high against a lower oscillator high for a bearish warning, and a lower price low against a higher oscillator low for a bullish warning. It promotes a named system, but the demonstrated favorable turns do not reveal all of that system's detection and execution rules.

## How to reproduce the observable analysis

1. Use the same instrument and bar construction when comparing the example. The page references NQ futures, and visible labels indicate a 500-tick chart in sampled frames. A 500-tick bar is not a five-minute bar.
2. Add MACD and record its actual parameters and whether divergence is measured on the line or histogram. The screen includes a 12/26/9-style label, but the speech does not establish the complete formula or proprietary modifications. Treat the observed label as an example setting requiring visual confirmation, not as proof of the full system.
3. Pair two already confirmed price highs with the corresponding oscillator highs. A higher price high with a lower oscillator high is the bearish relationship shown.
4. Pair two confirmed lows for the opposite relationship.
5. Define a separate entry trigger and exit policy. A divergence warning alone does not specify when to enter.

## Rules that cannot be recovered

The clip does not establish swing lookback, oscillator-peak matching tolerance, minimum divergence magnitude, confirmation delay, required VWAP context, order type, stop placement, target calculation, position size, or expiry. Although the caption advertises easy stops and targets, it does not give their formulas. The name of a commercial indicator is not a reproducible specification.

## How to research it without hindsight

Additional implementation choices: select a causal pivot algorithm and wait until each pivot is confirmed; align oscillator observations to those price swings using a frozen rule. Do not backdate a signal to an extreme discovered only after subsequent bars. Track every divergence, including repeated bearish warnings during a continuing uptrend. Compare a fixed base reversal trigger with and without divergence on later data. Include fees, tick size, contract multiplier, spread, and slippage. A tick-bar dataset needs the underlying trade sequence or an equivalent historical construction; daily or minute OHLC cannot recreate it exactly. The advertised point moves are neither guaranteed attainable fills nor a full net-performance record.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 0–14s contrasts bearish and bullish divergence; 14–21s adds another bearish example; later frames display favorable point excursions and system branding. The screen-text record retains the tick-chart and MACD labels, including recognition uncertainty.

# An anchored-VWAP pullback with explicit EUR/USD example levels

Source: [Time To Trade](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1DWh4piyuK/). Downloaded duration: 39.84 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The lesson anchors VWAP at a swing low, waits for an upward move and a pullback that holds the average, then illustrates a long toward the recent high. Unlike item 002's filter-only explanation, this source provides example execution levels in its caption. The chart is an educational EUR/USD fifteen-minute example, not independently verified trade history.

## How to reproduce the example

1. Mark the illustrated swing low at 1.0874 after it is recognizable and anchor the VWAP there.
2. Observe price advancing above the anchored average toward the prior high of 1.0928.
3. Watch the retracement toward the average, described near 1.0905, and require the example candle to wick into the area and close above it.
4. The caption's proposed entry is 1.0907, with invalidation at 1.0898 and a target of 1.0928. These are historical teaching levels from the post, not current market instructions.
5. Specify executable order timing independently. Knowing a candle closed above the average does not establish that an order could have been filled at that same already-completed close.

## Arithmetic and indicator meaning

The entry-to-stop distance is 0.0009, conventionally 9 pips for this EUR/USD quotation. Target distance is 0.0021, or 21 pips, giving about 2.33R before costs. The caption says a later price reached 1.0933, but no broker fills or complete trade record establish the result. AVWAP is a volume-weighted price from the chosen anchor, not literally the average cost of every remaining buyer. A spot-FX feed may use tick volume or another provider-specific proxy rather than a consolidated total of global trading.

## Missing rules and validation

Anchor selection, swing confirmation, price source, volume source, pullback tolerance, stop-buffer formula, sizing, maximum holding period, and failed-touch treatment are not generalized by the example. 5. Specify executable order timing independently. Knowing a candle closed above the average does not establish that an order could have been filled at that same already-completed close.

The entry-to-stop distance is 0.0009, conventionally 9 pips for this EUR/USD quotation. Target distance is 0.0021, or 21 pips, giving about 2.33R before costs. # 50/100 EMA crossover with a LuxAlgo SuperTrend oscillator filter

Source: [TRADING CHART](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1KAreoR3Nu/). Downloaded duration: 36.466 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The presenter combines two exponential averages with a color change in the LuxAlgo SuperTrend oscillator. A short is illustrated when the averages cross downward and the oscillator agrees, with an oscillator-based exit. The stated claim of 200 tests is not accompanied by the underlying trades or a reproducible performance report. The chart screenshots include a daily crypto chart, so the title's scalping and stock-trading framing should not be treated as proof of an intraday stock test.

## How to configure the stated method

1. Add two EMAs and set their lengths to 50 and 100 as instructed in the narration. Use a declared price source; close is visible in the settings dialog.
2. Search for the SuperTrend Oscillator from LuxAlgo. The sampled search screen highlights SuperTrend Oscillator [LUX]. Record the actual script version and settings before testing because similarly named scripts are different tools.
3. For the illustrated short, require the 50 to cross beneath the 100 and a bearish oscillator color transition. The source does not establish whether both events must happen on exactly the same bar or within a tolerance window.
4. The machine transcript, including a second isolated-audio transcription, renders the short exit as the histogram going above 33. The sampled chart does not establish a readable numerical threshold or unambiguously identify the plotted series. Treat 33 as an unconfirmed transcription, not a validated constant for implementation; obtain a clearly audible/legible exit rule before coding it.
5. The presenter suggests reversing the logic for longs, but does not fully state the mirrored numerical exit. Do not silently assert a negative threshold as a confirmed source rule.

## Ambiguities that matter

A sampled input dialog around 10s still shows the default length 9 during editing, while the narration explicitly asks for 50 and 100. It is a transitional UI frame, not evidence that 9 is a third required average. The oscillator length, multiplier, smoothing, precise color-state definition, full exit-series mapping, stop, sizing, and signal expiry remain unspecified. A reproducible implementation needs those choices or the actual frozen indicator code.

## Failure modes and evaluation

Crossovers lag and can alternate repeatedly in a range. Requiring two signals may reduce opportunities without improving expectancy. # Daily trend bias, an opposing opening sweep, and a fair-value-gap pullback

Source: [The Trading Apprentice](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/19gTYpeiaK/). Downloaded duration: 91.95 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker calls this a daily sweep setup. A higher-timeframe directional assessment is paired with a shorter-timeframe excursion against that assessment, followed by a return in the preferred direction. The intended entry is a pullback into a newly formed fair-value gap, with a prior-day extreme as the objective. The payout and consistency statements are promotional claims, not validated results.

## How to reproduce the described sequence

1. Inspect daily swings. Higher highs and higher lows favor the long branch; lower highs and lower lows favor the short branch. The source gives no formal swing-confirmation algorithm.
2. Mark the previous day's high for the long branch or low for the short branch. Define the daily session boundary before calculating those levels.
3. Move to the one-hour chart and observe the New York opening period. The exact clock time and instrument-specific opening convention are not fully established.
4. Look for an excursion through a shorter-term reference against the daily bias. Wait for evidence that the move fails rather than assuming every opposing break is a trap.
5. Drop to the five-minute chart for confirmation: the video changes from H1 to a visibly labeled M5 chart around 61–65s. Look for the three-candle fair-value gap after the opposing move, then wait for a pullback into it. The daily chart sets bias, H1 locates the opening fakeout, and M5 supplies the depicted entry setup.
6. Target the selected prior-day extreme. The long-position illustration puts the stop below the nearby M5 low; the narration only calls it a clear invalidation point. The exact gap-fill percentage and stop buffer are not specified.

## Rules needed for an actual detector

Additional choices include the daily pivot rule, whether an opening sweep requires recovery by a candle close, which short-term level qualifies, displacement size, exact gap geometry, first versus repeated retest, entry order, and maximum wait. An implementation of a bullish three-bar wick gap can compare the first bar's high with the third bar's low, but the spoken description alone does not establish every variant or input. No gap exists as a confirmed three-bar condition until the third bar has completed.

## Failure modes and evaluation

Daily bias can be wrong, an apparent opening failure can resume its original direction, and a gap can be crossed without support. The prior-day target might already have been reached or offer insufficient room by the time entry becomes eligible. Freeze the trend and level selection, log every eligible opening event, and compare the same gap entry with and without the higher-timeframe and sweep filters on later data. Include unfilled pullbacks, costs, and executable timing. The clip's clear-invalidation language is not a complete risk policy until the price and order behavior are specified.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximately 13–37s establishes daily direction and prior-day targets; 37–58s describes the opening excursion on a one-hour chart; 58–81s describes the gap and pullback; 81–91s gives conceptual invalidation and target.

Reviewed using: manual synthesis of the complete machine transcript and timestamped screen-text observations.

# Repeated support tests: measure the reactions rather than assuming each touch adds strength

Source: [bhsledu](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/19twX6VmVY/). Downloaded duration: 127.221 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The lesson challenges the idea that the fourth support touch must be safer than the first. It suggests watching for shrinking rebounds, progressively faster returns, and lower intervening highs. Its order-consumption story is a conceptual explanation: price history alone cannot measure the full standing order book or establish that no new buyers replenish it.

## How to apply the observation

1. Mark a support zone using earlier price reactions and freeze its width and boundaries.
2. For each later visit, record the rebound distance and the time until price next returns.
3. Compare the highs achieved between visits. A descending sequence can indicate that upward responses are weakening.
4. At a new touch, evaluate the actual reaction rather than buying solely because of the touch count.
5. The speaker contrasts a stronger response with a weak response followed by a close beneath support, and notes that broken support can later behave as resistance. The video does not provide an executable entry rule for either case.

## How to turn the warning signs into measurements

These are additional research definitions: rebound strength could be peak excursion from the zone before the next return, normalized by recent volatility; return speed could be elapsed bars; pressure could be the slope or ordering of intervening highs. Choose a maximum observation horizon and define how much separation makes two contacts distinct. Otherwise one prolonged visit can be counted as several independent touches. These choices are not numerical settings supplied by the source.

## What remains missing

The instrument, timeframe, support algorithm, zone width, minimum rebound, definition of fast return, confirmation trigger, stop, target, size, and expiry are unspecified. The clip's explanation that clustered stops can accelerate a break is plausible market intuition, but the chart does not prove where all stops sit. A heavily watched area can hold, fail quietly, or fail sharply; attention does not guarantee any one outcome.

## How to evaluate it

Study subsequent outcomes at every qualifying touch and compare count alone with the three reaction measures. Calculate those measures only from information completed before the new decision. Avoid using the eventual rebound maximum to authorize an entry at the initial touch. Compare later-period results and include costs if converting the observations into a strategy. This video teaches a contextual warning, not a verified threshold at which support always breaks.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Roughly 0–37s introduces repeated tests and replenishment; 38–73s discusses attention and potential stop activity; 75–98s lists the three warning signs; 98–114s emphasizes the actual reaction and a possible support-to-resistance change.

# An AI-to-replay strategy-development workflow, with replay distinguished from forward testing

Source: [DAS Replay](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/19n9EM1vxz/). Downloaded duration: 35.083 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The clip describes connecting an AI application to a replay-data service through MCP, requesting a strategy, editing the generated script, and testing it in replay. Its advertised speed improvement is not a performance benchmark or evidence that the resulting strategy works. The video does not include a complete installable server configuration or order-executing strategy. Around 20s it does show a Pine v6 indicator called Momentum Cross: `fast = ta.ema(close, 9)`, `slow = ta.ema(close, 20)`, buy markers on `ta.crossover(fast, slow)` and sell markers on `ta.crossunder(fast, slow)`. It plots averages and shapes; it contains no strategy orders, protective exits, or sizing.

## The four steps shown

1. Connect the specific DAS Replay MCP service to the AI application. The claimed data scope includes multiple asset classes and fine-grained data, but the source does not establish the endpoint, authentication, account entitlement, or exact schema.
2. Ask the application to create a momentum strategy using that connection. A reproducible prompt must additionally specify universe, timeframe, trigger, risk policy, costs, and evaluation dates; the caption's short request leaves these open.
3. Inspect the resulting Pine Script in the editor shown by the video, modify it if needed, and run it in the service's supported chart environment. The claimed editor compatibility was not tested here.
4. Replay the strategy bar by bar or event by event and inspect fills and decisions. That can reveal causal or execution mistakes that a favorable summary metric conceals.

## A necessary terminology correction

Historical replay remains historical testing even if the user advances time manually. Forward testing uses observations that arrive after the rules are frozen, such as a subsequent paper-trading period. The clip blends those terms. A replay engine can be useful without making replay equivalent to an untouched future sample, and order-flow detail does not automatically remove selection bias.

## How to make the workflow reproducible

Additional implementation steps: save the full prompt, generated code, code revision, data version, timezone, indicator warmup, and execution assumptions. Require the script to use information available at each simulated decision. A rule based on a completed close should become eligible only under an executable later-price convention. Keep training/tuning data separate from later evaluation and retain every tested revision rather than reporting only the best one.

## What is not supplied or authorized by this clip

No server installation, third-party credential use, strategy deployment, broker connection, or trade is performed as part of this video review. The actual signal rules, stop, target, position size, and full test output are absent. The useful result is a development checklist; a conversational interface and fast code generation do not establish realistic execution or positive expectancy.

# Candle-body reference levels, failed excursions, and closes beyond a zone

Source: [Dumb Hunter](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1F8yiSJB7A/). Downloaded duration: 142.566 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker builds reference areas from candle bodies, distinguishes wicks that fail beyond them from closes that accept beyond them, and studies retests across weekly and daily charts. He favors less-traversed levels over repeatedly crossed ones. The final assertion that the approach works universally is unsupported; the clip gives selected examples without a complete trade record.

## How to reproduce the stated analysis

1. Mark a candle-body zone that the speaker describes as untested. A detector still needs an exact candle-selection and zone-boundary rule, which the clip does not fully define.
2. When price attempts to extend beyond the zone but does not maintain a close there, treat a move toward the opposite reference as a scenario. A wick and a later close back inside are related failure observations with different timing.
3. When price closes beyond the area, evaluate a retest and continuation in the break direction.
4. If that accepted break is later reclaimed by a close inside, reconsider the return toward the move's origin.
5. Count pass-throughs and compare higher- and lower-timeframe levels. The speaker's example uses weekly context and daily reference areas; those frames can describe different stages at once.

## Making the terms precise

Additional implementation choices must specify body-only versus full-candle zone width, which close constitutes acceptance, how far a wick may extend, whether a retest needs a rejection bar, and when a level expires. Define a pass-through as a particular observable crossing event so a prolonged oscillation does not generate arbitrary counts. The claim that every level remains relevant indefinitely is not a validated retention policy; storing levels forever can produce an overwhelming and hindsight-sensitive set.

## Missing risk rules and validation

There is no complete entry trigger, exact stop, target-selection hierarchy, position size, timeframe reconciliation rule, or maximum holding period. A failed break can fail again, and an opposite-side target is not guaranteed. Freeze level construction before replay, delay decisions until the relevant close is known, and evaluate both accepted-break and recovery branches separately. Compare fresh and repeatedly traversed levels over later data, including levels that never generate a trade, losses, fees, and slippage. Do not choose the best historical candle body after seeing where the market subsequently reacted.

About 15–48s discusses wick failures; 48–76s compares closes beyond a level and recovery inside; 79–114s discusses timeframes and pass-throughs; 114–139s illustrates weekly versus daily context.

# Eleven claimed AI trading skills and a simulation that leaves many paths unresolved

Source: [Thomas Smith](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1FU6cKYrMk/). Downloaded duration: 40.82 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The clip advertises a third-party day-trading skill package that purportedly scans charts, tracks news and filings, times entries, and plans stops and targets. Its featured tool simulates many remaining-day paths and reports barrier-hit proportions. The source says paper trading is the default and that execution requires user agreement; these are advertised behaviors, not a security or code audit performed here.

## How to reproduce the useful planning workflow

1. Obtain the exact package, version, and supported data sources from its actual documentation before considering installation. The clip's invitation to paste a GitHub link is not a substitute for reviewing code and permissions.
2. Specify a proposed instrument, direction, entry, stop, target, position size, and time horizon.
3. Supply a clearly identified return/path model and calibration period. Without those, ten thousand simulations cannot be independently reproduced.
4. Review target-hit, stop-hit, and unresolved probabilities, along with model assumptions and execution costs.
5. Keep analysis and simulated orders separate from real execution. This review does not install the package, connect accounts, or submit trades.

## Interpreting the numerical example

The narration rounds the example to 29% target first and 25% stop first. The actual displayed table around 29s reads 29.4% target first, 25.5% stop first, and 45.1% open at the close, totaling 100%. It also shows TSLA, five-minute bars, 10,000 paths, and seed 19. Use the displayed 45.1% unresolved fraction rather than inferring exactly 46% from rounded speech. A seed helps repeat a specified model, but the model is not disclosed. Calling the proposal a coin flip omits that large unresolved category, the target/stop payoff ratio, and costs. Normalizing only the resolved cases answers a different conditional question from the probability of a profitable full trade. The clip does not disclose enough detail to calculate net expectancy.

## Limitations and validation

The simulator algorithm, training data, sampling scheme, dependence between returns, time-to-barrier treatment, gap behavior, simultaneous barrier touches, filing-publication latency, and live order controls are absent. A Monte Carlo estimate is conditional on those choices; more paths do not make an incorrect model truthful. An added research validation should compare predicted outcome frequencies with subsequent untouched observations, measure calibration and cost-adjusted returns, and test sensitivity to assumptions. The advertised installation and safety behavior require separate code inspection. A list of skills is not a complete trading strategy or proof of profitable automated operation.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 6–19s lists claimed functions; 21–30s gives simulation size and the 29/25 example; 30–38s describes paper mode, agreement before orders, and installation promotion.

# A four-step liquidity-sweep strategy around supply/demand zones, plus a stacked-zone variant

Source: [Trade Sharpe](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1Kj5JZbcpy/). Downloaded duration: 806.966 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source first identifies a closing break of structure, marks the candle area that originated the move, and then seeks an intervening obvious reference whose failure would lead price into that area. It places a limit order at the farther supply/demand zone. An advanced branch substitutes a smaller nearby zone for the obvious double-bottom/top-style reference. The advertised daily dollar income and universal market applicability are not verified outcomes.

## Basic long setup

1. Identify an uptrend and a candle that closes above the relevant prior high. The source explicitly excludes a wick-only break from its break-of-structure condition.
2. Look back to the candle immediately before the sharp move that caused that break. Box its full low-to-high range as the demand zone. The exact departure-selection rule remains qualitative.
3. Find an obvious repeated-low reference above that demand zone, such as a double/triple bottom or repeated rejection. The hypothesis is that a later downward excursion through it reaches the lower demand zone.
4. Place the illustrated buy limit at the top of the demand zone, invalidation slightly below its bottom, and an objective at 2R or, as a separately stated more aggressive choice, a prior high.
5. The favorable example sweeps the upper low reference, touches the lower demand entry, and reverses. The reversal is the outcome; a resting-limit version cannot require seeing that outcome before claiming the earlier fill.

## Basic short setup

1. Identify a closing break below the relevant prior low.
2. Mark the full candle area before the sharp decline as supply.
3. Seek an obvious repeated-high reference below that supply zone.
4. Place the illustrated sell limit at the bottom of supply, invalidation slightly above it, and an objective at prior lows in the worked short example.
5. Keep this target choice distinct from an automatic 2R exit. The source discusses both, but they are not always the same price or payoff.

## Advanced stacked-zone branch

The same sequence begins with a major structure break and its originating zone. The nearer apparent liquidity reference is then another, smaller supply/demand zone generated by a smaller swing break. For a long, a minor demand zone lies above major demand; for a short, minor supply lies below major supply. The intended trade is at the farther major zone after the nearer minor zone fails. The source classifies major versus minor through qualitative swing prominence, not a fixed numerical lookback or ratio.

The example long enters at the top of major demand with a stop below and target at prior highs. The example short enters at the bottom of major supply with a stop above and target at prior lows. Rejections at the minor zone are context; they do not guarantee its eventual break or the farther zone's defense.

## Information needed for reproducible orders

The speaker favors five- to fifteen-minute examples but leaves the instrument/feed, swing rule, departure threshold, candle selection, equality tolerance, zone spacing, freshness, maximum retests, buffer, order expiry, risk fraction, and simultaneous positions open. A resting order needs a specific placement time and cancellation policy. If its zone has already been reached before the order is placed, a later screenshot cannot establish a historical fill. A causal detector must delay the zone until its defining structure break has completed.

## Liquidity terminology and failure modes

Resting limit orders and stop-triggered market orders have different execution roles; a chart-based liquidity label is not a complete view of actual depth. The source's suggestion that counterparties always exist at every desired price is too strong during gaps or illiquid conditions. Orders can slip, a limit can remain unfilled, and price can cut through both the minor and major zones. A stop cluster or institutional motive cannot be verified solely from the repeated highs/lows.

## How to evaluate it

Freeze the basic and advanced definitions separately, retain all valid setups, and compare the major-zone entry with and without the intervening-reference filter. Model gap-aware stops, costs, unfilled orders, and ambiguous same-bar entry/exit paths. Evaluate 2R and prior-extreme targets as distinct variants on later data. Report outcomes in R and realistic account units; a fixed daily dollar income is not a consequence of a chart setup without size, frequency, loss distribution, and capital assumptions. The closing exchange-affiliate promotion is not part of the strategy and is not endorsed or acted on here.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximate chapters: 0–153s promotional liquidity explanation; 166–233s closing structure break; 235–289s originating zone; 289–365s intervening reference; 370–407s basic long orders; 451–535s short example; 565–754s stacked major/minor zones; 759–807s exchange-affiliate promotion.

Reviewed using: manual reading of the complete machine transcript in timestamped sections, supported by recognized screen text; the generic repost caption does not define the method.

# A three-loss stopping rule as a guard against revenge trading

Source: [WOZ Capital](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EWhW8wisH/). Downloaded duration: 23.2 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker proposes ending trading after three losing trades to interrupt attempts to win back losses impulsively. The described benefit is limiting a behavioral escalation, not improving the underlying signal's accuracy. The example contrast between a smaller loss and a much larger bad day is illustrative, not a verified account history or a prescribed monetary budget.

## How to implement the process rule

1. Decide before a session what counts as a losing trade and what resets the counter. The narration says three losing trades but does not settle whether it means consecutive losses or cumulative losses in a day.
2. Track completed outcomes under that fixed definition, including fees if the policy is based on net P&L.
3. Once the declared threshold is reached, halt new discretionary entries for the predefined cooling-off period.
4. Keep any existing position under its previously defined risk and exit policy. Stopping new entries and abruptly liquidating every position are separate actions; the video does not specify the latter.
5. Review decisions later, rather than increasing size or creating a new setup solely to recover the day's money.

## Operational details the source leaves open

A reproducible policy needs session boundaries, partial-exit treatment, break-even classification, multiple-account handling, whether simultaneous trades count separately, how failed or canceled orders are treated, and the restart condition. The number three is the speaker's suggestion, not a statistically demonstrated universal optimum. A daily monetary loss limit is another possible policy but is not equivalent to a trade-count limit.

## How to evaluate it

Additional research choices could compare the same frozen strategy with and without a new-entry halt under several prespecified thresholds. Preserve trades that the halt would reject, include days where a later valid trade would have recovered losses, and measure both drawdown reduction and missed opportunity. Separately record whether the rule reduces off-plan decisions. A compliant losing session can remain a normal strategy outcome, while a profitable revenge trade can still violate the plan. This clip provides a behavioral constraint; it gives no market entry, target, stop, or position-sizing strategy.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The opening 6s gives the three-loss suggestion; approximately 6–19s describes escalating recovery attempts; the closing seconds emphasize avoiding revenge trading.

# Five smart-money terminology slides: gaps, sweeps, swings, structure breaks, and order blocks

Source: [Cloud Cabin Quantum AI](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1HpmPA7JbF/). Downloaded duration: 49.922 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This is a visual glossary. It introduces fair-value gaps, liquidity sweeps, higher-high/higher-low structure, breaks of structure, and order blocks. It does not combine them into a fully defined entry-and-exit system. Its institutional language is an interpretation of chart behavior rather than evidence identifying specific market participants.

## How to annotate the illustrated concepts

1. For the gap slide, inspect the three-bar price geometry and mark the unoverlapped outer-wick region rather than assuming every strong candle creates the same structure. The source describes an imbalance but supplies no numerical minimum.
2. For the sweep slide, mark a known high or low, the excursion through it, and the subsequent rejection. A break without recovery is a different observable path.
3. For trend structure, label confirmed swing highs and lows and compare their order.
4. For a structure break, mark which earlier swing is exceeded and when the chosen break condition becomes known. The source does not specify wick versus close.
5. For an order block, mark the candle area preceding the strong move shown by the slide. The source's broad definition does not settle body versus full range, displacement requirements, or subsequent validity.

## Turning a glossary into a usable specification

Additional research rules must define pivot confirmation, gap calculation, sweep recovery, displacement strength, zone boundaries, retest eligibility, and expiry. Each object should have both a price area and an availability timestamp. A gap that requires a third candle is not known when the middle candle begins; a confirmed pivot may require later bars. Preserve those delays in replay.

## Limitations and evaluation

No instrument, timeframe, session, setup sequence, entry, stop, target, size, or statistical result is established. A zone can be crossed, an apparent sweep can resume its initial direction, and repeated swing labeling can be sensitive to arbitrary lookback choices. If researching a combined method, first write its full sequence, then compare the contribution of each condition on later data. The glossary itself should not be counted as an executable strategy, and its favorable diagrams cannot establish that a gap must fill or that an order-block revisit must reverse.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Around 6s the gap slide is visible; 12–19s covers sweeps; 25s shows higher swings; 31–38s shows a structure break; 44–50s defines and illustrates an order-block area.

# Wait for a liquidity reaction, bullish displacement, and an order-block pullback

Source: [Hsbed Shx](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1KTP5meFz7/). Downloaded duration: 44.58 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The lesson avoids an entry in the middle of an undefined area, waits for a reaction at a liquidity reference, observes a bullish expansion, and then enters on a return to the last bearish candle before that expansion. The stop is described as slightly beneath that candle area. The fuel and supercar comparison is an analogy, not a measurable explanation of actual order flow.

## How to reproduce the described long sequence

1. Mark a specific prior reference where a liquidity interaction will be observed. The clip does not fully define which high or low qualifies.
2. Wait for price to reach that reference and react; do not predict direction merely because the level exists.
3. Identify the strong bullish breakout that the speaker treats as directional evidence.
4. Mark the last bearish candle before the expansion as the example order block. Define its body/full-range boundaries independently.
5. Wait for price to pull back into that area rather than buying the expansion immediately.
6. Use the stated invalidation beneath the order-block area with an explicit buffer. The video supplies no exact target, trailing method, size, or time exit.

## Confirmation and assumptions

The speaker calls the pullback confirmation, but a touch and a confirmed rejection are different events. A research implementation must choose whether to use a resting limit, a completed rejection bar, or another causal trigger. It also needs a displacement threshold, a rule for selecting the preceding bearish candle, and a maximum number of bars or retests before expiry. Those choices materially change fills and risk and are not established in the narration.

## Failure modes and validation

An expansion can fail, a retest can trade straight through the selected candle, and the move can continue without giving any pullback entry. A liquidity metaphor does not guarantee future acceleration. Freeze level and zone selection, timestamp when the expansion becomes confirmed, and log filled, unfilled, failed, and expired candidates. Compare the same order-block entry with and without the initial location and expansion conditions using later data and costs. Without a defined exit, the attractive final move cannot be converted into a reproducible return series.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximately 0–23s gives the waiting/location narrative; 24–29s establishes bullish expansion; 29–44s describes the return to the last bearish candle and invalidation below it.

# Personal trading preferences: written rules, one main setup, and a bounded session

Source: [James A. Strong](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1FSGwCHYmT/). Downloaded duration: 106.068 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker answers a series of either-or questions. He prefers price action, a fifteen-minute view over a one-minute view, one primary strategy, process rules before entry techniques, written decisions over intuition, planned targets, a personal account, and a single session. He also favors keeping other employment while learning. These are individual preferences, not a demonstrated optimal plan or a complete strategy.

## How to translate the useful process advice

1. Select one explicitly documented setup for a controlled study instead of changing among loosely defined methods after each loss.
2. Write its eligibility, entry, invalidation, target, size, and stop-trading conditions before replay or paper practice.
3. Choose a session and timeframe that match the data and execution model being studied. The video's fifteen-minute preference is not evidence that every one-minute strategy is inferior.
4. Track whether exits follow the selected policy. A fixed target, partial exit, and trail are different policies; choose and test one rather than treating discretionary early profit-taking as an invisible exception.
5. Record process adherence separately from profit so a lucky deviation does not become an undocumented strategy change.

## Claims that require qualification

The claim that all indicators are merely lagging price ignores tools that also use volume, order-book, options, or external inputs. Even a price-derived indicator can be useful as a precisely defined transformation; its usefulness requires testing. The suggestion that futures and foreign exchange are essentially identical also understates differences in contract terms, trading venue, settlement, margin, quotation, and execution. The claim that one strategy will produce large profits is not established by the preference list.

## What is missing and how to evaluate it

No actual entry pattern, instrument, indicator settings, stop formula, target distance, sizing, or measured outcomes are supplied. A personal account and a funded-account arrangement also impose different constraints; the clip's preference cannot determine suitability for a reader. To study the operational ideas, hold the strategy fixed and compare declared session or exit variants on later data, including missed trades, costs, and time demands. The employment discussion is commentary on pressure and lifestyle, not a financial plan established by the video.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 0–29s discusses tools, markets, timeframe, and focus; 29–58s emphasizes process and written rules; 58–75s covers targets; 75–91s covers account/session preferences; 91–106s discusses learning alongside employment.

# Fair-value gaps: three-bar geometry, midpoint entries, and invalidation ambiguities

Source: [The Xau Cartel](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1E25NS4grY/). Downloaded duration: 153.2 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The lesson defines a three-candle fair-value gap, distinguishes bullish, bearish, and invalidated/inverse interpretations, and proposes waiting for a retracement instead of chasing the expansion. It favors a stronger move associated with a sweep and structure break, plus alignment with trend. The caption correctly qualifies that not every gap fills; the magnet analogy is not a certainty.

## How to identify and use the demonstrated bullish case

1. Label three consecutive completed bars. A bullish wick gap exists when the first bar's high is below the third bar's low; mark that interval. The middle bar's movement traverses the area, so this is an outer-bar overlap condition rather than proof that nothing traded there.
2. Examine whether the expansion is meaningful relative to context and whether the source's sweep/structure/trend conditions have been met. Numerical strength thresholds are not supplied.
3. Mark the gap on the higher timeframe being studied. The exact higher timeframe is not specified.
4. Wait for a return to the area. The speaker offers entry around its midpoint or after a fifteen-minute rejection. These are alternative execution conventions, not equivalent fills.
5. Use a recent high as the illustrated long objective. Define the actual stop and execution timing before testing.

## Two corrections and an unresolved stop rule

The narration suggests that only buyers traded during the gap. Every executed trade has both a buyer and seller; candle geometry cannot establish that counterparties were absent. It can describe rapid movement without showing all orders.

The detailed entry section says to place the stop beneath the first candle, while the recap says beyond the gap. Those are not necessarily the same price: the first candle's low can lie well below the gap's lower boundary at its high. Preserve the difference as an unresolved choice instead of quietly selecting whichever produces the better result.

## Additional rules and evaluation

A detector needs a minimum gap size, displacement measure, swing/break definition, freshness criterion, trend filter, body-versus-wick invalidation convention, expiry, partial-fill policy, buffer, size, and exit timing. A close through the gap may invalidate the original direction, but an inverse trade still requires its own trigger. Price may never revisit the midpoint, fill the entire area and continue against the setup, or reach the intended target before an executable entry. Test every eligible gap using only information available after the third bar completes. Compare midpoint-limit and confirmed-rejection branches separately on later data, including unfilled orders and costs. Confluence with an order block is another condition to test, not proof that the setup must work.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

# An Elliott-style A–B–C–D–E triangle and a measured breakout guide

Source: [bhsledu](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1RLStdErAh/). Downloaded duration: 171.5 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The lesson treats a triangle as a five-leg corrective structure labeled A through E, with smaller three-part subdivisions inside each leg. It contrasts contracting and expanding forms, locates the pattern within the presented Elliott-wave counting framework, and suggests waiting for a break rather than trading every internal oscillation. This is a model for labeling structure, not proof that the next move must follow the drawing.

## How to annotate the proposed pattern

1. Identify the alternating A–B–C–D–E legs and draw boundaries through their alternating extremes. The source says each corrective leg subdivides into three; no objective algorithm for those subdivisions is supplied.
2. For a contracting version, inspect whether the boundaries converge and later alternating extremes stay within the relevant earlier extremes.
3. Classify the visible shape as symmetrical, rising-support/flat-resistance, or falling-resistance/flat-support.
4. Keep expanding versions separate: their swings grow rather than contract. The video notes that these are less common within its framework, without supplying data.
5. Relate the triangle to the larger count. The source places it in a fourth wave, B wave, or the final portion of a complex correction, and excludes a second-wave label under the rules it teaches.

## The trading idea and open decisions

The speaker avoids internal chop, waits for the E leg to finish and the boundary to break, and uses the triangle's widest price span as a target guide. If treated as a fourth-wave correction, the following thrust is labeled a fifth wave, after which the source expects the larger move to be vulnerable. These are framework-dependent scenarios, not guaranteed market events.

An implementation still needs a definition of E completion, closing-versus-wick breakout, permissible overshoot, entry order, stop location, projection origin, time limit, size, and what invalidates the larger wave count. The widest span alone does not settle those details.

## A causal evaluation

Additional research choices should freeze pivot recognition and boundary fitting before the breakout. Do not relabel an unsuccessful triangle as another correction only after seeing it fail while excluding it from results. Compare the measured objective with the actual entry/stop distance and costs, and include false breaks, no-break expiries, and expanding candidates separately. Nested three-part counts can be subjective and sensitive to timeframe. The claim that a triangle cannot be wave two is a rule of the presented counting system; it does not mean a geometric triangle cannot physically appear during a move that someone had previously called a second pullback.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 15–45s introduces five corrective legs and subdivisions; 50–75s gives larger-count placement; 81–124s distinguishes triangle forms; 127–156s describes waiting for E, the break, and the widest-span objective guide.

# Drop-base-rally demand zone: wait for the first return instead of chasing

Source: [CreedFx](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1FugYKakuM/). Downloaded duration: 28.233 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source marks a short pause between a decline and a strong upward departure as a demand zone. It then waits for price to revisit that zone, places a long within it, invalidates beneath the base, and uses the previous high as an objective. The term demand is an interpretation of a chart pattern; the bars do not reveal all unfilled institutional buy orders.

## How to reproduce the four-step example

1. Find a decline followed by a compact pause and then a stronger rally. The source calls the pause the base.
2. Box that base and keep its boundaries fixed. The source does not specify whether the box includes full wicks, bodies only, or a subset of base candles.
3. Wait for a return to a fresh zone. The word fresh suggests a zone not already retested, but the exact counting and expiration rule must be defined.
4. Evaluate a buy in the box, with invalidation below it and the last high as the stated target. The clip does not say whether the entry is a resting limit or requires a new rejection candle.

## How to make it reproducible

Additional choices include the maximum number of base bars, allowable base width, minimum departure distance, how the preceding decline is recognized, whether a structure break is required, and how long a zone persists. A demand zone cannot be recognized from the pause alone when the subsequent rally is part of its definition. Timestamp its eligibility only after the declared departure condition becomes known. Keep its original boundary and first-return status in the research record.

## Risk arithmetic and limitations

As an added example, an entry at 100 with invalidation at 98 and a target at 105 offers 2.5R before costs. A different point inside the same zone can materially change that ratio. The clip supplies no numerical buffer, size, timeframe, instrument, session, or time exit, and its favorable target-hit animation is not a full performance sample. A fresh zone can fail on its first return, a shallow pullback can miss the order, or the rally can have already consumed the target opportunity.

## How to evaluate it

Freeze zone construction and entry timing, then record every eligible return, unfilled order, stop, and target on later data. Compare a touch entry with a separately defined rejection-confirmed entry using realistic spreads and slippage. A long-term zone archive must avoid repainting the base after observing later reactions. The course-launch date in the promotional ending is not part of the trading specification and was not independently verified.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The first 17s describes the entire four-step process; the saved caption states the same sequence. The remainder promotes a course and shows a favorable outcome rather than adding risk or test rules.

# A bearish structure shift followed by an order-block and gap retest

Source: [MSI Trading Lab](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/14uvxxDNTgq/). Downloaded duration: 13.466 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The animation shows an upward move giving way to a bearish structural break, marks a zone above price labeled as an order block plus gap, and illustrates a short on a return toward that zone. The stated objective is lower-side liquidity. The diagram's Trade With Jade branding differs from the list's page label; both are retained as source observations rather than assuming who originally created the material.

## How to reproduce the visible sequence

1. Mark the preceding swing structure and the support whose break constitutes the bearish shift. The source names the shift but supplies no numerical swing rule.
2. After the downward move, box the highlighted overhead candle area and associated gap as shown. The animation does not settle every boundary-selection convention.
3. Wait for price to recover toward the overhead zone.
4. The illustrated entry is short from that area. The position overlay places invalidation above the zone.
5. Use the chosen low-side reference as the objective. The animation adjusts the target overlay before revealing the decline, so the precise target-selection rule is not established by the rectangle alone.

## Rules required before implementation

Additional choices include completed-bar confirmation of the structure break, how the last bullish candle is selected, the gap geometry and minimum size, entry at edge versus midpoint, a rejection requirement, stop buffer, which prior low is the target, size, and expiry. A box identified because of a later strong decline becomes available only after that decline satisfies the declared confirmation rule. A retrospective short marker at a perfect retest is not evidence that an order existed there in real time.

## Failure cases and evaluation

The recovery can cross the entire zone, the move can continue down without retesting it, or the target can be reached before the intended order fills. A prior low is a chart reference, not a directly observed inventory of stop orders. Test all qualifying shift-and-retest sequences with causal zone availability, include failed and unfilled examples, and compare the combined zone/gap condition with each component separately on later data. The clip contains no instrument, timeframe, risk fraction, or performance sample, so it should be treated as a schematic setup rather than a complete measured system.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 1–4s introduces the structure shift and marks the zone; 4–7s identifies liquidity and the entry area; 8–13s adds the short overlay, extends the objective, and reveals a favorable decline.

# Four volume-profile shapes as context, with the day's midpoint kept separate from the profile's center

Source: [Peteonthebid](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1G3a8Pg4br/). Downloaded duration: 86.169 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker classifies a profile as D-shaped, P-shaped, b-shaped, or thin and associates those shapes with balance or directional movement. He explicitly says a profile cannot predict the next move or time an entry. A volume profile groups activity by price, so this is context analysis rather than a complete trading trigger.

## How to read the four shapes

1. A D-like distribution has much of its activity near the center and suggests a more balanced rotation; after a directional move it may also reflect a pause.
2. A P-like distribution concentrates activity higher in the range with a lower tail. The speaker adds a close above the day's price-range midpoint before accepting the bullish interpretation.
3. A b-like distribution concentrates activity lower with an upper tail. He adds a close beneath that midpoint before accepting the bearish interpretation.
4. A thin distribution spreads less accumulated activity across a faster price move. The speaker avoids fading that movement and notes possible rapid traversal of a low-volume area on a later return.

## Configuration needed to reproduce a profile

The source does not give the instrument, session window, bin size, data granularity, volume measure, or an objective shape classifier. Additional research choices must specify all of those. The midpoint condition means (session high + session low)/2 under a declared session, not necessarily the point of control, VWAP, or center of a value area. These different prices must not be silently substituted for each other. Exact volume at price cannot be recovered from a daily OHLCV bar alone.

## Causal timing and interpretation limits

A completed day's profile and final high/low are unavailable earlier that day. A study using the final shape to justify an early-session entry would look ahead. Either use a completed prior-session profile or explicitly use a developing profile whose history is stored as it evolves. Shape does not prove participant identity, inventory, or future direction. The source's claim of one side being completely in control should be understood as a directional interpretation rather than direct order-book evidence.

## How to evaluate it

Freeze a shape rule and profile settings, then test a separate entry system with and without the contextual condition on later dates. Include profiles that change classification intraday and distinguish descriptive accuracy from net trading returns. The lesson supplies no stop, target, position size, or exit rule. A trend can reverse even with a thin profile, and a balanced profile can break into a new trend; neither the never-fade preference nor a rotation expectation is guaranteed.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximately 11–23s covers D; 23–37s covers P and its midpoint filter; 37–51s covers b and the opposite filter; 52–68s covers thin profiles; 69–79s explicitly limits prediction and entry timing.
