# A fifteen-minute structural reversal into a Fibonacci-marked long point of interest

Source: [SMC GOLD](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1BWTnGUydj/). Downloaded duration: 16.8 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The video starts with an earlier bearish structure/zone annotation, then shows low-side activity, a subsequent bullish structural change, and a long from a lower point of interest toward an overhead reference. The narration names structure breaks, change of character, and Fibonacci tools. The final objective is described as buy-side liquidity. Despite the page name, the chart's displayed quotation alone does not establish that the instrument is gold.

## How to reproduce the visible long scenario

1. Mark the prior bearish structure and the earlier low-side reference. Keep that earlier short illustration separate from the later bullish trade.
2. Wait for the structural recovery labeled change of character and a further break in the new direction. The source does not formalize pivot or closing-bar rules.
3. Draw the displayed Fibonacci retracement over the chosen swing and identify the marked point-of-interest area below the recovery. Several numerical labels are small and change as the drawing is edited; no universal retracement ratio is established confidently here.
4. Wait for a return to that area and evaluate the long illustrated by the second position overlay.
5. The overlay places invalidation below the point of interest and projects an objective at a prior overhead high. Exact buffer and entry trigger are not supplied.

## What must be specified independently

The narration says the analysis is fifteen-minute, but leaves the instrument, swing-selection algorithm, Fibonacci anchor timestamps, retracement tolerance, point-of-interest geometry, gap/order-block requirement, entry order, size, expiry, and risk policy open. A chart-editing sequence can move anchors as context changes; a backtest must preserve which anchor pair was actually known at each decision rather than borrowing the final attractive drawing.

## Failure modes and evaluation

An apparent structural recovery can fail and resume the decline. The retracement may not reach the point of interest, may cross it without support, or may occur only after the target has been reached. Define the exact recovery and entry sequence before replay, timestamp when each pivot and zone becomes eligible, and test all candidates with costs on later data. Compare the structural rule with and without the chosen retracement filter. The clip's favorable final rally and high reward/risk rectangle are examples; they do not establish a reproducible win rate or that the Fibonacci tool predicted the reversal.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The opening frames show the earlier bearish map; around 5–7s the new structural labels and Fibonacci drawing appear; 9–12s marks the long point of interest and position overlay; 14–17s reveals the favorable overhead move.

# RSI double rejection: trendline location, a 50-line trigger, and higher-timeframe agreement

Source: [Trade Empire](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/18gtftgH79/). Downloaded duration: 525.683 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The tutorial replaces an unconditional 30/70 reversal interpretation with trend-following pullbacks. It combines rejection of a price trendline, rejection in a middle RSI band, a return across RSI 50, and agreement on one-hour/four-hour RSI. The worked chart is fifteen-minute. The author calls this double rejection because price location and momentum turn together.

## Configuration

Use RSI and disable its RSI-based moving-average overlay, as the speaker does. The source says to retain other defaults but does not explicitly pin every numerical input in the narration; save the actual period, source, smoothing, and platform/script version rather than assuming defaults never change. The decision frames are fifteen-minute for the example entry, with one-hour and four-hour context.

## Four-rule short branch

1. In an established downtrend, draw a falling line through prior lower highs and wait for price to touch it during a rally.
2. Require a bearish candle showing rejection: the source accepts a strong downward body from the line or an upper-wick rejection.
3. Require RSI to have recovered into 50–60, turned down, and returned beneath 50.
4. Require both one-hour and four-hour RSI to be below 50. They need not be crossing 50 on the same bar.
5. Invalidate above the rejection candle's high and use the author's stated fixed objective of 1.5R. His illustrations of a later 6R excursion do not change that fixed-exit result.

## Long branch and setup invalidation

For longs, the line joins higher lows; price touches it and produces a bullish rejection. RSI pulls into 40–50, turns upward, and crosses back above 50, while both higher-frame values are above 50. The stop is beneath the rejection candle's low and the stated objective remains 1.5R.

The short setup is rejected if a candle closes above its trendline or RSI closes above 60. The long setup is rejected after a close beneath its line or RSI beneath 40. The source permits a wick through the line when the closing reaction still satisfies the setup. It does not fully specify whether these invalidation conditions also force early exits after entry or only disqualify a candidate.

## How to make it reproducible

Additional choices must define trendline construction, pivot delay, minimum touches, line tolerance, allowable time between RSI zone visit and crossing, candle geometry, stop buffer, order type, expiry, and size. Use only higher-timeframe values already observable at the entry timestamp. A retrospective one-hour/four-hour final close cannot approve an earlier fifteen-minute order inside that unfinished bar. If confirmation is based on a completed rejection candle, use an executable later-price convention rather than retroactively filling at the already-known close.

## Failure modes and validation

A trendline can break, RSI can remain in a new regime, and a higher-frame filter can lag the reversal. RSI 50 describes its calculation's balance, not direct proof of who owns market inventory. Test all qualifying pullbacks, include invalid and expired cases, and compare price-only, RSI-only, and combined variants on later data with costs. The selected winning shorts are examples; the clip supplies no complete net-performance report, and no signal is guaranteed.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 80–99s changes the overlay; 117–209s discusses higher-timeframe disagreement; 237–338s introduces middle-band trend pullbacks; 347–463s gives the exact short rules and invalidation; 463–511s mirrors them for longs.

# Rolling Z-score: three applications, explicit settings, and limits of the probability claims

Source: [Trade Empire](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/19ovVRNftK/). Downloaded duration: 369.08 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source demonstrates Rolling Z Score Trend by QuantAlgo on a four-hour EUR/USD example. It describes a standardized price-deviation line, momentum columns, and applications to reversion, divergence, and trend context. Standardization is a calculation, not certainty about future extremes or reversal probabilities. The video's scientific and universal-accuracy framing overstates what those calculations establish.

## Baseline and market-specific settings stated

The general setup uses lookback 50, EMA smoothing 3, an enabled information table, and visible momentum columns. General extreme references are +2 and -2. Later suggestions are major FX lookback 60/smoothing 3/extremes ±1.8; crypto lookback 30/extremes ±2.5; gold lookback 40/extremes ±2; and SPY/QQQ lookback 50/extremes ±1.6. These are settings proposed by the source, not validated optimal parameters. Smoothing is not restated for every later row, so its carryover should be recorded as an assumption if used.

## Application 1: mean reversion

Wait for the standardized reading to exceed the selected positive/negative threshold, then require momentum columns to turn against the extension: red above the positive extreme for the illustrated short, green below the negative extreme for a long. The speaker describes a stop around a 2.5-Z boundary and a first objective at zero.

A broker price stop cannot be set directly in oscillator units. A reproducible version needs either a monitored indicator-exit rule or an explicitly frozen conversion using the mean and scale known at entry. The source does not settle the sign/buffer for every branch, whether zero is a moving target, or whether an intrabar value or completed-bar value triggers an exit.

## Applications 2 and 3

For divergence, compare new price extremes with weaker Z-score peaks/troughs and momentum columns. The transcript labels a lower-price-low/higher-Z-low case bearish, although that geometry is normally the bullish warning; the directional wording needs checking rather than being copied as a short rule. No complete divergence entry/exit policy is supplied.

For trend context, the source uses sustained Z above +1 with positive columns as an upward-strength condition. It also proposes checking one-hour and four-hour readings for alignment. That is a separate trend-following application; simultaneously treating every positive extreme as a mandatory short would contradict it without a regime rule.

## What the statistics do and do not say

A conventional rolling Z-score is (price minus rolling mean) divided by rolling standard deviation, subject to the actual script's source and smoothing. Zero variance needs an explicit handling rule. A two-sided ±2 probability near 5% requires a suitable normal-distribution model; rolling financial prices and smoothed, overlapping scores are not automatically independent standard-normal draws. Even a correctly estimated tail probability is not the chance that the next trade reverses profitably. Claims of a 10–15-bar forecasting advantage and optimal asset presets are not backed by supplied tests.

## How to evaluate it

Freeze the script/version, variance convention, smoothing, signal timing, regime selection, stop conversion, size, and expiry. Compare threshold and lookback variants on training data and report only subsequent evaluation outcomes. Assess reversion and trend branches separately, include persistence beyond extremes, costs, and missing fills, and use only completed higher-frame values. A long trend can remain statistically extended and a moving mean can shift away from the proposed target.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximate chapters: 31–89s indicator and components; 93–127s baseline setup; 149–203s reversion; 204–244s divergence; 246–282s trend/timeframe context; 304–367s market presets.

Reviewed using: manual reading of the complete machine transcript and timestamped recognized chart text; no indicator source-code audit was performed.

[Downloaded video](video.mp4) · [Page description](video.description) · [Timestamped machine transcript](transcript.txt) · [Sampled frames](frames/contact-sheet.jpg) · [Metadata](video.info.json) · [Integrity record](source.json)

Machine transcripts may misrecognize names, numbers, and music. Settings and claims that could not be established are identified above. Any implementation examples added in this writeup are research choices, not extra rules attributed to the video.

# Step Channel Momentum Trend: pivot midpoint, ATR bands, and sustained color states

Source: [Trade Empire](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1A14HuVYRn/). Downloaded duration: 290.806 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source demonstrates Step Channel Momentum Trend by ChartPrime, using a fifteen-minute GBP/JPY example. A step-like center based on confirmed pivot high/low information is surrounded by ATR-based bands. Price beyond the upper band is shown green, beneath the lower band red, and between them orange. These colors describe a calculated state, not direct observation of future momentum.

## Baseline setup and proposed presets

The general inputs are pivot length 10, ATR period 200, and multiplier 0.6. Body, wick, and border coloring are enabled, along with a current-state label. Later presets are scalping on one- to five-minute charts with pivot 5, ATR 100, multiplier 0.4; daily swing analysis with pivot 20, ATR 300, multiplier 0.8; major FX pivot 12/multiplier 0.5; crypto pivot 8/multiplier 0.3; and stocks pivot 15/multiplier 0.7. The source does not restate an ATR period for every asset row. All are source suggestions, not verified optimum settings.

## How to follow the demonstrated state logic

1. Wait for price to move beyond a band and generate the corresponding color.
2. Do not enter on the first colored candle in the main example; the speaker waits for two or three consecutive green candles for a long or red candles for a short. Choosing exactly two versus three is an unresolved implementation setting.
3. Treat the structural center as a contextual support/resistance reference rather than a fully stated initial stop.
4. For longs, the first orange after green is described as a reason to take profit or tighten risk; a red transition is described as an immediate exit.
5. For shorts, orange after red warns of fading movement. The source does not fully specify the symmetric opposite-color rule, trailing distance, or initial protective stop.

## Why confirmed pivots do not eliminate lag

The described midpoint averages the latest confirmed high and low. A confirmed pivot generally needs later observations under its chosen rule, so the claim of eliminating lag entirely is not established. The actual availability time matters more than where the line is visually drawn. The code shown around 249s explicitly calculates `avg = math.avg(p_h, p_l)`, `atr = ta.atr(100) * mult`, `upper = avg + atr`, and `lower = avg - atr`. This corroborates the band formula and the narrated scalping ATR period of 100; it does not establish that the separate 200/300-period presets were actually applied. The visible `label.new(bar_index-len, ...)` also places pivot labels on earlier bars, so their display position is not their detection time. The complete pivot/state code is still needed to reproduce every colored candle.

## Missing rules and evaluation

Entry timing, choice of two/three bars, first stop, sizing, orange-state action, trail calculation, costs, and expiry remain open. Near a boundary, colors can alternate and produce repeated poor entries; wider bands can delay a move and narrower ones can increase churn. Freeze the version and parameters, record states as known on each completed bar, and test sustained-state entries with realistic later-price fills. Compare presets on genuinely later data rather than calling the most attractive historical coloring accurate. The claim of testing over 500 indicators is not a supplied reproducible comparison.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 25–79s explains the indicator; 98–144s gives baseline inputs; 147–181s gives sustained-state entries; 191–216s discusses exits; 236–290s lists presets.

# Rally-base-drop sequence labels: reversal and continuation branches with different timing

Source: [Trade Empire](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1DzAZY7zky/). Downloaded duration: 410.853 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source demonstrates a LuxAlgo rally/base/drop sequence indicator on a one-hour EUR/USD example. It groups two-or-more same-direction candles with an intervening base and labels RBD, DBR, RBR, or DBD. It then separates reversals at key areas from continuation after a structural change. The exact code is not supplied, so the natural-language sequence description is not a full reconstruction of the indicator.

## Configuration and a repainting distinction

Enable only RBD/DBR when studying the source's reversal branch and only RBR/DBD for its continuation branch. The display offers full historical coloring, coloring on detection, or labels without color; label size is cosmetic. The speaker explicitly says full coloring can paint the first candle of a sequence historically, while detection coloring begins when the sequence is recognized, described as the second directional candle. A study must use that actual detection time, not treat the first historically recolored bar as a signal known then.

## Reversal branch

At resistance, wait for rally, base, then drop and the RBD label. The source permits entry when the label appears or after an added bearish structural confirmation. Invalidation is above the resistance/sequence extreme, with a stated 1.5R objective or the next major support in the short example. At support, the DBR mirror is used for a long, with invalidation below support and a 1.5R example objective. Immediate and structure-confirmed entries are distinct variants and should not be blended retrospectively.

## Continuation branch

First identify a bullish or bearish structural change. Then use RBR for upward continuation or DBD for downward continuation, entering on the detected sequence before waiting for an additional later structure break. The narration suggests optional RSI/stochastic timing but gives no complete settings for those tools. It specifically mentions RSI above 50 in the bearish discussion; that unusual condition is not silently changed to below 50 here. Its role and timing need clarification before implementation. The continuation branch's full stop/target rules are not as clearly specified as the reversal branch.

## Market suggestions and contradictions

The source suggests default inputs and London/New York overlap observation for FX; five-minute to one-hour crypto charts; daily stocks for swing studies and five-minute stocks for intraday; and fifteen-minute to one-hour futures charts. It gives no controlled evidence that these are optimal. A later crypto sentence calls RBR and DBR continuation patterns, conflicting with the earlier definition that continuation is RBR and DBD. Preserve the original four-pattern definitions and flag that mismatch rather than merging DBR into both branches without a rule.

## How to evaluate it

Additional choices must define the exact script version, base classification, structure algorithm, key-zone construction, detection-close convention, order type, buffer, size, expiry, and exits. Freeze whether optional confirmations are enabled. Record detection events as they occur, include false labels and unfilled entries, and compare each branch on later data with costs. Historical coloring can make the first part of a completed pattern appear obvious; it does not establish that the label was available before the confirming candles. The narrative's claims about institutional accumulation/distribution are interpretations, not direct evidence from these candle tags.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Approximate chapters: 21–116s sequence definitions; 140–202s display settings and detection delay; 209–284s reversals; 284–347s continuation; 364–411s asset/timeframe suggestions.

Reviewed using: manual reading of the complete machine transcript and timestamped recognized chart text; generic repost caption is unrelated to implementation.

# Fifteen-minute demand context refined to a five-minute point of interest

Source: [CariosFx](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1CrBbDTTEk/). Downloaded duration: 29.233 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The animation identifies an earlier bullish structure break, marks a lower higher-timeframe point of interest, and follows a decline toward it. It then switches from a fifteen-minute label to five-minute detail, shows an inducement/inner reference and an upward structural recovery, and illustrates a long from a refined lower zone toward prior highs. The brief narration names the objects but does not fully formalize their detection.

## How to reproduce the visible scenario

1. On the example fifteen-minute view, mark the known swing break and the demand-origin area before the earlier upward move.
2. Wait for price to return toward that higher-timeframe area rather than buying in the middle of the preceding advance.
3. Inspect five-minute structure inside the area. The illustration marks an internal inducement reference and a recovery through a nearer swing.
4. Mark the smaller point of interest shown within the broader zone and evaluate the illustrated long from that location.
5. The position overlay invalidates below the refined zone and targets the overhead high-side reference. Exact prices, order type, and trigger are not supplied.

## What is required for a causal rule

Define the fifteen-minute pivot and break condition, zone boundaries, five-minute internal reference, recovery confirmation, entry depth, stop buffer, target selection, maximum wait, and size. A higher-timeframe zone whose existence depends on a later break is not available before that break completes. Likewise, a refined zone cannot be selected because it later gave the cleanest bounce. If the entry depends on the five-minute recovery, the order must be placed only after that recovery becomes known.

## Failure cases and evaluation

The broad zone can fail, a refined zone can be too narrow for spread/noise, or the rally can leave without retesting the intended order. Inducement and liquidity labels do not prove the location of actual stop orders. Compare the same broader-zone setup with and without the five-minute refinement on later data. Include fills missed by the narrower entry, invalidations, costs, and realistic timing. The final high-reaching rally is a selected illustration, not a complete statistical record or proof that every higher-timeframe zone deserves a long.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The first 8s shows the fifteen-minute context and return; around 12s the chart is labeled five-minute; 16–21s adds the internal reference and trade overlay; 25–29s reveals the favorable rally toward the overhead reference.

# A five-minute high-break trigger after an apparent selling-exhaustion setup

Source: [G Street Trades](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/19giFToCHs/). Downloaded duration: 58.77 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker distinguishes where a mean-reversion opportunity might occur from the event that makes an entry eligible. A downward extension, a sweep, and an apparent exhaustion candle can still be followed by further decline. His additional long-side trigger is a five-minute candle exceeding the prior candle's high, ideally the exhaustion candle's high. The claimed 80% win rate and the caption's 40-to-80 comparison are not supported by a supplied trade sample.

## How to follow the described long setup

1. Identify the source’s proposed reversion context: acceleration away from a mean, an excursion through a reference, and an exhaustion candidate. The diagram labels the reference Key Level on 4HR, while the trigger is on five-minute candles. The clip does not define the mean, the four-hour level-selection rule, or numerical acceleration/exhaustion thresholds.
2. Wait instead of buying solely because the exhaustion candidate begins to form.
3. On the five-minute chart, require a later bar to break the previous bar's high, preferably the selected exhaustion bar's high.
4. Treat that break as the proposed trigger and record when it becomes observable. The source says break, not necessarily a completed close above, so an intrabar trigger and close-confirmed trigger must be kept as distinct implementation choices.
5. Define protective risk and an exit objective separately; the clip does not supply them.

## Rules still missing

A reproducible version needs the mean calculation, extension threshold, sweep definition, exhaustion geometry, exactly which prior candle is referenced, maximum waiting period, entry buffer/order type, stop, target, position size, and session. If the high is not broken, the illustrated losing example remains ineligible under this filter. A later high break after the original context has expired should not automatically resurrect a stale setup.

## Failure modes and evaluation

A high break can occur during a brief countertrend bounce before another decline. Waiting for it can avoid some premature entries but can also worsen price and reward/risk or miss a fast reversal. Test the same base setup with and without the trigger on later data, preserving every candidate and costs. Compare entry timing, missed moves, drawdown, and net expectancy rather than relying only on win rate. Any short-side mirror is a separate extension; the clip's fully described confirmation is for the illustrated long case.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 7–23s defines the setup-versus-trigger problem; 24–37s shows a failed early entry without a high break; 38–54s gives the five-minute confirmation.

# Supply-zone retests explained through a remaining-order hypothesis

Source: [Geek's Trading Edge](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EbsUQZd5a/). Downloaded duration: 23.242 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker describes a sharp decline from a supply area and proposes that unfilled sell interest may remain there, producing another downward reaction when price returns. This is a conceptual explanation for watching an earlier origin zone. A historical price chart cannot establish that particular orders still exist, their sizes, or that they will execute on a later visit.

## How to use the observable part

1. Identify the earlier area preceding a meaningful decline using a rule chosen before a later retest.
2. Mark and preserve that area as a candidate supply reference.
3. Observe subsequent approaches and actual reactions rather than assuming every return must fall.
4. Define a separate entry, invalidation, and exit if converting the observation into a strategy. The clip does not provide them.
5. Track the age and number of prior visits so a fresh and repeatedly traded area are not treated as identical without testing.

## Where the explanation is incomplete

Displayed or undisplayed orders can be canceled, replenished, moved, or executed elsewhere. A strong decline does not prove an enduring inventory of sell limits at a particular candle. The source gives no zone boundary convention, displacement threshold, timeframe, instrument, retest count, confirmation, stop, target, size, or expiry. Those are necessary operational choices, not details that can be recovered merely from the supply label.

## How to evaluate it

As additional research, freeze a zone-construction rule, timestamp when its defining departure becomes known, and study every later approach under fixed validity limits. Compare a touch entry with a confirmed-rejection entry and include unfilled and failed cases on later data. A microstructure explanation about remaining orders should be tested with suitable order-level data if that is the actual claim; an OHLC reaction study can test price behavior but cannot identify those hidden orders. The selected downward response is an illustration rather than a guaranteed consequence of a retest.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The first 14s presents the remaining-sell-interest story; 14–22s links a later return to the shown downward reaction. No complete executable method is stated.

# A failed bearish order-block scenario followed by a bullish gap-entry illustration

Source: [isfak trading official](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EtDhMeUSm/). Downloaded duration: 15.033 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The nearly static diagram begins with a labeled downtrend, successive structure breaks, and an overhead order-block area. A later bullish structural change and recovery invalidate the apparent bearish continuation. The image calls an earlier area a trap order block and labels a long from a gap-entry area, followed by a large upward extension. These are the visible annotations; the image does not reveal a complete real-time detector.

## How to reconstruct the pictured scenario

1. Mark the earlier bearish swing sequence and its support breaks.
2. Record the overhead zone that would otherwise be interpreted as a bearish order block.
3. Observe the later upward structural change rather than continuing to assume the original short thesis.
4. Mark the smaller bullish gap-entry area shown after the recovery and evaluate the depicted long from that location.
5. The green/red overlay places invalidation beneath that entry region and a profit area above. The visible annotation reads RR1:5 (a nominal 5R illustration). It is a source example, not a universal target rule or verified achieved return.

## Information not supplied

There is no instrument, timeframe, pivot rule, closing-break convention, gap definition, minimum displacement, entry trigger, order type, buffer, target formula, size, or maximum holding period. The word trap is a retrospective interpretation, not proof that a participant intentionally engineered the move. An early zone can fail without the opposite trade automatically becoming eligible.

## How to turn the illustration into a study

Additional research choices should define the original short thesis, its invalidation, and a separately confirmed long sequence. Timestamp each transition and do not assume a fill at the lowest historical gap touch before the bullish conditions became known. Include failed recoveries, unfilled retests, costs, and later-period outcomes. Compare an ordinary structural-reversal entry with the additional failed-zone/gap condition. The displayed strong rally is an example outcome, not a measured expectation or a complete risk policy.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The same annotated structure remains visible across the 0–15s samples: bearish breaks, an order block, a later change of character, a trap-zone label, and a bullish gap entry with a favorable extension.

Reviewed using: manual inspection of all eight timestamped visual samples; no meaningful speech or descriptive caption was available.

# Volume profile basics: point of control, a 70% value area, rejection, and acceptance

Source: [Peteonthebid](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1JjJGCB4E5/). Downloaded duration: 73.445 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The clip distinguishes volume over time from volume grouped by price and explains point of control and a value area. It offers two contextual scenarios: a weak excursion outside value that returns toward the point of control, and sustained activity outside value that establishes acceptance. It explicitly says the profile is context rather than a complete entry signal.

## How to reproduce the display

1. Select and record the profile's instrument, session or other interval, volume source, and price-bin size. The profile aggregates activity within that chosen interval; saying it ignores time means its bars are arranged by price, not that the interval is irrelevant.
2. Identify the largest-volume price bin as the point of control. Tie-breaking needs an implementation rule if bins have equal volume.
3. Construct the example value area containing about 70% of the selected volume, then mark its upper and lower edges. The source gives the percentage but not the expansion/tie algorithm.
4. Preserve those reference levels as-of the decision time, or explicitly maintain a developing profile rather than borrowing the final completed session.

## The two scenarios

For a return-to-value idea, the speaker looks for price outside the value area on lower activity and anticipates rejection toward the point of control. For acceptance, he watches price hold outside value while activity builds and then uses that region as new context. Low, building, stays, and rejection have no numerical thresholds in the clip. A separate entry, stop, target-execution rule, size, and expiry are therefore still required.

## Limitations and validation

The point of control is not necessarily the price midpoint or VWAP. Final-session volume and value edges are not known earlier in the session. A sparse excursion can continue trending, while apparent acceptance can later fail; the video explicitly does not promise a return to value. To research the scenarios, freeze profile construction and acceptance/rejection definitions and compare a fixed base entry with and without them on later data. Include every eligible excursion, costs, and changing developing levels. Fine volume-at-price analysis also needs suitably granular data; a daily OHLCV bar does not reveal the exact distribution of volume across its prices.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 3–22s contrasts time and price grouping; 22–38s defines point of control and the 70% value area; 38–57s describes rejection and acceptance; 57–70s states the limitations.

# Do not treat an unconfirmed internal low as the protected higher low of an uptrend

Source: [Smartvaultfx](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1HbP1XkRSK/). Downloaded duration: 46.833 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker rejects a seemingly attractive bearish retest because the broken low did not produce a subsequent equal or higher major high under his structure definition. He argues that this internal low should not be used as the protected higher-low reference for a major bearish shift. This is a swing-selection filter, not a complete entry strategy.

## How to follow the source's reasoning

1. Identify the prior meaningful high and the pullback low that followed it.
2. Check what the next upward leg actually accomplished. Under the speaker's framework, the low becomes a confirmed higher low only after price reaches an equal or new higher high.
3. If the rally fails well short of that high area, keep the internal low separate from the confirmed protected low.
4. Do not interpret the break of that unconfirmed internal point alone as proof that the major uptrend has changed.
5. Reassess a proposed short-retest zone using the properly defined structural origin rather than its visual neatness. The video does not state an alternative complete trade to take instead.

## Operational choices still needed

A detector needs a major/minor swing rule, equality tolerance, completed-bar confirmation, level width, and a policy for updating the protected reference. Equal and higher highs require a precise price and timing condition, not visual hindsight. Different structure methods can use different definitions, so the source's convention should be recorded explicitly rather than presented as the only possible use of the words higher low.

## Failure modes and evaluation

An unconfirmed low's break can still precede a genuine decline, and a confirmed protected-low break can still fail. The clip's assertion that the illustrated retest will be violated is not a universal outcome rule. Test a fixed retest strategy with and without this protected-swing filter on later data, preserving every rejected candidate, losses, costs, and timing. Do not use a future high to retroactively confirm a low at an earlier decision. The source provides no exact entry, stop, target, size, session, or timeframe, so the practical takeaway is better structural bookkeeping rather than a guaranteed reversal forecast.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 0–22s introduces the apparently clean but rejected retest; 23–38s gives the higher-low confirmation condition; 38–47s applies it to the illustrated failed rally.

# Volume-profile-filtered pivots with delta color and retest entries

Source: [Trade Empire](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1ETvXzV7so/). Downloaded duration: 336.361 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source demonstrates Volume Profile + Pivot Levels by ChartPrime on a one-hour EUR/USD example. It describes a rolling price-volume distribution, a point of control, and pivot levels promoted only when their associated bin clears a fraction of point-of-control volume. Profile color reflects an up-volume-minus-down-volume calculation. Historical activity at a price is not the same as presently available order-book liquidity, and this color is not necessarily trade-classified bid/ask delta.

## Settings stated by the source

The general profile period is 200 with resolution 50 price bins. The final settings panel around 336s also visibly shows pivot Length 10; the exact left/right confirmation convention still requires the script. The speaker suggests period 150 on lower frames and 250 on daily charts. For the main entry examples, promoted levels need at least 40% of point-of-control bin volume. Later suggestions are FX period 200/filter 25–30%; crypto period 150/filter 15–20%; stocks period 250 for daily swing or 180 intraday/filter 20%; and gold period 200/filter 35–40%. These later promotion thresholds differ from the stricter 40% entry filter; they should be recorded as separate conditions rather than conflated. None is a verified optimum.

## How to follow the long branch

1. Require a teal profile and the corresponding positive up/down-volume measure.
2. Select a promoted pivot low beneath current price with the stated main-example volume ratio.
3. Wait for price to move away and then revisit the level.
4. Require a wick into the reference without a close through it.
5. Enter on the following candle under an executable order convention, invalidate beneath the pivot, and use 1.5R or the next promoted resistance as separately selected objectives.

## Short branch and an ambiguity

Require maroon/negative context, select a promoted pivot high overhead, and wait for a bearish retest that does not close above the level. The stated entry is on the following candle, invalidation above the level, and objective 1.5R. One sentence describes price moving away upward before rallying back to an overhead level, which is geometrically unclear. Preserve the intended rejection-from-below scenario and define the departure/retest sequence independently rather than copying that sentence literally.

## Implementation and evaluation

The script's actual pivot delay, volume allocation to bins, up/down classification, rolling-level revision, sources, stop buffer, size, and expiry are not fully established. Spot-FX volume may be provider-specific rather than consolidated traded volume. A pivot is not known at its extreme if confirmation requires later bars; a rolling bin and its percentage can also change later. Save promoted status as-of each decision. Compare fixed retest entries with and without the profile gate and color condition on later data, include failed/unfilled orders and costs, and distinguish historical volume from claims of institutional backing.

Approximately 41–126s explains the tool; 148–181s gives profile settings; 186–239s gives longs; 239–272s gives shorts; 295–336s gives asset-specific suggestions.

# An intraday trendline break reaching an older demand area: wait for the actual reaction

Source: [Trading Bull](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/14utksN3z52/). Downloaded duration: 44.605 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The clip presents a buy-or-sell question. It first describes an uptrend losing momentum and breaking its rising line, then notes that price has reached an earlier demand area. The proposed long is conditional on rejection from that area, not an immediate buy merely because the level exists. The narration's bearish shift and later bullish possibility describe different stages.

## How to reproduce the analysis

1. Label the earlier higher highs/higher lows and draw the existing rising reference line using only earlier points.
2. Observe the downward break and avoid assuming the old upward momentum continues unchanged.
3. Mark the earlier demand/rejection zone reached by the decline.
4. Wait for a defined bullish reaction there before making a long eligible. The source uses conditional language and does not supply a specific candle pattern or closing threshold.
5. The long-position overlay around 38s places its stop below the demand zone and a target above the earlier swing high. Treat those as illustrated placements, not a fully stated stop buffer or target formula. Size and expiry remain absent.

## What still needs a rule

Trendline construction, swing prominence, zone boundaries, reaction strength, whether a close is required, order timing, and the relationship between the broken trend and older demand must be specified. A trendline break alone is not equivalent to a break of every protected structural low. A demand label is also not proof that the same buyers remain present.

## How to evaluate it

As additional research, freeze the old demand zones before the approach and compare a touch entry with a completed-reaction entry after a line break. Include failures, no-reaction cases, missed reversals, costs, and later data. A weak bounce can be only a pause in a new decline, while waiting can lose favorable entry price. The quiz framing and successful-looking example do not establish that a correct answer can be known with certainty from one static chart.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 4–22s describes the earlier uptrend and its weakening; 25–40s gives the demand-area context and explicitly conditional long reaction.

Reviewed using: manual synthesis of complete machine transcript, saved description, and timestamped recognized chart text.

# SuperTrend signals filtered by an Elliott-wave oscillator: an incomplete two-indicator recipe

Source: [TRADING CHART](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1CHuXECU2E/). Downloaded duration: 44.372 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source adds a SuperTrend script and an Elliott-wave oscillator, then illustrates accepting a buy when the oscillator agrees. The frames show a positive green histogram accompanying the long example. The headline's perfect-signal description and a displayed 40% move do not establish net profit, a complete sample, or universal accuracy.

## How to reproduce the established portion

1. Search for SuperTrend in TradingView and identify the highlighted script by KivancOzbilgic, preserving its exact version and inputs.
2. Add the intended Elliott-wave oscillator. The search screen contains several similarly named results and the recognized author spelling is uncertain; do not assume every result has the same formula or scale.
3. Observe a SuperTrend buy marker and check the oscillator's bullish state, shown as a green positive histogram in the example.
4. Define when the confirmation must occur relative to the buy marker and whether a completed bar is required. The clip does not quantify a tolerance window.
5. Specify stops, exits, size, and expiry independently, because no reliable complete rule is recoverable from the available narration and frames.

## Uncertainties that matter

The later machine transcript becomes incoherent and switches languages; it cannot be used as a confident translation of exit instructions. The indicator periods, ATR multiplier, oscillator calculation, exact second-script identity, instrument, and short-side rule are not established. The toolbar around 38s visibly selects D (daily), so the shown example should not be relabeled as an intraday scalping test. A mirrored bearish combination is a possible research branch, not an extra confirmed instruction. The highlighted search row in a menu also need not be the final clicked script.

Obtain and freeze the actual scripts, then compare the SuperTrend entry alone with the oscillator-filtered version on later data. Log signal availability at completed bars, avoid repainting/backdated pivots, and include costs and all losing transitions. Trend tools can whipsaw in ranges and a confirming oscillator can delay entry. A chosen percentage excursion does not account for leverage, stops, position size, fees, or the fraction of the move that a declared exit could capture.

# A thirty-minute opening range with closing-break confirmation and a fixed ten-point objective

Source: [Erick Jablonski](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EsBNHj5MJ/). Downloaded duration: 43.033 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The speaker uses the first two fifteen-minute candles after the example US cash open to define a range, waits until 10:00 Eastern, and trades a close beyond a boundary. A wick alone is explicitly insufficient. The illustrated short invalidates at the opposite range edge and targets ten price points. The chart is visibly labeled ES · 15. Its one-contract illustration shows a ten-point target with $500 gross P&L, consistent with ES’s $50-per-point multiplier. That is a hypothetical order display, not evidence of a broker fill.

## How to reproduce the stated rule

1. Select the correct regular-session instrument/calendar and a fifteen-minute chart.
2. At 10:00 Eastern, freeze the high and low of the first two opening candles, corresponding to the 09:30–10:00 example window.
3. Wait for a candle to close above the upper boundary for the long branch or below the lower boundary for the short branch. A temporary excursion that closes inside remains ineligible.
4. For the short, the narration places invalidation at the opposite range edge and uses a ten-point downward objective. The displayed example adds a buffer: the upper blue boundary is about 5106.75, entry 5095.50, stop 5108.00, and target 5085.50. That is 12.50 points of planned risk for 10 points of reward (0.8R before costs); the buffer is not generalized by the narration. The opposite-edge long invalidation is the natural mirrored research interpretation, but the worked spoken stop example is short.
5. Specify actual fill timing after the confirming close and record the attainable entry price.

## Risk/reward and missing decisions

A fixed ten-point objective does not imply a fixed reward/risk ratio. If the range is wide, the opposite-edge stop can risk more than the objective; if narrow, spread and noise can dominate. The source leaves size, stop buffer, maximum range width, number of attempts, reentry, session cutoff, gaps, and time exit unspecified. It describes a variation learned from another trader but does not establish that person's complete system.

## How to evaluate it

Build the range only after the opening window is complete, use a timezone-aware Eastern calendar, and log all later eligible closes. Compare fixed ten-point targets across the actual intended instrument and volatility regimes rather than transferring them to every stock or market. Include failed first breaks, costs, gap-aware stops, and next-executable-price fills. The caveman/easy framing is presentation; a simple definition can still have unfavorable expectancy.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 3–12s defines the two opening candles and clock time; 13–25s distinguishes closes from wicks; 26–33s gives the opposite-edge stop and ten-point target.

# Candle-range theory as a failed excursion beyond a selected candle's extremes

Source: [FX Smart Trade](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/18jv5o2V9i/). Downloaded duration: 28.885 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The clip selects one reference candle, retains its high and low, and watches the following price action for an excursion outside those extremes that closes back inside. The proposed observation is a failed boundary break. The reference candle's open/close are excluded from the range definition, but a later close is essential to the described recovery condition.

## How to reproduce the observable setup

1. Choose a reference candle at a predefined time and timeframe. The source says a key time but does not specify a clock, market, or selection rule.
2. After that candle completes, freeze its high and low.
3. Observe the next candle or declared subsequent window.
4. Mark a high-side or low-side excursion and require a close back inside the reference range.
5. Treat the failed excursion as reversal context. The final short-position illustration sells after an upside failure, places invalidation above the sweep wick, and targets the reference candle’s low. The narration does not generalize an exact entry, stop buffer, sizing, or expiry rule; the downside-failure long mirror is not separately demonstrated.

## Rules still needed

Define whether only the immediately following candle qualifies, whether equality counts as outside/inside, the minimum excursion, which side wins if both extremes are crossed, and whether entry requires another confirmation. A final closing recovery is unavailable earlier within that candle. A resting order anticipating the recovery and an order placed after confirmation are different strategies and should not be assigned the same historical fill.

## Failure modes and evaluation

Price can recover inside and then resume the initial break, sweep both edges, or remain inside without producing any signal. The clip's two-possibility description is a broad classification, not a probability model. As additional research, freeze the reference selection and horizon, record every qualifying excursion, and compare subsequent returns with ordinary boundary touches. Use later data, realistic execution, and costs. The name candle range theory alone does not supply absent clock settings or justify importing a different instructor's complete model.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The opening 0–10s defines the reference extremes; approximately 10–23s describes a later excursion and closing recovery. The available narration supplies no complete execution policy.

Reviewed using: manual synthesis of complete machine transcript, saved caption, and timestamped recognized chart text.

# A return to an older bearish order block despite an intervening bullish recovery

Source: [ICT liquidity trader](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1ByQfSbVfU/). Downloaded duration: 15.0 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

A schematic and matching chart show an earlier high-side order-block area, a decline, an internal recovery with sweep/shift labels, and a final return toward the older overhead zone. A short-position overlay at that zone projects a decline toward the earlier low. The message is a higher-level bearish area can remain relevant despite smaller upward structural labels; the picture does not define how to rank those levels mechanically.

## How to reconstruct the shown scenario

1. Mark the original overhead bearish zone before the initial decline.
2. Record the lower reference low and the internal recovery sequence separately.
3. Keep the smaller internal order-block and break labels distinct from the older overhead zone.
4. Wait for the illustrated return toward that older area and define an actual rejection/entry trigger independently. The diagram places a short overlay there but gives no candle-close or order rule.
5. The visual invalidation is above the overhead zone and the objective lies near the prior low. Exact buffer, size, and expiry are not supplied.

## Missing rules and caution about labels

No instrument, timeframe, formal pivot hierarchy, zone-selection criterion, freshness condition, sweep definition, risk fraction, or objective formula is established. The internal MSS/BOS labels do not by themselves prove a major reversal, just as the old bearish area does not guarantee a later short will succeed. The word inducement in the schematic is an interpretation, not proof of counterparties' intentions.

An additional study should freeze a hierarchy of structural levels and log when each zone first becomes known. Test the return-to-older-zone setup with and without internal-recovery conditions, using every eligible approach and later data. # A bullish recovery, renewed low-side visit, and continuation from a marked order-block area

Source: [Liquidity Sniper Club](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/14wRpyQyx5R/). Downloaded duration: 26.167 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The silent animation marks a bullish change of character, a later low-side liquidity reference near a lower order-block area, a new consolidation, and a subsequent upward break toward a high-side target. The box labeled high probability is an assertion in the chart, not a measured success rate.

## How to reconstruct the visual setup

1. Identify the earlier recovery through a local high labeled change of character.
2. Mark the lower origin zone and the later pullback reference above or around it.
3. Observe the return toward the lower region and the subsequent base rather than assuming an immediate rebound at the first touch.
4. The animation later marks a new structure-break level and shows continuation above it. Define which of the zone return or later break is the actual entry event before testing; the source's large position rectangle alone does not settle this.
5. The displayed stop region lies below the lower setup area and the objective is the prior overhead liquidity line.

## Rules still absent

There is no instrument/timeframe, zone formula, pivot delay, liquidity-build-up threshold, confirmation trigger, order type, stop buffer, position size, or expiry. The final BOS annotation appears after the original position rectangle has already been drawn, so it must not be used to retroactively justify an earlier fill unless it was genuinely part of the entry policy.

## How to evaluate it

As additional research, separate a zone-touch entry from a later confirmed-break entry, preserve their different prices and risk, and include failed bases, no-retest moves, costs, and later-period results. Level labels do not prove actual stop inventory or institutional activity. A selected animation reaching an overhead line is not evidence that the large illustrated reward/risk was consistently attainable.

The 0–7s samples show the original shift and lower-region return; around 11–15s consolidation and a newer break reference appear; 18–26s shows favorable continuation to the high-side objective.

# First five-minute candle range, one-minute displacement, gap retest, and engulfing confirmation

Source: [Robert Mitchell](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1E6kS4y3Vr/). Downloaded duration: 85.402 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source uses the first five-minute candle after the example 09:30 opening time as a reference range, then moves to one-minute analysis. It requires a displacement-style boundary break that creates a three-bar fair-value gap, followed by a retest and engulfing confirmation. The stated objective is 3R. The video's claims of working every day and extensive testing are unsupported by a supplied complete sample.

## How to reproduce the sequence

1. After the example opening candle completes, freeze its high and low. The narration gives 09:30 but does not fully establish instrument/calendar details, so use the actual intended regular session.
2. Switch to one-minute bars and wait for price to break a boundary with the stated gap-producing displacement. A wick or ordinary close alone is explicitly insufficient.
3. Require the three-bar outer-wick gap to be established; the third candle must exist before the condition is known.
4. Wait for price to return into that gap and then form the described engulfing candle.
5. After the engulfing candle completes, make the trade eligible under an executable later-price rule and use a 3R objective relative to the chosen protective stop.

## The major omission

The narration does not specify a protective-stop formula. The illustrated short-position overlay places risk above the retest/engulfing candle cluster and shows $1,000 planned risk versus $3,000 reward. That supplies the pictured side of invalidation, but not an exact choice of wick, gap edge, or buffer for every setup. A reproducible 3R target still requires a declared entry and stop. The source also leaves the exact engulfing body/range convention, gap minimum, retest depth, signal expiry, attempt limit, position size, and market-data source open. A statement that winning trades make three times losing trades is a planned payoff structure, not an established outcome after gaps, costs, and partial execution.

## Failure modes and evaluation

The displacement can fail, a retest can cross the gap, or confirmation can arrive after room to the objective is reduced. Build the opening range only after its candle closes, use completed one-minute conditions, and never fill retrospectively at a confirming close merely because the close is visible. Test every eligible opening event on later data, include unfilled retests and false breaks, and compare the gap-plus-engulfing filter with a simpler opening-range break. Costs and realistic stop behavior are especially relevant on one-minute bars.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 18–34s defines the opening range; 34–62s requires displacement and the gap; 62–77s requires retest/engulfing and states 3R; the original position drawing places the stop above the engulfing/retest cluster, while an exact buffer/formula is not supplied.

Reviewed using: manual synthesis of complete machine transcript and timestamped recognized chart text.

The QQE MOD primary panel shows RSI length 6, smoothing 5, QQE factor 3, threshold 3, and close as source. Its secondary panel shows RSI length 6, smoothing 5, QQE factor 1.61, threshold 3, and close. The visible style settings include primary up/down signals and a zero line.

The right-hand numeric input values are not reliably readable in the sampled camera view; do not invent a baseline length or ATR multiplier from common defaults. Some display controls are changed during the demonstration, so record the final actual configuration before attempting replication.

## How to use the established visual idea

1. Add the exact two intended scripts and save their versions.
2. Reproduce the readable QQE inputs and independently obtain the missing SSL numerical configuration.
3. Observe agreement between the price-line state and histogram direction.
4. Define whether entry requires a crossover, a first aligned bar, or sustained agreement. Those are research choices, not confidently recovered instructions.
5. Specify invalidation, objective, size, expiry, and signal timing before testing. None is clearly established by the usable evidence.

## Failure cases and evaluation

Two smoothed tools can agree late or whipsaw together in a range. Agreement does not prove independent confirmation because both can transform the same price history. Test a frozen executable rule on later data, compare each indicator alone with the combination, and retain all failed transitions and costs. Verify the original audio or a reliable transcript before attributing more specific rules to the speaker. The marked historical turns and long favorable stretches do not constitute a measured win rate.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The first roughly 80s points to aligned line/histogram turns; 86–108s shows SSL controls; 113–124s shows QQE primary/secondary inputs and style. The full-resolution frames preserve settings more clearly than the garbled transcript.

# A static accumulation–upside excursion–bearish redistribution illustration

Source: [SMC ICT FX Signals Community](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1AMwJcttnu/). Downloaded duration: 15.0 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The diagram labels an initial range as accumulation, an upward excursion as manipulation, a bearish structural shift, and a recovery into an overhead gap/order-block area before a later decline toward low-side liquidity. This is an AMD-style story for a completed chart. The labels cannot establish actual manipulative intent or identify which participants held orders.

## How to reconstruct the visible sequence

1. Mark the initial range and its high/low before the excursion.
2. Observe the move above the range and the subsequent downward structural change.
3. Mark the bearish gap and overhead order-block region left by the decline.
4. Wait for a return toward that region and define an actual short trigger independently. The drawing's arrows suggest the scenario but provide no closing-bar or limit-order condition.
5. The intended objective lies toward the lower reference shown as sell-side liquidity; exact stop placement, buffer, target tolerance, size, and expiry are absent.

## Implementation requirements

A reproducible model needs range selection, excursion/recovery definitions, pivot confirmation, gap geometry, order-block boundaries, and a clear branch for a breakout that holds instead of failing. Record when each object becomes known. A completed-history distribution label must not be used as evidence that the final decline was already certain at the initial high.

## Failure modes and evaluation

The high-side move can continue, the structural break can fail, or the retest can cross the overhead zone. Some moves will never retest. Test every eligible range event with a frozen entry and exit, include costs and failed scenarios, and compare the added gap/zone filters with a simpler failed-break model on later data. A detailed annotated diagram is an educational map, not a complete strategy or a verified probability estimate.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

The same annotated chart is visible throughout 0–15s, including the initial range, high-side excursion, MSS, gap, negative order-block labels, and lower objective.

# Mitigated versus untouched zones: a lifecycle definition, not a new entry signal

Source: [StocksJet Advisory](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EeFoTB75S/). Downloaded duration: 28.188 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

The source calls a previously created supply area, order block, or fair-value gap mitigated after price departs and later returns to interact with it. It teaches a state change in a zone's lifecycle. 1. Define and mark the original zone using a separate construction rule.
2. Record when it becomes available and when price first departs from it.

4. Mark the zone as mitigated at the first qualifying interaction.

Interaction can mean touching the near edge, crossing a midpoint, fully traversing the area, or closing inside. Those alternatives produce different lifecycle timestamps; the clip does not select a numerical convention. A mitigated zone may still produce a reaction under some systems; others reject it after the first touch. That trading policy is separate from this source's definition.

Additional research can store zone states such as forming, fresh, departed, first-touch, repeatedly-tested, invalidated, and expired. Transition only on information available at that bar. Compare a frozen strategy's first-touch and later-touch outcomes on later data, including no-return zones and costs. A state label is useful bookkeeping, but its usefulness for returns must be measured. # Optimized Trend Tracker signals with period 7 and a WWMA setting

Source: [TRADING CHART](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EeiLqGoEy/). Downloaded duration: 27.237 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source adds an Optimized Trend Tracker script and trades its buy/sell labels. Unlike the speech's vague instructions to choose this average and check this box, the visible final settings allow several inputs to be recovered. The large dollar-profit headline and expanding risk/reward rectangle are promotional examples, not independently verified returns.

## Visible configuration

The final panel shows close as source, OTT period 7, OTT percent 1.4, and moving-average type WWMA. Show Support Line and Show Support Line Crossing Signals are enabled, as is the highlighter. Price/OTT crossing and OTT-color-change signal options are unchecked in the visible panel. An earlier frame still shows VAR before the average-type change; that transitional value should not replace the later WWMA choice.

## How to reproduce the stated signal idea

1. Identify and freeze the exact Optimized Trend Tracker script/version rather than choosing any similarly named bands, oscillator, or strategy variant.
2. Apply the visible settings above.
3. The source buys on the displayed buy label and sells or considers a short on the sell label. Exiting a long and initiating a short are different actions and need an explicit position-policy choice.
4. Decide whether labels must persist through a completed bar and model the actual later executable fill.
5. Add a protective stop, objective or opposite-signal exit, size, and expiry. The video does not fully specify those rules, despite showing example position overlays.

## Failure modes and evaluation

Trend trackers can alternate signals in a range and lag abrupt reversals. The same label can behave differently if a script repaints or the bar is unfinished. Audit signal availability, freeze the version/inputs, and test all transitions on later data with costs. Do not assume the displayed very large reward/risk ratios were attainable under an unstated exit; the rectangle is moved to show larger historical excursions. A dollar result cannot be reproduced without position size, leverage, fees, and exact fills.

Around 7–15s shows the script search and configuration; the 15.48s panel clearly displays WWMA after the earlier VAR frame. About 18–27s illustrates buy and sell labels.

# A 9/20 EMA crossover gated by repeated levels, role reversal, and the swing midpoint

Source: [Cipher ィ ۦۦ](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1CbzEBjPEm/). Downloaded duration: 681.783 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The tutorial treats the 9/20 EMA cross as timing within a location/context framework. It first requires support or resistance established by a departure and another hold, then favors role-reversal areas and alignment with the broader swing. The author claims 68 winners from 100 trades across gold, Bitcoin, and EUR/USD, but supplies no complete independently auditable ledger or frozen test protocol.

## Configuration and first trigger

Add two EMAs: length 9 shown green and length 20 shown white. The colors are visual identifiers rather than predictive inputs. A 9-above-20 cross is the bullish trigger and the opposite cross bearish. The worked context examples use a five-minute chart. The source's description of EMAs reading only the last named number of candles is simplified: an EMA retains progressively smaller weight on older observations, so its source, initialization, and warmup still matter.

## Location filter

1. Mark a potential support/resistance area after an initial departure.
2. Require price to return and hold it a second time before treating it as established under the source's rule.
3. At a later return, wait for the correctly directed EMA cross rather than trading the level touch alone.
4. If price cuts through the zone in the wrong direction, reject the candidate.
5. The source's long invalidation is beneath support and the short invalidation above resistance; the illustrated objective is 1.5R, with a prior swing extreme offered as another variant.

## Role reversal and final context

A resistance area that breaks and later holds from above is called a flip zone for longs; broken support retested from below is the bearish mirror. This is different from repeated holds on the same side. The final short example also zooms out on the same five-minute chart to verify lower highs/lower lows, measures the last major downward leg, and places the short location above that leg's 50% midpoint. A mirrored long discount filter is a research extension of the stated idea, while the final detailed premium illustration is short.

## Rules and evidence limits

The source leaves zone width, touch separation, pivot delay, trendline/major-leg selection, cross timing tolerance, stop buffer, order type, position size, and expiry open. It enters at the crossover candle close in the narration; an executable test must define how an order becomes eligible after that close is known. A losing illustration uses a one-touch area that violates the stated filter. Including such discretionary mistakes in the claimed 100-trade result makes it unclear whether that percentage estimates the frozen rules or the trader's actual decisions.

## How to evaluate it

Freeze the base cross, repeated-level filter, flip condition, and midpoint context separately. ## Experiment overview

The tutorial treats the 9/20 EMA cross as timing within a location/context framework. It first requires support or resistance established by a departure and another hold, then favors role-reversal areas and alignment with the broader swing. The author claims 68 winners from 100 trades across gold, Bitcoin, and EUR/USD, but supplies no complete independently auditable ledger or frozen test protocol.

**Proposed evaluation scope:** Evaluate the particular setup or indicator sequence described here on a frozen historical universe. First produce causal features and candidate events; promote it to a trade simulation only after the unresolved entry, invalidation, exit and sizing decisions below have an explicit versioned specification. A daily-equity adaptation must be labeled when the source uses another interval or product.

## Rules and inputs

**Evidence boundary:** The source interpretation below retains the writeup’s own wording, including its qualifications, corrections and explicitly added research examples. A numbered procedure can contain a proposed operational choice; it is not automatically a rule attributed to the video. No unstated timeframe, conventional default, mirrored trade or numerical stop/target becomes source-backed through inclusion here.

### Writeup: Configuration and first trigger

Add two EMAs: length 9 shown green and length 20 shown white. The colors are visual identifiers rather than predictive inputs. A 9-above-20 cross is the bullish trigger and the opposite cross bearish. The worked context examples use a five-minute chart. The source's description of EMAs reading only the last named number of candles is simplified: an EMA retains progressively smaller weight on older observations, so its source, initialization, and warmup still matter.

### Writeup: Location filter

1. Mark a potential support/resistance area after an initial departure.
2. Require price to return and hold it a second time before treating it as established under the source's rule.
3. At a later return, wait for the correctly directed EMA cross rather than trading the level touch alone.
4. If price cuts through the zone in the wrong direction, reject the candidate.
5. The source's long invalidation is beneath support and the short invalidation above resistance; the illustrated objective is 1.5R, with a prior swing extreme offered as another variant.

### Writeup: Role reversal and final context

A resistance area that breaks and later holds from above is called a flip zone for longs; broken support retested from below is the bearish mirror. This is different from repeated holds on the same side. The final short example also zooms out on the same five-minute chart to verify lower highs/lower lows, measures the last major downward leg, and places the short location above that leg's 50% midpoint. A mirrored long discount filter is a research extension of the stated idea, while the final detailed premium illustration is short.

Additional datasets and source-specific dependencies below are mandatory only for the branch that needs them. A signal-only study can proceed once its event definition is complete; trade P&L additionally requires explicit entry/fill, invalidation, exit and sizing policies.

## Proposed integration

**Indicators:** [analysis/rule_catalog.py](../../analysis/rule_catalog.py) and [analysis/rule_engine.py](../../analysis/rule_engine.py) supply typed indicator operands/comparisons; [analysis/indicator_engine.py](../../analysis/indicator_engine.py) supplies MACD, SMA, Wilder RSI and other series. [indicators/_math.py](../../indicators/_math.py) has Wilder ATR/EMA/DEMA building blocks. Stateful sequences or missing formulas need a dedicated adapter rather than forced Builder conditions.

**Swings:** [patterns_v2/patterns/common.py](../../patterns_v2/patterns/common.py) exposes causal ZigZag pivots with separate pivot and confirmation indices; [core/rsi_divergence.py](../../core/rsi_divergence.py) demonstrates evidence carrying pivot/confirmation dates. Freeze the base cross, repeated-level filter, flip condition, and midpoint context separately. Use only confirmed swing endpoints available at the decision and retain every failed, rejected, and unfilled candidate on later data. Compare the contribution of each condition with costs. Role-reversal stories about trapped traders are interpretations, not proof of inventory. A crossover near a well-tested zone can still fail, and the same-side hold count does not guarantee that future support becomes stronger.

**Indicators evidence:** Export feature values and each condition’s pass/fail reason. Test exact numeric fixtures, cross equality, recursive seeds and constant-price/zero-variance cases. Compare individual filters before the combined stack.

**Swings evidence:** Log pivot origin and confirmation, protected-level updates and every failed or stale candidate. Change bars after a decision and assert identical prior levels/signals. Backdated chart labels must never become backdated fills.

Freeze interpretation, parameters and execution before testing. Expose only completed decision bars and prior data to the adapter; close-generated signals fill no earlier than the next tradable open. Limit/stop orders become eligible only after their conditions are known. Preserve pivot confirmation, external publication and higher-frame availability times. Test prefix invariance by changing/removing future bars and requiring unchanged earlier features, signals and orders. Use raw market prices for fills, keeping synthetic Heikin-Ashi/regression prices as features.

For fully specified trades, report candidate/accepted/rejected/expired/unfilled counts, trade and signal/fill timestamps, rule/level evidence, fees/slippage, net expectancy/R where defined, win rate, profit factor, realized/unrealized P&L, marked-to-market equity, exposure, turnover and drawdown by market. Compare a frozen baseline with identical dates/universe/costs; label independent-notional versus finite-capital accounting. Without entry/exit rules, report event coverage and predeclared forward-return/MAE/MFE horizons or forecast calibration, leaving trading P&L unavailable. Outcome windows never enter features and are censored at end_date with incomplete horizons reported.

Use fixtures alongside [core/test_stream_backtest.py](../../core/test_stream_backtest.py), [core/test_rule_backtest.py](../../core/test_rule_backtest.py), [core/test_backtest_service.py](../../core/test_backtest_service.py) and [web/test_paper_api.py](../../web/test_paper_api.py): source positives/near-misses, date boundaries, warm-up without orders, missing/invalid data, owner/remote parity, `.PS` and market isolation, enumeration/auth/partial-bulk failures, progress/cancel/retry and valid no-signal runs. Use untouched later holdouts and retain all trials, failures and costs.

The source leaves zone width, touch separation, pivot delay, trendline/major-leg selection, cross timing tolerance, stop buffer, order type, position size, and expiry open. # A deep bullish-gap retracement with lower-edge rejection and an impulse-high objective

Source: [Smart Forex Pips](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/18kLiGb5o7/). Downloaded duration: 72.748 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The source shows a bullish three-bar gap followed by a deep return that rejects near the gap's lower edge, then a long toward the preceding impulse high. It argues against chasing the initial expansion. The claimed explanation that buyers and sellers never met in the gap is inaccurate: the outer-bar gap geometry does not mean the middle candle's traversed prices had no counterparties.

## How to reproduce the illustrated case

1. Identify the completed three-bar bullish structure and mark the interval between the first bar's high and third bar's low.
2. Wait for the later retracement; in this example, touching the near edge is not treated as the completed entry because price continues deeper.
3. Observe the lower-edge wick and upward closing reaction.
4. The narration places entry at that edge and invalidation beneath the candle that created it, with the impulse high as target. Decide independently which candle and exact boundary that stop phrase means.
5. Choose whether to place a resting edge order or wait for the described closing rejection. Those choices have different fills and must not be combined retrospectively.

## Unspecified settings

No instrument, timeframe, gap-size threshold, trend requirement, first-touch policy, stop buffer, position size, order expiry, or time exit is established. The caption's buy/sell question and selected outcome do not provide those inputs. A full-gap fill and a successful reversal are separate observations; filling the region does not oblige price to rise.

## How to evaluate it

Freeze gap geometry, depth, confirmation, and stop selection, then compare near-edge, midpoint, and lower-edge entries as distinct variants on later data. Include gaps that never retest, cross entirely, or reverse before filling the intended order. Model costs and executable timing. The attractive final rally is a favorable example, not proof that price had a duty to collect skipped orders or that a lower-edge touch reliably predicts the next move.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

About 8–27s defines the gap and gives the overstated microstructure story; 30–48s shows the deep retest/rejection; 53–60s gives entry, stop concept, and impulse-high target; the remainder reveals the favorable result and promotes a guide.
