# Four-stage bullish reversal: higher low, structure break, consolidation, and final breakout

Source: [Trading for Beginners](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1HVxNeSP4C/). Downloaded duration: 15.0 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Trading for Beginners explicitly sequences the reversal rather than buying one candle. After a downtrend it requires a higher low, a break of the last lower high, consolidation with another higher low, and a break of the consolidation high with volume.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Establish the initial downtrend and its last major lower high.
2. Observe the first higher low as an early warning, not final confirmation.
3. Wait for the upward break of the lower-high reference.
4. Let the new range form and identify its final higher low.
5. Require the caption’s breakout above the consolidation high with volume before the final confirmed branch.
6. Define entry timing, stop, target and size separately.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

Pivot confirmation, range duration, volume threshold, buffer and risk rules are missing. Consolidation does not prove smart-money accumulation, and the claim one will never buy a top/sell a bottom again is unsupported. Confirmed patterns can still fail.


## Local evidence and reproducibility

The full caption lists all four stages; the original image labels first/second reversal indication and final confirmation.

# A minor downtrend inside a larger rising channel

Source: [Tristan Ford](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1Esi9LvUQi/). Downloaded duration: 30.37 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Tristan Ford contrasts shorting a newly formed minor downtrend with buying its correction inside a larger upward channel. The wider view shows price returning toward lower rising support and a final bullish continuation rectangle.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Mark the broad rising-channel anchors and major bullish lows before the pullback.
2. Identify the smaller descending correction as a separate scale.
3. Check whether the larger bullish invalidation has actually failed.
4. The preferred illustration waits for lower-channel/support confluence, then a bullish reaction rather than chasing the minor decline.
5. Define the exact long trigger, stop, upper objective and size independently.

# Five short bodyweight demonstrations promoted as a daily 100-repetition routine

Source: [Bryan Lee](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1GgNZPcfLx/). Downloaded duration: 22.84 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This URL is a fitness reel, so it is archived as fitness content. Bryan Lee demonstrates kneeling/bodyweight movements and promotes 100 repetitions of each per day, with waist/glute/core claims and a fitness-app invitation. It is not trading material.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Kneeling squat/hip extension: from tall kneeling on a padded surface, sit the hips back toward the heels, then extend the hips to return upright without throwing the lower back.
2. Hands-and-feet-supported bent-knee drive/rotation: the demonstrator brings a bent leg inward beneath the torso, then returns toward the support position. The fast clip does not name the exact variation or establish that it is a full sit-through.
3. Bird-dog-style reach: from hands/knees, extend one leg backward and the opposite arm forward while keeping the trunk controlled, then return and switch.
4. Kneeling up/down plank: move between hand support and forearm support with knees down, keeping the trunk steady.
5. Forearm kneeling rock-back: from forearm/knee support, move the hips back/up and return forward, using a comfortable range.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

The source does not define cadence, sets, rest, left/right counting, progression or individualized suitability. Its 100-per-move daily target is a promotional prescription, not a required starting dose. The short clips do not establish that this routine is better than 10,000 steps, which trains a different activity pattern. Stop a repetition when control is lost rather than racing to match a headline count.

## How to assess the body-composition claims

The [American Council on Exercise explanation of common fitness myths](https://www.acefitness.org/about-ace/press-room/press-releases/319/ace-lists-most-common-fitness-myths/) does not support spot reduction. Training the trunk or glutes can challenge those muscles, but this reel does not establish localized belly/arm fat loss from these movements. The before/after photos are not a controlled comparison of this routine. For a reproducible exercise record, note movement variation, controlled repetitions on each side, rest, range of motion and how the next session progresses. Treat the advertised seven-day app access as an external promotion; no signup was performed.

## Local evidence and reproducibility

Full 23-second narration plus original frames at 1/4/7/10/13/16/19/21/22s were inspected to distinguish the five movements.

Reviewed using: manual synthesis of full transcript, caption and original chart evidence.

# Six bullish pattern examples for recognition

Source: [Mananjay Capital](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1CgYEF3ADo/). Downloaded duration: 5.04 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Mananjay Capital’s sheet labels flag, falling wedge, pennant, cup and handle, ascending triangle and inverse head-and-shoulders, all shown with favorable upside completion.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Flag/pennant: distinguish a corrective channel from a smaller converging pause after an impulse.
2. Falling wedge: identify converging descending boundaries.
3. Cup/handle: separate the rounded base from its smaller near-rim correction.
4. Ascending triangle: flat resistance with rising lows.
5. Inverse head-and-shoulders: three troughs and the neckline.
6. Require a declared completed breakout/confirmation and add risk/exit rules before using a picture as an entry.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

No duration, touch count, ratio tolerance, volume filter, timeframe, stop or size is supplied. The sheet excludes failed versions and therefore cannot establish reliability. A bullish-family label does not make the next candle bullish.


## Local evidence and reproducibility

All original samples show the same six labeled bullish patterns.

Reviewed using: manual inspection of original sampled frames, recognized chart text and saved caption; music is not treated as instruction.

Source: [writeup.md](writeup.md). Planning only: this document proposes future integrations and does not implement a tab, strategy or engine. Source snapshot SHA-256: `9c6945393208a6b600a8079adffcd1ec53ee2fd411e9feb7bf576ba6d163764f`.

## Experiment overview

Prime Order Flow’s static reference pairs schematics and charts for double top, double bottom, triple top and triple bottom. It illustrates the common neckline break rather than giving a complete order-flow strategy.

**Proposed evaluation scope:** Start with a causal annotation or filter event study of the described condition. Measure all qualifying cases and compare a separately frozen entry model with and without that condition. A descriptive label or selected reference picture is not automatically an order.

## Rules and inputs

**Evidence boundary:** The source interpretation below retains the writeup’s own wording, including its qualifications, corrections and explicitly added research examples. A numbered procedure can contain a proposed operational choice; it is not automatically a rule attributed to the video. No unstated timeframe, conventional default, mirrored trade or numerical stop/target becomes source-backed through inclusion here.

### Writeup: How to use or reproduce it

1. Mark the two or three comparable peaks/troughs before the final break.
2. For tops, identify the intervening support/neckline and require a declared bearish confirmation.
3. For bottoms, identify the intervening resistance and require the bullish break.
4. Choose entry on close or retest as distinct variants.
5. Add stop, measured/structural target, size and expiry independently.

**Experiment input contract (proposed):** timestamped open, high, low, close and volume, market/session identity, versioned source interpretation and all declared parameters. Additional datasets and source-specific dependencies below are mandatory only for the branch that needs them. A signal-only study can proceed once its event definition is complete; trade P&L additionally requires explicit entry/fill, invalidation, exit and sizing policies.

## Proposed integration

Create a source-specific adapter for the sequence in the Rules and inputs section, preserving the order in which each illustrated reference and confirmation becomes known. Store candidate, armed, confirmed, expired and invalidated events separately. [patterns/base_pattern.py](../../patterns/base_pattern.py) supplies signal/annotation structures, while [indicators/_signal.py](../../indicators/_signal.py) demonstrates latest-bar output; neither supplies the missing source rules. A recap or undisclosed indicator stays blocked until its actual generator and execution specification are available.

The future Experiments page would extend [web/app.py](../../web/app.py) and [web/templates/base.html](../../web/templates/base.html), using Paper’s [template](../../web/templates/paper.html) and `initPaper` in [web/static/app.js](../../web/static/app.js) for US/PH controls, status, tables and chart inspection. Add experiment selection, start/end dates, parameters, requirements, Start/Cancel and saved results. Use [web/static/backtest_runs.js](../../web/static/backtest_runs.js), [web/runs.py](../../web/runs.py) and [core/backtest_jobs.py](../../core/backtest_jobs.py) as lifecycle references: background execution, run IDs, polling/reconnect, loading/warm-up/session progress, cancellation, errors, interrupted runs and explicit retry.

Propose a versioned catalog and typed contracts in `core/experiments/`, source-specific adapters and `web/experiments.py` (new components, not existing APIs). Register this directory’s source ID/digest; requests freeze market, inclusive dates, parameters, universe/data hashes and execution policy. A proposed `/api/experiments/catalog` and `/api/experiments/runs[/{id}]` flow would validate requirements → load → warm up → replay → persist/poll results, with a run-specific cancel action. Missing specifications/data should produce explicit preflight blockers.

[core/backtest_service.py](../../core/backtest_service.py) offers frozen-input/artifact contracts but is currently coupled to pinned pattern versions; extend or wrap its lifecycle rather than assume an arbitrary-strategy plug-in API. [core/stream_backtest.py](../../core/stream_backtest.py) demonstrates a growing causal store, pending next-open fills, warm-up without orders and explicit end policy; [core/rule_backtest.py](../../core/rule_backtest.py) is a simpler rule-replay reference. Audit their detector, sizing and exit contracts before reuse. Keep experiment state separate from live Paper books and the immutable pattern registry. Paper’s DII/Kronos/Laya gates and loss/trailing/exposure policies apply only when explicitly selected as experimental assumptions. Durable run storage and history-owner routing are separate deployment concerns.

## Data handling

Determine warm-up from the longest declared indicator, reference range and formation window, plus prior-value comparisons and pivot confirmation delays. Retain pre-start zone/anchor state when required. If the source leaves these windows open, finalize them before declaring a minimum; insufficient history produces a per-symbol not-ready reason, not fabricated values.

Use [docs/daily-bars-api.md](../../docs/daily-bars-api.md) and [data/history.py](../../data/history.py): snapshot `list_history_symbols(market=...)`, then `load_daily_bars(symbol, market=...)`. When `STOCKS_HISTORY_URL` is empty and the process owns history (`STOCKS_HISTORY_OWNER` or existing deployment/host detection), `local_history_backfill_enabled()` selects local PostgreSQL `stocks_history` through `data/db.py`. Otherwise the existing authenticated `data/history_client.py` uses the history HTTP API; `enable_ui_web_history()` supplies the remote default for a non-owner web process. Preserve that routing in workers, with existing credentials and no silent CSV/Yahoo/TradingView fallback.

Snapshot each market’s available symbols, optionally narrowed by explicit tickers; current membership/delistings and corporate-action adjustments are unverified. PH keys use `.PS` through `core.market.ph_history_symbol`. Use `core.market.get_market` for separate USD/PHP reporting, New York/Manila session calendars and PH long-only eligibility. Report unsupported short branches explicitly; do not invent a long mirror. Freeze costs and use tick/lot helpers with the historical `as_of` date where relevant.

Validate start ≤ end; filter inclusively by market-session `date`/`bar_date`, retaining `ts` identity. The facade offers exclusive `after_ts` and newest-N `limit`, with no end-date bound. Fetch enough pre-start history (or all history), then filter locally; newest-N can omit an old interval entirely and bulk’s 2,000-bar cap is not historical pagination. Pre-start bars only warm features/state. Sort/validate completed, finite OHLCV and conflicting/duplicate sessions; preserve missing sessions and zero/missing-volume status. Higher-frame context must use completed calendar periods.

`None` from `load_daily_bars` means failure; `[]` means no bars. Preserve this distinction before candle/frame conversion and report insufficient warm-up separately. Symbol enumeration currently collapses remote errors to `[]`: propose an explicit failure status before treating an empty universe as success. Bulk helpers can return partial maps after chunk failure; reconcile every requested symbol, retry missing keys and bound concurrency/cancellation. Surface auth/transport/503 errors without exposing credentials. No history ingestion or repair is part of an experiment run.

## Results and validation

Freeze interpretation, parameters and execution before testing. Expose only completed decision bars and prior data to the adapter; close-generated signals fill no earlier than the next tradable open. Limit/stop orders become eligible only after their conditions are known. Preserve pivot confirmation, external publication and higher-frame availability times. Test prefix invariance by changing/removing future bars and requiring unchanged earlier features, signals and orders. Use raw market prices for fills, keeping synthetic Heikin-Ashi/regression prices as features.

For fully specified trades, report candidate/accepted/rejected/expired/unfilled counts, trade and signal/fill timestamps, rule/level evidence, fees/slippage, net expectancy/R where defined, win rate, profit factor, realized/unrealized P&L, marked-to-market equity, exposure, turnover and drawdown by market. Compare a frozen baseline with identical dates/universe/costs; label independent-notional versus finite-capital accounting. Without entry/exit rules, report event coverage and predeclared forward-return/MAE/MFE horizons or forecast calibration, leaving trading P&L unavailable. Outcome windows never enter features and are censored at end_date with incomplete horizons reported.

Use fixtures alongside [core/test_stream_backtest.py](../../core/test_stream_backtest.py), [core/test_rule_backtest.py](../../core/test_rule_backtest.py), [core/test_backtest_service.py](../../core/test_backtest_service.py) and [web/test_paper_api.py](../../web/test_paper_api.py): source positives/near-misses, date boundaries, warm-up without orders, missing/invalid data, owner/remote parity, `.PS` and market isolation, enumeration/auth/partial-bulk failures, progress/cancel/retry and valid no-signal runs. Declare gap-through-stop and conservative same-bar stop/target ordering; daily OHLC cannot reveal intrabar order. Freeze end-date treatment (mark open positions or labeled liquidation), with last-bar orders unfilled if no later eligible bar exists. Use untouched later holdouts and retain all trials, failures and costs.

## Gaps and assumptions

### Writeup: Missing rules and evidence limits

No equality tolerance, required separation, timeframe, volume rule, buffer or measured performance is supplied. More peaks/troughs do not automatically imply a more reliable trade. The bullish promotional caption is broader than the sheet, which includes bearish patterns too.

**Practical next step:** Agree one causal annotation/event definition and audit it against hand-labeled examples with future bars hidden. Only then attach a separately specified entry/exit baseline and test whether the condition adds value.

**Proposed assumptions, not source facts:** the experiment catalog/API paths, adapters, daily-stock adaptation, warm-up/seed conventions where unspecified, next-open execution convention, costs/slippage, sizing, finite-account policy, same-bar ordering and end-date handling are design proposals. Keep source-established values and unresolved alternatives in separate manifest fields. Claims of institutional activity, guaranteed moves, AI confidence or advertised profitability require independent evidence; OHLCV labels alone cannot establish them.

# Bearish symmetrical-triangle break, retest, and Stochastic RSI context

Source: [Rahul Singh](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1A4vTWxsL2/). Downloaded duration: 6.899 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Rahul Singh’s static chart begins in a downtrend, forms a symmetrical triangle, breaks lower, retests a horizontal/diagonal confluence and continues down. A Stochastic RSI pane is labeled as bearish pressure context.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Establish the prior downtrend and converging triangle boundaries.
2. Require the illustrated downside break.
3. Wait for the return to the broken boundary/old horizontal support region.
4. Check the pictured bearish oscillator state, but define its exact cross/threshold independently.
5. The retest inset specifically labels Bearish Engulfing. Define that candle geometry and its completed-bar timing before using it for the short; set invalidation, target and size separately.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

No Stochastic RSI inputs, thresholds, timeframe, instrument, breakout-close rule, buffer or result sample is supplied. Symmetrical triangles can break upward; prior direction and the eventual selected chart do not guarantee continuation.


## Local evidence and reproducibility

All original samples show Symmetrical Triangle, breakout/retest/confluence and the lower Stoch.RSI pane.

Reviewed using: manual inspection of original sampled frames, recognized chart text and saved caption; music is not treated as instruction.

Machine transcripts may misrecognize names, numbers, and music. Settings and claims that could not be established are identified above. Any implementation examples added in this writeup are research choices, not extra rules attributed to the video.

# Three returns to demand: balanced, corrective, and a failed-zone reversal

Source: [The AI Trade Matrix](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1SiJo62gcv/). Downloaded duration: 5.04 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The AI Trade Matrix contrasts a simple return, a multi-wave correction and a liquidity-sweep/zone-failure path. The first two are shown as bullish demand reactions; the third breaks demand and is labeled Sell(Break).

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Mark the bullish BOS and demand origin before the return.
2. Balanced-return branch: observe the direct retracement and defined bullish reaction.
3. Corrective branch: track the A/B/C-style waves and internal CHoCH/BOS before the bullish response.
4. Reversal branch: observe the upper liquidity sweep, later lower structural failure and actual break of demand; do not keep buying solely because the old zone existed.
5. Define confirmation, invalidation, target and size separately for each branch.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

Balanced/corrective are qualitative, and wave boundaries, pivot delay, timeframe, close requirement, buffer and execution are not supplied. The green checks/red cross summarize selected paths, not calibrated likelihoods. A demand-zone break can also reclaim, so the bearish branch needs an explicit rule.


## Local evidence and reproducibility

All original samples show Different Returns to the Demand Zone and the three labeled paths; the full caption describes the distinction.

Reviewed using: manual inspection of original sampled frames, recognized chart text and saved caption; music is not treated as instruction.

[Downloaded video](video.mp4) · [Page description](video.description) · [Timestamped machine transcript](transcript.txt) · [Sampled frames](frames/contact-sheet.jpg) · [Metadata](video.info.json) · [Integrity record](source.json)

Machine transcripts may misrecognize names, numbers, and music. Settings and claims that could not be established are identified above. Any implementation examples added in this writeup are research choices, not extra rules attributed to the video.

# Integration plan: Three returns to demand: balanced, corrective, and a failed-zone reversal

Source: [writeup.md](writeup.md). Planning only: this document proposes future integrations and does not implement a tab, strategy or engine. Source snapshot SHA-256: `bb6fed378fe6e2cb744ed05c4196b9124e6b22e2d360172fd84cdbc3550e05ce`.

## Experiment overview

The AI Trade Matrix contrasts a simple return, a multi-wave correction and a liquidity-sweep/zone-failure path. The first two are shown as bullish demand reactions; the third breaks demand and is labeled Sell(Break).

**Proposed evaluation scope:** Evaluate the particular setup or indicator sequence described here on a frozen historical universe. First produce causal features and candidate events; promote it to a trade simulation only after the unresolved entry, invalidation, exit and sizing decisions below have an explicit versioned specification. A daily-equity adaptation must be labeled when the source uses another interval or product.

## Rules and inputs

**Evidence boundary:** The source interpretation below retains the writeup’s own wording, including its qualifications, corrections and explicitly added research examples. A numbered procedure can contain a proposed operational choice; it is not automatically a rule attributed to the video. No unstated timeframe, conventional default, mirrored trade or numerical stop/target becomes source-backed through inclusion here.

### Writeup: How to use or reproduce it

1. Mark the bullish BOS and demand origin before the return.
2. Balanced-return branch: observe the direct retracement and defined bullish reaction.
3. Corrective branch: track the A/B/C-style waves and internal CHoCH/BOS before the bullish response.
4. Reversal branch: observe the upper liquidity sweep, later lower structural failure and actual break of demand; do not keep buying solely because the old zone existed.
5. Define confirmation, invalidation, target and size separately for each branch.

**Experiment input contract (proposed):** timestamped open, high, low, close and volume, market/session identity, versioned source interpretation and all declared parameters. Additional datasets and source-specific dependencies below are mandatory only for the branch that needs them. A signal-only study can proceed once its event definition is complete; trade P&L additionally requires explicit entry/fill, invalidation, exit and sizing policies.

## Proposed integration

**Zones and gaps:** Propose a stateful zone/gap adapter with origin, first-known, active, touched, invalidated and expired timestamps. [patterns/011_breakout_retest.py](../../patterns/011_breakout_retest.py) offers a price-break/retest reference but does not implement a universal order-block/FVG specification. Freeze the writeup’s wick/body boundaries and trigger sequence before reuse.

The future Experiments page would extend [web/app.py](../../web/app.py) and [web/templates/base.html](../../web/templates/base.html), using Paper’s [template](../../web/templates/paper.html) and `initPaper` in [web/static/app.js](../../web/static/app.js) for US/PH controls, status, tables and chart inspection. Add experiment selection, start/end dates, parameters, requirements, Start/Cancel and saved results. Use [web/static/backtest_runs.js](../../web/static/backtest_runs.js), [web/runs.py](../../web/runs.py) and [core/backtest_jobs.py](../../core/backtest_jobs.py) as lifecycle references: background execution, run IDs, polling/reconnect, loading/warm-up/session progress, cancellation, errors, interrupted runs and explicit retry.

Propose a versioned catalog and typed contracts in `core/experiments/`, source-specific adapters and `web/experiments.py` (new components, not existing APIs). Register this directory’s source ID/digest; requests freeze market, inclusive dates, parameters, universe/data hashes and execution policy. A proposed `/api/experiments/catalog` and `/api/experiments/runs[/{id}]` flow would validate requirements → load → warm up → replay → persist/poll results, with a run-specific cancel action. Missing specifications/data should produce explicit preflight blockers.

[core/backtest_service.py](../../core/backtest_service.py) offers frozen-input/artifact contracts but is currently coupled to pinned pattern versions; extend or wrap its lifecycle rather than assume an arbitrary-strategy plug-in API. [core/stream_backtest.py](../../core/stream_backtest.py) demonstrates a growing causal store, pending next-open fills, warm-up without orders and explicit end policy; [core/rule_backtest.py](../../core/rule_backtest.py) is a simpler rule-replay reference. Audit their detector, sizing and exit contracts before reuse. Keep experiment state separate from live Paper books and the immutable pattern registry. Paper’s DII/Kronos/Laya gates and loss/trailing/exposure policies apply only when explicitly selected as experimental assumptions. Durable run storage and history-owner routing are separate deployment concerns.

## Data handling

Determine warm-up from the longest declared indicator, reference range and formation window, plus prior-value comparisons and pivot confirmation delays. Retain pre-start zone/anchor state when required. If the source leaves these windows open, finalize them before declaring a minimum; insufficient history produces a per-symbol not-ready reason, not fabricated values.

Retain the zone-formation/impulse history before the chosen date range. A three-candle gap becomes known only after its third candle; a block validated by later displacement becomes available only after that validation. Missing formation history makes it unavailable.

Use [docs/daily-bars-api.md](../../docs/daily-bars-api.md) and [data/history.py](../../data/history.py): snapshot `list_history_symbols(market=...)`, then `load_daily_bars(symbol, market=...)`. When `STOCKS_HISTORY_URL` is empty and the process owns history (`STOCKS_HISTORY_OWNER` or existing deployment/host detection), `local_history_backfill_enabled()` selects local PostgreSQL `stocks_history` through `data/db.py`. Otherwise the existing authenticated `data/history_client.py` uses the history HTTP API; `enable_ui_web_history()` supplies the remote default for a non-owner web process. Preserve that routing in workers, with existing credentials and no silent CSV/Yahoo/TradingView fallback.

Snapshot each market’s available symbols, optionally narrowed by explicit tickers; current membership/delistings and corporate-action adjustments are unverified. PH keys use `.PS` through `core.market.ph_history_symbol`. Use `core.market.get_market` for separate USD/PHP reporting, New York/Manila session calendars and PH long-only eligibility. Report unsupported short branches explicitly; do not invent a long mirror. Freeze costs and use tick/lot helpers with the historical `as_of` date where relevant.

Validate start ≤ end; filter inclusively by market-session `date`/`bar_date`, retaining `ts` identity. The facade offers exclusive `after_ts` and newest-N `limit`, with no end-date bound. Fetch enough pre-start history (or all history), then filter locally; newest-N can omit an old interval entirely and bulk’s 2,000-bar cap is not historical pagination. Pre-start bars only warm features/state. Sort/validate completed, finite OHLCV and conflicting/duplicate sessions; preserve missing sessions and zero/missing-volume status. Higher-frame context must use completed calendar periods.

`None` from `load_daily_bars` means failure; `[]` means no bars. Preserve this distinction before candle/frame conversion and report insufficient warm-up separately. Symbol enumeration currently collapses remote errors to `[]`: propose an explicit failure status before treating an empty universe as success. Bulk helpers can return partial maps after chunk failure; reconcile every requested symbol, retry missing keys and bound concurrency/cancellation. Surface auth/transport/503 errors without exposing credentials. No history ingestion or repair is part of an experiment run.

## Results and validation

**Zones and gaps evidence:** Export original zone bounds, formation/availability, every return and invalidation. Test early touches before zone availability, overlapping zones, no-return moves and failed retests. Do not treat institutional-order narratives as OHLCV-observed facts.

Freeze interpretation, parameters and execution before testing. Expose only completed decision bars and prior data to the adapter; close-generated signals fill no earlier than the next tradable open. Limit/stop orders become eligible only after their conditions are known. Preserve pivot confirmation, external publication and higher-frame availability times. Test prefix invariance by changing/removing future bars and requiring unchanged earlier features, signals and orders. Use raw market prices for fills, keeping synthetic Heikin-Ashi/regression prices as features.

For fully specified trades, report candidate/accepted/rejected/expired/unfilled counts, trade and signal/fill timestamps, rule/level evidence, fees/slippage, net expectancy/R where defined, win rate, profit factor, realized/unrealized P&L, marked-to-market equity, exposure, turnover and drawdown by market. Compare a frozen baseline with identical dates/universe/costs; label independent-notional versus finite-capital accounting. Without entry/exit rules, report event coverage and predeclared forward-return/MAE/MFE horizons or forecast calibration, leaving trading P&L unavailable. Outcome windows never enter features and are censored at end_date with incomplete horizons reported.

Use fixtures alongside [core/test_stream_backtest.py](../../core/test_stream_backtest.py), [core/test_rule_backtest.py](../../core/test_rule_backtest.py), [core/test_backtest_service.py](../../core/test_backtest_service.py) and [web/test_paper_api.py](../../web/test_paper_api.py): source positives/near-misses, date boundaries, warm-up without orders, missing/invalid data, owner/remote parity, `.PS` and market isolation, enumeration/auth/partial-bulk failures, progress/cancel/retry and valid no-signal runs. Declare gap-through-stop and conservative same-bar stop/target ordering; daily OHLC cannot reveal intrabar order. Freeze end-date treatment (mark open positions or labeled liquidation), with last-bar orders unfilled if no later eligible bar exists. Use untouched later holdouts and retain all trials, failures and costs.

## Gaps and assumptions

### Writeup: Missing rules and evidence limits

Balanced/corrective are qualitative, and wave boundaries, pivot delay, timeframe, close requirement, buffer and execution are not supplied. The green checks/red cross summarize selected paths, not calibrated likelihoods. A demand-zone break can also reclaim, so the bearish branch needs an explicit rule.

**Practical next step:** Write and approve a small explicit research specification resolving the source gaps above, then validate numeric/event fixtures and a short causal replay before a full historical run. Missing rules should block the faithful trading mode; a labeled feature/event study may be the practical first milestone.

**Proposed assumptions, not source facts:** the experiment catalog/API paths, adapters, daily-stock adaptation, warm-up/seed conventions where unspecified, next-open execution convention, costs/slippage, sizing, finite-account policy, same-bar ordering and end-date handling are design proposals. Keep source-established values and unresolved alternatives in separate manifest fields. Claims of institutional activity, guaranteed moves, AI confidence or advertised profitability require independent evidence; OHLCV labels alone cannot establish them.

# Twelve bullish and bearish schematic examples, with naming caveats

Source: [Tradinguniverscity](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1PXq9pDBwE/). Downloaded duration: 15.0 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Tradinguniverscity shows a Koinly-branded reference with six bullish and six bearish examples: flag, wedge, triangle, pennant, cup/handle and head-and-shoulders variants. It includes entry/target arrows but no complete trade model.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Bullish row families: a pictured converging pause labeled Flag, falling wedge, ascending triangle, pennant, cup/handle and an inverse reversal formation.
2. Bearish families: flag, rising wedge, descending triangle, pennant, inverse cup/handle and head-and-shoulders.
3. Judge geometry as well as the label: the bullish Flag and Pennant pictures are very similar, and the inverse-reversal label is garbled.
4. Require an actual boundary break/confirmation before treating the arrow as eligible.
5. Set risk and exits independently.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

No timeframe, instrument, exact pattern tolerance, entry timing, stop, size or validation is supplied. The sheet’s naming inconsistencies should not be converted into precise detector rules. It is a recognition aid, not twelve proven systems.

The original full-size reference was inspected to distinguish all twelve cells and the ambiguous labels.

1. Preserve the archival date and source feed; the narration’s now/today refers to that historical scene.
2. Mark the broken rising trendline and overhead 4400 region as the author’s resistance.

# Overhead kettlebell-lunge descending ladder with a 20-minute cap

Source: [Dan Ford](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/14uRsrBoWRh/). Downloaded duration: 12.3 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This URL is a fitness workout, not trading content. Dan Ford prescribes left and right overhead-lunge blocks in a 21–18–15–12–9–6–3 descending ladder, for time with a 20-minute cap. The demonstration uses one kettlebell held overhead while lunging.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Understand the load-free lunge first: take a controlled split stance, lower by bending hips/knees, keep the front foot planted and knee tracking with its foot, then return under control.
2. For the demonstrated overhead version, establish a stable overhead arm position before the lunge, keeping the trunk controlled rather than compensating with a large back arch.
3. Perform the left-side block then the right-side block at the chosen rung, following the source’s side order. The caption does not fully resolve whether left/right names the carrying arm or working-leg convention; use the actual demonstration consistently.
4. Complete 21 each side, then 18,15,12,9,6,3, with the stated 20-minute limit.
5. One complete ladder totals 84 repetitions per side,168 combined if every rung is completed on both sides.

# Bullish breaker-block retest after a downside sweep and structural recovery

Source: [Forex Insights](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1Drw5S71Ci/). Downloaded duration: 5.04 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The static Forex Insights poster illustrates a bullish reversal following a clean bearish move. Price reaches a sideways range, breaks beneath support into the area labeled Bullish Liquidity, then recovers and breaks the former resistance. CHoCH and BOS labels describe that recovery. A later pullback reaches the green Break Block band, where a blue circle marks entry; a red stop-loss area sits underneath and a green target sits above. FVG annotations appear in both the earlier decline and the later rise. The illustration is dated October 26, 2023.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Reconstruct the original support/resistance range before the sweep, keeping the sweep low separate from the later breaker band.
2. Follow the recovery through the labeled CHoCH and subsequent bullish breaks rather than buying solely because price traded below support.
3. Mark the former resistance/breaker region and inspect the later return into it.
4. Treat the blue circle, red invalidation area and upper objective as the depicted trade geometry. An actual candle trigger, order type and precise prices still require definitions.
5. Keep the FVGs as contextual annotations unless a separate gap requirement is explicitly adopted.

# Selecting an order-block retest with fixed-range volume profile

Source: [Rohit Prasad](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1CocU39nzV/). Downloaded duration: 99.705 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Rohit Prasad explains in Hindi how to choose among several fair-value gaps and an order block created during an upward impulse. He selects fixed-range volume profile and draws it from the swing low to the swing high. The small horizontal bars beside the FVGs are rejected as low-volume areas; the larger bars near the order block make that lower zone his preferred return location. 4. Wait for price to return; distinguish the halfway-zone rejection from the deeper-sweep branch.

# Late bull-flag breakout entries versus waiting for a lower demand reaction

Source: [Trade Vision](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1C6oJ4koaC/). Downloaded duration: 5.04 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Trade Vision compares three pairs of bullish continuation drawings under Bad Setup vs Good Setup. The left versions buy higher, around a descending flag’s breakout, and list unattractive risk to reward, chasing price, retail pattern and late entry. The right versions extend the pullback into a lower horizontal demand area, sometimes below the flag’s lower boundary, before the rebound. Their bullets emphasize attractive risk to reward, confluences, demand and good timing. The same broad idea is repeated across different final candle paths.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Mark the preceding bullish impulse and its demand/origin area before drawing the corrective flag.
2. Compare the higher breakout entry with the lower demand-retest location using an identical invalidation and target convention.
3. Under the preferred illustrated branch, wait for the deeper pullback and reaction instead of assuming the first diagonal breakout is the entry.
4. Record cases that rally immediately without returning, as well as demand zones that fail. A cheaper entry may never become available.
5. Specify what constitutes the reaction or confirmation; the caption’s liquidity-sweep language does not turn every touch into an order.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

The drawings do not provide an instrument, timeframe, numerical ratio, stop buffer, demand-zone construction or precise candle trigger. A green profit rectangle compares geometry, not the probability of reaching that profit. The sheet does not demonstrate that breakout strategies are universally bad, nor that lower entries outperform after missed trades and failed demand are included. Institutional intent is not observable from these stylized candles.


## Local evidence and reproducibility

0.00–4.88 s: original three-row comparison; inspected demand zones, deeper pullbacks, trade rectangles and all left/right bullet labels; caption adds the sweep/demand preference.

# Choosing chart timeframes by intended holding style

Source: [TRADING CHART](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1A8hCeQhzv/). Downloaded duration: 23.451 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The narrator links chart interval to the kind of trading being attempted. For swing trading he recommends medium intervals from one hour through one day. For day trading he lists one minute, fifteen minutes and thirty minutes, then advises looking at monthly charts for the bigger picture. This is an organizational suggestion for analysis rather than a setup. The montage’s broader message is to choose a useful level of detail instead of treating the fastest chart as automatically superior.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. State the intended holding period and available monitoring time.
2. If studying the source’s swing branch, begin with hourly through daily charts; if studying its intraday branch, examine the listed 1 m/15 m/30 m intervals. These are the author’s examples, not mandatory market rules.
3. Review a monthly chart separately for long-range context and record how that context is allowed to influence an intraday decision.
4. Keep one execution interval fixed during a comparison so that changing timeframes after an adverse move does not disguise a failed rule.
5. Select an actual strategy and risk policy independently; interval selection alone supplies no entry or exit.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

There is no instrument-specific rationale, session definition, lookback, trigger, stop, target or evidence that these are the best intervals. The short visual montage includes a five-minute example, whereas the spoken day-trading list names 1 m/15 m/30 m. Neither list establishes a complete hierarchy or makes every chart in it appropriate for every trader. Monthly context is not itself a directional forecast.

# Integration plan: Choosing chart timeframes by intended holding style

Source: [writeup.md](writeup.md). Planning only: this document proposes future integrations and does not implement a tab, strategy or engine. Source snapshot SHA-256: `a5af0ad502c96e2305bd711984021de82de4a2cc4c33f77b0e4e733a988d7bc0`.

## Experiment overview

The narrator links chart interval to the kind of trading being attempted. For swing trading he recommends medium intervals from one hour through one day. For day trading he lists one minute, fifteen minutes and thirty minutes, then advises looking at monthly charts for the bigger picture. This is an organizational suggestion for analysis rather than a setup. The montage’s broader message is to choose a useful level of detail instead of treating the fastest chart as automatically superior.

**Proposed evaluation scope:** Use this initially as a research-process or comparison protocol. A planning workflow, preference or motivational claim is not itself an OHLCV strategy. A run can evaluate a separately specified baseline only after its signals and risk rules are frozen; no psychological or product claim should become a price signal.

## Rules and inputs

**Evidence boundary:** The source interpretation below retains the writeup’s own wording, including its qualifications, corrections and explicitly added research examples. A numbered procedure can contain a proposed operational choice; it is not automatically a rule attributed to the video. No unstated timeframe, conventional default, mirrored trade or numerical stop/target becomes source-backed through inclusion here.

### Writeup: How to use or reproduce it

1. State the intended holding period and available monitoring time.
2. If studying the source’s swing branch, begin with hourly through daily charts; if studying its intraday branch, examine the listed 1 m/15 m/30 m intervals. These are the author’s examples, not mandatory market rules.
3. Review a monthly chart separately for long-range context and record how that context is allowed to influence an intraday decision.
4. Keep one execution interval fixed during a comparison so that changing timeframes after an adverse move does not disguise a failed rule.
5. Select an actual strategy and risk policy independently; interval selection alone supplies no entry or exit.

**Experiment input contract (proposed):** timestamped open, high, low, close and volume, market/session identity, versioned source interpretation and all declared parameters. Additional datasets and source-specific dependencies below are mandatory only for the branch that needs them. A signal-only study can proceed once its event definition is complete; trade P&L additionally requires explicit entry/fill, invalidation, exit and sizing policies.

## Proposed integration

Create a source-specific adapter for the sequence in the Rules and inputs section, preserving the order in which each illustrated reference and confirmation becomes known. Store candidate, armed, confirmed, expired and invalidated events separately. [patterns/base_pattern.py](../../patterns/base_pattern.py) supplies signal/annotation structures, while [indicators/_signal.py](../../indicators/_signal.py) demonstrates latest-bar output; neither supplies the missing source rules. A recap or undisclosed indicator stays blocked until its actual generator and execution specification are available.

The future Experiments page would extend [web/app.py](../../web/app.py) and [web/templates/base.html](../../web/templates/base.html), using Paper’s [template](../../web/templates/paper.html) and `initPaper` in [web/static/app.js](../../web/static/app.js) for US/PH controls, status, tables and chart inspection. Add experiment selection, start/end dates, parameters, requirements, Start/Cancel and saved results. Use [web/static/backtest_runs.js](../../web/static/backtest_runs.js), [web/runs.py](../../web/runs.py) and [core/backtest_jobs.py](../../core/backtest_jobs.py) as lifecycle references: background execution, run IDs, polling/reconnect, loading/warm-up/session progress, cancellation, errors, interrupted runs and explicit retry.

Propose a versioned catalog and typed contracts in `core/experiments/`, source-specific adapters and `web/experiments.py` (new components, not existing APIs). Register this directory’s source ID/digest; requests freeze market, inclusive dates, parameters, universe/data hashes and execution policy. A proposed `/api/experiments/catalog` and `/api/experiments/runs[/{id}]` flow would validate requirements → load → warm up → replay → persist/poll results, with a run-specific cancel action. Missing specifications/data should produce explicit preflight blockers.

[core/stream_backtest.py](../../core/stream_backtest.py) demonstrates a growing causal store, pending next-open fills, warm-up without orders and explicit end policy; [core/rule_backtest.py](../../core/rule_backtest.py) is a simpler rule-replay reference. ## Data handling

**Source interval constraint:** This writeup includes intraday/tick or hourly branches. Select any source-supported daily branch explicitly; the following constraint applies to the finer-interval branches. Daily OHLCV cannot reconstruct its internal ordering, session windows or lower-frame confirmation. The owner has local hourly loaders but the history API has no hourly route, and hourly bars cannot recover one-/five-/fifteen-minute or tick data. A faithful branch remains blocked until a suitable historical source and remote access contract exist. Any added daily-bar equity adaptation needs a separate identity and explicit changed rules; do not present it as the original experiment.

Determine warm-up from the longest declared indicator, reference range and formation window, plus prior-value comparisons and pivot confirmation delays. Retain pre-start zone/anchor state when required. If the source leaves these windows open, finalize them before declaring a minimum; insufficient history produces a per-symbol not-ready reason, not fabricated values.

Use [docs/daily-bars-api.md](../../docs/daily-bars-api.md) and [data/history.py](../../data/history.py): snapshot `list_history_symbols(market=...)`, then `load_daily_bars(symbol, market=...)`. When `STOCKS_HISTORY_URL` is empty and the process owns history (`STOCKS_HISTORY_OWNER` or existing deployment/host detection), `local_history_backfill_enabled()` selects local PostgreSQL `stocks_history` through `data/db.py`. Otherwise the existing authenticated `data/history_client.py` uses the history HTTP API; `enable_ui_web_history()` supplies the remote default for a non-owner web process. Preserve that routing in workers, with existing credentials and no silent CSV/Yahoo/TradingView fallback.

Snapshot each market’s available symbols, optionally narrowed by explicit tickers; current membership/delistings and corporate-action adjustments are unverified. PH keys use `.PS` through `core.market.ph_history_symbol`. Use `core.market.get_market` for separate USD/PHP reporting, New York/Manila session calendars and PH long-only eligibility. Report unsupported short branches explicitly; do not invent a long mirror. Freeze costs and use tick/lot helpers with the historical `as_of` date where relevant.

Validate start ≤ end; filter inclusively by market-session `date`/`bar_date`, retaining `ts` identity. The facade offers exclusive `after_ts` and newest-N `limit`, with no end-date bound. Fetch enough pre-start history (or all history), then filter locally; newest-N can omit an old interval entirely and bulk’s 2,000-bar cap is not historical pagination. Pre-start bars only warm features/state. Sort/validate completed, finite OHLCV and conflicting/duplicate sessions; preserve missing sessions and zero/missing-volume status. Higher-frame context must use completed calendar periods.

`None` from `load_daily_bars` means failure; `[]` means no bars. Preserve this distinction before candle/frame conversion and report insufficient warm-up separately. Symbol enumeration currently collapses remote errors to `[]`: propose an explicit failure status before treating an empty universe as success. Bulk helpers can return partial maps after chunk failure; reconcile every requested symbol, retry missing keys and bound concurrency/cancellation. Surface auth/transport/503 errors without exposing credentials. No history ingestion or repair is part of an experiment run.

## Results and validation

For the initial incomplete-specification state, report the missing dependencies and any captured configuration/signal evidence; trading metrics remain unavailable. Product slogans, floating P&L, dashboards and selected chart rectangles are not validated performance.

Freeze interpretation, parameters and execution before testing. Expose only completed decision bars and prior data to the adapter; close-generated signals fill no earlier than the next tradable open. Limit/stop orders become eligible only after their conditions are known. Preserve pivot confirmation, external publication and higher-frame availability times. Test prefix invariance by changing/removing future bars and requiring unchanged earlier features, signals and orders. Use raw market prices for fills, keeping synthetic Heikin-Ashi/regression prices as features.

For fully specified trades, report candidate/accepted/rejected/expired/unfilled counts, trade and signal/fill timestamps, rule/level evidence, fees/slippage, net expectancy/R where defined, win rate, profit factor, realized/unrealized P&L, marked-to-market equity, exposure, turnover and drawdown by market. Compare a frozen baseline with identical dates/universe/costs; label independent-notional versus finite-capital accounting. Without entry/exit rules, report event coverage and predeclared forward-return/MAE/MFE horizons or forecast calibration, leaving trading P&L unavailable. Outcome windows never enter features and are censored at end_date with incomplete horizons reported.

Use fixtures alongside [core/test_stream_backtest.py](../../core/test_stream_backtest.py), [core/test_rule_backtest.py](../../core/test_rule_backtest.py), [core/test_backtest_service.py](../../core/test_backtest_service.py) and [web/test_paper_api.py](../../web/test_paper_api.py): source positives/near-misses, date boundaries, warm-up without orders, missing/invalid data, owner/remote parity, `.PS` and market isolation, enumeration/auth/partial-bulk failures, progress/cancel/retry and valid no-signal runs. Declare gap-through-stop and conservative same-bar stop/target ordering; daily OHLC cannot reveal intrabar order. Freeze end-date treatment (mark open positions or labeled liquidation), with last-bar orders unfilled if no later eligible bar exists. Use untouched later holdouts and retain all trials, failures and costs.

## Gaps and assumptions

### Writeup: Missing rules and evidence limits

There is no instrument-specific rationale, session definition, lookback, trigger, stop, target or evidence that these are the best intervals. The short visual montage includes a five-minute example, whereas the spoken day-trading list names 1 m/15 m/30 m. Neither list establishes a complete hierarchy or makes every chart in it appropriate for every trader. Monthly context is not itself a directional forecast.

**Practical next step:** Choose a separately documented baseline strategy and measurable protocol before using daily data. Preserve this writeup as process context. Do not infer a profitable entry, psychological outcome or automated deployment permission from the lesson.

**Proposed assumptions, not source facts:** the experiment catalog/API paths, adapters, daily-stock adaptation, warm-up/seed conventions where unspecified, next-open execution convention, costs/slippage, sizing, finite-account policy, same-bar ordering and end-date handling are design proposals. Keep source-established values and unresolved alternatives in separate manifest fields. Claims of institutional activity, guaranteed moves, AI confidence or advertised profitability require independent evidence; OHLCV labels alone cannot establish them.

# Long reversal from horizontal support after a local descending-line break

Source: [Tristan Ford](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/154wpJUdFqW/). Downloaded duration: 30.348 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Tristan Ford’s animation introduces bullish/bearish impulse and corrective waves, then develops a declining channel toward a lower horizontal support zone. Near that zone the final correction compresses under a smaller descending line. The illustrated trade is a long after price turns upward out of this local structure. A red stop-loss area sits around/below the lower support and a tall green target reaches the earlier upper reaction area. Despite the long preceding decline, the final rectangle is a bullish reversal example, not a short continuation.

1. Separate the broad declining channel from the smaller corrective line close to support.
2. Mark the lower horizontal zone from prior price structure before the final reversal.
3. Follow the local upward break near that zone; the animation does not justify buying every touch during the decline.
4. Reproduce the pictured trade geometry with invalidation around the lower support and the upper reaction zone as the objective.
5. Decide whether a completed break, a retest or a particular candle confirms entry. The drawing does not state a precise order rule.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

Trendline anchors, support width, timeframe, instrument, penetration tolerance and buffer are missing. The oversized green rectangle is visual rather than a disclosed numerical reward ratio. # Four proposed replacements for familiar chart-analysis tools

Source: [Ahmed On Chart](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1FAYWgsaDP/). Downloaded duration: 17.877 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Ahmed On Chart argues for replacing a conventional volume indicator with volume profile, moving averages with anchored VWAP, trendlines with market structure, and RSI/MACD with order flow and cumulative volume delta. The format is an emphatic four-item preference list followed by a course invitation. It does not show a trade with all four tools, establish their settings or compare their performance. Volume profile and anchored VWAP are themselves calculated chart tools, so the distinction is about how information is organized rather than eliminating indicators.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Write down the question each proposed replacement is meant to answer: where volume traded, average traded price since an anchor, swing relationships, or signed trading activity.
2. Specify the profile range, VWAP anchor, swing definition and order-flow feed before using any of them.
3. Compare each tool with its proposed replacement on the same market and information available at the time. Their outputs answer different questions and are not numerically interchangeable.
4. Choose an actual entry/exit policy separately. The commands to never use the older tools are opinions, not executable conditions.
5. Record whether access to appropriate volume/order-flow data is available for the chosen instrument.

The video supplies no anchor-selection method, delta classification, indicator lengths, timeframe, market, stop, target, size or test results. # Clean market structure versus a cluttered indicator chart

Source: [Algo Signal AI](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1F6pSHMNsa/). Downloaded duration: 5.04 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

The Algo Signal AI card contrasts a top panel labeled as a new trader’s crowded chart with a lower professional-style chart emphasizing price structure. Its saved caption explains a decline through lower highs and lower lows, a failed attempt to make a new low, a break above a previous lower high and a subsequent correction/retest. The lower chart marks the failed lower low, bullish correction and an entry area. The intended lesson is to recognize a structural transition with fewer overlays.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Identify the existing lower-high/lower-low sequence without using the later rally to choose only convenient pivots.
2. Record the failed lower low and distinguish that early warning from the later upward break of the previous lower high.
3. Wait for the depicted correction/retest after the break if studying the caption’s preferred sequence.
4. Define exactly which level is retested and what reaction permits an entry. The card’s entry label alone does not settle whether a touch, close or secondary break is required.
5. Set invalidation, objective and size independently before testing the simplified chart.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

No swing lookback, equality tolerance, required displacement, timeframe, instrument or risk policy is provided. Removing indicators can improve visual clarity, but the image does not prove that clean charts are profitable or that many indicators cause losses. Nor does the failed low guarantee a trend reversal; price can resume downward. The favorable example is a teaching illustration, not a complete signal record.


## Local evidence and reproducibility

0.00–4.88 s: repeated original New Trader/Pro Trader comparison and lower structural labels; complete caption supplies the failed-LL, prior-LH-break and correction narrative.

Reviewed using: manual review of the complete saved transcript and caption, original sampled frames and legible chart labels; promotional claims are treated as claims rather than performance evidence.

Source: [Ijaz Ahmed Metla](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1A1Yzndfkm/). Downloaded duration: 34.727 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

1. Draw the descending line using information available before the initial break.

# Red-day cash-secured-put checklist with incomplete loss and assignment rules

Source: [Market Moves](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1GDhSdZEwC/). Downloaded duration: 6.166 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Market Moves supplies a ten-step options-selling checklist in the caption: wait until 9:45 AM; use a familiar watchlist; skip all-green days; look for a ticker down at least 3%; require IV above 50%; sell a put around 30 days to expiration; seek 5% of collateral in premium; set an alert to take 50% profit; then stop watching. The short visual presents a no-loss streak claim, but there is no trade ledger. The collateral language resembles cash-secured put selling, although the exact collateral convention and contract are not established.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Preserve the source’s thresholds as a proposed screening experiment, including the assumed US-equity opening time. Do not interpret a red day alone as sufficient compensation for risk.

3. State the cash required and the shares deliverable on assignment for the actual contract.
4. Resolve the exit arithmetic: capturing half a premium initially equal to 5% of collateral realizes about 2.5% of that same collateral before costs, not the full 5%.
5. Specify adverse-move, early-assignment and expiration handling before considering the checklist executable.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

The first 15 minutes being pure noise, green days always paying less and 30 days being universally optimal are unsupported generalizations. No stop/loss limit, concentration limit or assignment plan is supplied. An alert is not an executed closing order. A cash-secured put has capped premium income but potentially large downside if the stock falls; cash collateral does not remove that loss. The [Options Industry Council cash-secured-put reference](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/cash-secured-put) explains the obligation to buy assigned shares and the substantial downside. A historical winning streak cannot establish safety or future returns.

# Bearish double-top neckline break, gap return and support-to-resistance continuation

Source: [Marketpedia](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1M1ZiLqFoG/). Downloaded duration: 21.013 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This silent price-action lesson follows a downtrend under a descending line. A double-top formation appears within that decline, its neckline breaks, and price drops into a gap-like separation below the old support. A later return toward that broken level is presented as a gap fill and support-to-resistance retest, followed by another bearish continuation. The saved caption explains these elements more explicitly than the sparse moving labels: trend context, double top, neckline break, gap fill and retest confirmation.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Establish the lower-high/lower-low context and identify the two local highs before the neckline failure.
2. Mark the neckline from the intervening low and distinguish its break from the diagonal trendline.
3. Record the downward gap/separation and the former support band. The graphic does not establish whether this is a session-opening gap or an ICT three-candle FVG.
4. Observe the return into the old support now illustrated as resistance.
5. Define a bearish confirmation and invalidation above the relevant rejection before using a continuation entry. A lower objective and size must be specified separately.

The combination is a descriptive sequence, not a complete mechanical strategy. No instrument, timeframe, double-top tolerance, minimum separation, gap definition, confirmation candle, stop buffer or target formula is given. # Dr Copper as a macroeconomic warning narrative, with unverified timing claims

Source: [Nicholas Crown](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1E24sGS3Ds/). Downloaded duration: 94.101 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Nicholas Crown argues that copper demand links the metal to construction, electrification, EVs, data centers and the power grid, making its price a possible early growth indicator. He invokes the 2008 commodity peak and financial crisis, then claims copper is again falling sharply ahead of weaker GDP. The lesson is a macroeconomic interpretation of an industrial commodity, not a chart entry system. Statements such as 17% below January and a 6.7% weekly fall refer to the recording’s unidentified observation window; they are not current market readings.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Identify the actual copper benchmark, currency, contract/roll method and observation date before trying to reproduce the quoted returns.
2. Compare the proposed copper signal with dated GDP releases, using the GDP information available at each historical decision time rather than later revisions.
3. Define what counts as a copper decline, the forecast horizon and the economic outcome before testing the claimed lead.
4. Include false alarms and expansions as well as the 2008 example.
5. Separate a macro warning from a trade: the video gives no instrument selection, entry, invalidation, target, exposure or horizon for acting on it.

The claim that copper moves for one reason only omits supply and other price drivers. [CME’s copper supply-and-demand discussion](https://www.cmegroup.com/content/dam/cmegroup/education/files/copper-supply-and-demand-dynamics.pdf) also examines production and US-dollar relationships. The stated 50,000-ton requirement per data center, EV multiplier, government designation and exact historical peaks are not documented in the clip and are retained as claims rather than established inputs. No study supports the universal three-month GDP lead or the assertion that copper never misses. A single retrospective crisis example cannot establish reliable crash prediction, and an economic relationship need not remain stable.

# Subjective indicator rankings: moving averages, Donchian breakouts and volume favored

Source: [Nicholas Crown](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1EtWyrDVy3/). Downloaded duration: 111.253 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Nicholas Crown ranks MACD F, simple moving averages A, Stochastics D, Fibonacci retracement B, RSI C, Bollinger Bands B, Donchian Channels A and volume S. His explicit examples are 50/200-day averages, a 20-session Donchian range and RSI divergence rather than selling solely because RSI is overbought. He treats Bollinger Bands as volatility context requiring another directional signal, and favors simple breakout concepts. These are opinions about tool usefulness, not eight specified trading strategies.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Separate each concrete parameter from its grade: 50/200 days and 20 sessions are stated; most other settings are not.
2. For a Donchian breakout study, define whether the signal compares a completed close with the prior 20-session range and ensure the current bar is not used to create its own impossible breakout threshold. That implementation detail is additional research guidance.
3. For RSI divergence, define both pivot selection and oscillator length before judging examples.
4. Compare tools against the same task and benchmark; a volatility envelope and a directional breakout rule have different jobs.
5. Add entries, exits, risk and costs before comparing strategy returns.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

The cited average 11-day MACD delay in 2022, 34 consecutive overbought crude sessions and 70% algorithmic-trading figure are unsupported by identifiable studies or settings. The assertion that every institution watches the same averages is too broad. Volume is not the only non-price information, and volume alone does not identify insiders or prove conviction. No controlled comparison supports the letter grades or the implication that a favored indicator anticipates moves. Lag is not by itself evidence of poor expectancy; the complete trading rule and objective matter.


## Local evidence and reproducibility

# Combining COT, prime-broker positioning and conditional dealer-gamma estimates

Source: [Nicholas Crown](https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1PahZixFbu/). Downloaded duration: 140.006 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Nicholas Crown introduces three positioning sources: public CFTC Commitments of Traders reports, prime-broker client exposure summaries such as gross/net and sector positioning, and dealer gamma. He says their combination can identify crowded trades and squeeze conditions. His gamma description is conditional: short-gamma hedging can amplify rises and declines, while long-gamma hedging can lean against them. He then overstates these concepts as getting ahead of every move and identifying the actual support/resistance. No composite calculation or executable setup is provided.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Obtain the relevant public COT series, preserving report date, release timestamp, trader category and futures-only versus combined format. Do not treat the observations as live orders.
2. Use only legitimately accessible prime-broker aggregates, documenting their client coverage and reporting period; one broker’s financed books are not the entire market. The mention of leaks is not an acquisition instruction.
3. For gamma, document the options universe, timestamp, dealer-position assumptions and pricing inputs. Estimated gamma exposure is not directly observed dealer inventory.
4. Align all sources to when they were actually available before constructing any crowding or squeeze hypothesis.
5. Define independent price confirmation, invalidation and risk; the clip gives none.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

The archived Friday 3:30 PM claim omits the traditional Tuesday observation date and holiday delays; see the [CFTC release schedule](https://www.cftc.gov/MarketReports/CommitmentsofTraders/ReleaseSchedule/index.htm). On October 27, 2026 the [CFTC announced plans for twice-weekly publication by year-end](https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/9316-26), so a timeless Friday-only rule would also become stale. Dealer counterparties and hedge behavior cannot be inferred from every trade indiscriminately. [Cboe’s gamma-squeeze research](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/education/research_publications/gammasqueezes.pdf) treats amplification as dependent on positioning and hedging conditions, not a guaranteed price magnet. The $20 trillion figure and claimed predictive superiority have no substantiation here. No squeeze probability, threshold, horizon, stop or performance series is supplied.


## Local evidence and reproducibility

0–18 s: positioning premise; 18–49 s: COT; 49–82 s: prime brokerage; 82–118 s: dealer gamma/support claims; 119–140 s: combination and newsletter. # Waiting for confirmation and accepting the middle of a move

Source: [The Disciplined Trader](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1cofk8uvb6/). Downloaded duration: 27.367 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

This discipline clip argues against trying to identify exact market tops and bottoms. The voice says waiting for confirmation means missing the first and last parts of a move but accepting that tradeoff to avoid the damage of being wrong while trying to boast about perfect timing. Archival portrait imagery accompanies subtitles; there is no demonstrated chart setup. The phrase about taking the safe middle expresses a preference for confirmation, not an assurance that any middle entry is safe.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Translate confirmation into an observable rule for an independently chosen strategy, such as a completed structural event. The clip itself does not select that event.

3. When reviewing trades, compare the actual rule-based entry with the earliest theoretically possible entry only as a hindsight benchmark.
4. Record the cost of waiting, including missed moves and worse entry prices, alongside any reduction in premature trades.
5. Judge the policy across a complete sample instead of celebrating isolated perfect tops or bottoms.

No instrument, timeframe, trend definition, confirmation threshold, stop, target, position size or test results are supplied. Waiting can reduce some premature entries but cannot eliminate losses. The portrait and edited narration do not independently verify authorship of the quote, so no historical attribution is asserted here. # Volume-profile context with a bullish structure break and supply-to-support retest

Source: [Trading 101](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1FoxTw6jTx/). Downloaded duration: 15.0 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Trading 101’s How To Spot A Real Reversal Using Volume Profile poster shows a downtrend, a descending line and a left-hand profile. A high-volume area coincides with an earlier supply region. Price breaks the descending line, rallies through that area and later retests it from above before the selected rise continues. The caption emphasizes waiting beyond the first line break: the earlier supply should be reclaimed and hold as support. It attributes the volume area to institutions, an identity claim the chart itself cannot establish.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Fix the profile range before the reversal and mark the high-volume area and earlier supply band.
2. Track the lower highs/lows and the bullish line/structure break.
3. Under the caption’s sequence, wait for price to reclaim the relevant high-volume supply area rather than treating the diagonal break alone as entry.
4. Observe the return from above and whether the band holds as support.
5. Define the retest confirmation, invalidation and next objective independently; the poster’s continued rally is not an order policy.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

A high-volume node and the unique point of control are related concepts but are not interchangeable labels. Profile range, row size, volume feed, supply boundaries, timeframe and numerical entry/stop/target are absent. # Weighted bench core-exercise montage with an unsupported fourteen-day appearance claim

Source: [Train With Dr. Godric](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1A8ZnG2WKi/). Downloaded duration: 27.433 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

## What it does

Train With Dr Godric shows a gym core-workout montage using a bench and weight plates. Early footage includes seated torso rotations with a plate held in front, followed by combinations of leaning back, bringing a knee upward and holding the plate higher. Later footage uses a green plate while reclining and drawing both knees toward the torso, including more fully reclined positions along the bench. The caption prescribes 3 × 30 repetitions of each. The large overlay promises a flat stomach in 14 days; the video contains no before/after evidence establishing that result.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Identify each movement separately from the edits: seated rotation, alternating knee/torso movement and the later two-knee tuck/recline variation. The clip does not supply standardized exercise names.

4. For reproduction, obtain suitable technique and load guidance; the montage does not explain how to choose a plate, progress repetitions or modify the movements.
5. Evaluate exercise performance separately from the appearance claim.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

Rest intervals, weekly frequency, tempo, breathing, load selection and what counts as one bilateral/alternating repetition are missing. There is no reason here to promise a particular abdominal appearance in 14 days. [ACE’s discussion of abdominal-fat claims](https://www.acefitness.org/resources/everyone/blog/6273/3-fat-loss-myths-to-stop-believing-now/) explains that abdominal exercise does not selectively remove abdominal fat. 0–5 s: seated plate rotations; 6–12 s: yellow-plate lean/knee movements; 14–20 s: green-plate recline/two-knee tuck; 22–27 s: more fully reclined variation. Original frames at 2-second intervals inspected, with useful detail frames preserved at 6, 18 and 22 s; saved caption contains 3 × 30.

## What it does

The last two sections discuss buying/selling imbalances, possible exhaustion and retesting the POC with imbalance confirmation. The intended workflow is contextual levels first, order-flow confirmation second, rather than trading every structural level in isolation.

1. Fix the profile’s session/range and row resolution, then mark POC, value-area high and value-area low. The 70% value-area setting is stated; other profile inputs are not.

# Previous-day point-of-control reaction as context for a separate execution model

Source: [Arthur Feyman](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1AyB8o3i9Y/). Downloaded duration: 27.446 seconds. The source is a lesson or demonstration, not independently verified performance evidence.

He describes the profile as something to combine with different execution models, so a touch of the prior-day POC is not presented as a fully explained standalone sell signal. The ending promotes a signal group with a high-win-rate claim.

## How to use or reproduce it

1. Define the previous trading day using the chosen market’s session and timezone before anchoring the profile.
2. Draw fixed-range volume profile across that completed day and identify its highest-volume price row.
3. Extend that POC forward and observe the next approach without extending the original profile to include future candles.
4. Apply a separately defined execution model at the level. The selected example is short, but the source does not make every prior-day POC inherently bearish.
5. Specify the trigger, stop, objective and sizing before evaluating reactions.

## Missing rules and evidence limits

Profile row size, value-area settings, feed, session boundaries and the exact execution model are missing. POC can provide a reference without guaranteeing rejection or attraction. The video does not disclose rules for a clean break through the level, repeated tests or a missed return. The stated roughly 90% gold-signal performance and screenshots are promotional evidence without a complete independent ledger, costs or drawdown. They do not establish the profile method’s accuracy.
